cards.front: Accruals: how to treat VAT on an accrual for a VAT-registered client?
cards.back: Accrue the net cost; VAT is claimed when the invoice arrives
cards.evidence: For a VAT-registered client, accrue the net cost. The VAT is claimed when the invoice arrives, in the VAT return period the invoice falls in.

cards.front: Accruals: how to treat VAT for a client that isn't VAT registered?
cards.back: Accrue the gross amount, as the VAT is a cost
cards.evidence: For a client that isn't VAT registered, the VAT is a cost, so accrue the gross amount.

cards.front: Time apportionment: formula for calculating it?
cards.back: Amount × months (or days) in the relevant period ÷ total months (or days) covered
cards.evidence: How to calculate a time apportionment: Amount × months (or days) falling in the relevant period ÷ total months (or days) covered.

cards.front: Year end adjustments: effect on profit and balance sheet of deferred income?
cards.back: Liability (deferred income); reduces profit
cards.evidence: Adjustment: Deferred income; What it means: Income invoiced or received in the year but not yet earned; Balance sheet: Liability (deferred income); Effect on profit: Reduces profit.

cards.front: Year end adjustments: effect on profit and balance sheet of a prepayment?
cards.back: Asset (prepayments); increases profit
cards.evidence: Adjustment: Prepayment; What it means: Cost paid or invoiced in the year that relates to next year; Balance sheet: Asset (prepayments); Effect on profit: Increases profit.

cards.front: Accruals: how many months after year end should post year-end invoices be checked?
cards.back: At least the first two months
cards.evidence: Check at least the first two months after the year end.

cards.front: Micro-entity limits for years beginning on/after 6 April 2025 (meet 2 of 3)?
cards.back: Turnover ≤£1m; balance sheet total ≤£500,000; ≤10 employees
cards.evidence: Size: Micro-entity; Turnover: Not more than £1m; Balance sheet total (gross assets): Not more than £500,000; Average employees: Not more than 10.

cards.front: Small company limits for years beginning on/after 6 April 2025 (2 of 3)?
cards.back: Turnover ≤£15m; balance sheet total ≤£7.5m; ≤50 employees
cards.evidence: Size: Small; Turnover: Not more than £15m; Balance sheet total (gross assets): Not more than £7.5m; Average employees: Not more than 50.

cards.front: Medium company limits for years beginning on/after 6 April 2025 (2 of 3)?
cards.back: Turnover ≤£54m; balance sheet total ≤£27m; ≤250 employees
cards.evidence: Size: Medium; Turnover: Not more than £54m; Balance sheet total (gross assets): Not more than £27m; Average employees: Not more than 250.

cards.front: Small/micro status: how does the two-year rule work for a change in size?
cards.back: Status changes only after meeting or failing the conditions in two consecutive years
cards.evidence: After that, its status only changes if it meets (or fails) the conditions in two consecutive years.

cards.front: Audit exemption: what member shareholding can force an audit (s476)?
cards.back: Members holding at least 10% of shares
cards.evidence: members holding at least 10% of the shares (by number or value) deposit a written notice requiring an audit, no later than one month before the end of the financial year (s476).

cards.front: Audit exemption: deadline for members' notice requiring an audit (s476)?
cards.back: No later than one month before the end of the financial year
cards.evidence: members holding at least 10% of the shares (by number or value) deposit a written notice requiring an audit, no later than one month before the end of the financial year (s476).

cards.front: FRS 105 micro-entities: how is deferred tax treated?
cards.back: Not recognised
cards.evidence: Deferred tax; FRS 105 (micro-entities): Not recognised; FRS 102 Section 1A (small): Recognised; Full FRS 102: Recognised.

cards.front: Deferred tax: do FRS 105 micro-entities recognise it?
cards.back: No, not recognised
cards.evidence: Framework: FRS 105 (micro-entities); Deferred tax: Not recognised.

cards.front: Deferred tax: do FRS 102 Section 1A small companies recognise it?
cards.back: Yes, same rules as full FRS 102
cards.evidence: Framework: FRS 102 Section 1A (small); Deferred tax: Recognised (same rules as full FRS 102).

cards.front: FRS 102 s29: are permanent differences given deferred tax?
cards.back: No; e.g. client entertaining and fines
cards.evidence: It's not recognised on permanent differences (items never taxable or deductible, e.g. client entertaining, fines).

cards.front: FRS 102 s29: is deferred tax discounted?
cards.back: No
cards.evidence: Deferred tax is not discounted.

cards.front: Deferred tax: when is a tax losses carried forward asset recognised?
cards.back: Only to the extent probable it will be recovered against future taxable profits
cards.evidence: unrelieved tax losses carried forward → an asset, but only to the extent it's probable they'll be recovered against future taxable profits;

cards.front: Deferred tax: which entry each year, closing balance or movement?
cards.back: Post the movement (closing less opening) to the tax charge
cards.evidence: Calculate the closing deferred tax balance, compare it with the opening balance, and post the movement to the tax charge (or to other comprehensive income if the underlying item went there, e.g. a property revaluation in a revaluation reserve).

cards.front: s455 tax: rate for loans made on or after 6 April 2026?
cards.evidence: - 35.75% for loans made on or after 6 April 2026.

cards.front: s455 tax: rate for loans made before 6 April 2026?
cards.evidence: - 33.75% for loans made before 6 April 2026;

cards.front: s455 tax: when is it due?
cards.back: 9 months and 1 day after the period end
cards.evidence: s455 tax is due at the same time as the corporation tax (9 months and 1 day after the period end).

cards.front: s455 tax: when is it repayable to the company?
cards.back: 9 months after the end of the accounting period in which the loan is repaid, released or written off
cards.evidence: It's repayable to the company 9 months after the end of the accounting period in which the loan is repaid, released or written off.

cards.front: Bed and breakfasting: what is the 30-day rule?
cards.back: Repayments of £5,000+ followed within 30 days by new loans of £5,000+ are matched to the new borrowing
cards.evidence: - 30-day rule: if repayments of £5,000 or more are followed within 30 days by new loans of £5,000 or more, the repayment is matched with the new borrowing, not the old loan.

cards.front: Bed and breakfasting: what is the arrangements rule?
cards.back: Balance £15,000+ and arrangements to re-borrow at repayment: the repayment is ignored
cards.evidence: - Arrangements rule: where the balance is £15,000 or more and there were arrangements to re-borrow at the time of repayment, the repayment is ignored.

cards.front: Director's loan: beneficial loan benefit in kind threshold?
cards.back: Loan over £10,000 at any time in the tax year, with interest below the official rate
cards.evidence: - Benefit in kind: if the loan exceeds £10,000 at any time in the tax year and interest below the official rate is charged, the director has a taxable beneficial loan benefit, and the company pays Class 1A NIC.

cards.front: Companies House: late filing penalty for accounts, starting amount?
cards.back: £150, doubling if late two years running
cards.evidence: Late filing penalties start at £150 and double if late two years running.

cards.front: HMRC: when is the CT600 due, and when is corporation tax usually payable?
cards.back: CT600: 12 months after period end; tax: 9 months and 1 day after
cards.evidence: - HMRC: the CT600 is due 12 months after the end of the accounting period, but tax is usually payable 9 months and 1 day after the end of the period (large companies pay by instalments).

cards.front: HMRC CT late filing penalties: when did they double?
cards.back: Returns with a filing date on or after 1 April 2026
cards.evidence: HMRC's CT late filing penalties were doubled for returns with a filing date on or after 1 April 2026.

cards.front: When did the free HMRC/Companies House joint accounts and CT filing service close?
cards.back: 31 March 2026
cards.evidence: HMRC and Companies House's free joint online service for filing accounts and the Company Tax Return closed on 31 March 2026, so every company now needs commercial software (or an agent using it).

cards.front: Small company: what may be omitted from accounts filed at Companies House?
cards.back: Profit and loss account and directors' report (filleted), with a balance sheet statement saying so
cards.evidence: It may omit the profit and loss account and directors' report ("filleted" accounts), with a statement on the balance sheet that it has done so.

cards.front: Companies House: what changes for filleted and abridged accounts from 1 April 2028?
cards.back: Abridged accounts abolished; small and micro companies must file a profit and loss account
cards.evidence: - abridged accounts are abolished;

cards.front: Companies Act: who signs the balance sheet for the board, and which section?
cards.back: A director, with name stated (CA 2006 s414)
cards.evidence: - The board approves the accounts, and the balance sheet is signed on behalf of the board by a director, with the director's name stated (CA 2006 s414).

cards.front: Fixed assets: how is profit or loss on disposal calculated?
cards.back: Proceeds − net book value at disposal
cards.evidence: Profit/(loss) = proceeds − net book value at disposal

cards.front: Fixed assets: typical depreciation policy for freehold buildings?
cards.back: 2% straight line
cards.evidence: Asset class: Freehold buildings; Typical policy: 2% straight line.

cards.front: Fixed assets: typical depreciation policy for motor vehicles?
cards.back: 25% reducing balance
cards.evidence: Asset class: Motor vehicles; Typical policy: 25% reducing balance.

cards.front: Fixed assets: typical depreciation policy for computer equipment?
cards.back: 33⅓% straight line
cards.evidence: Asset class: Computer equipment; Typical policy: 33⅓% straight line.

cards.front: Fixed assets: is freehold land depreciated?
cards.back: No, freehold land is not depreciated
cards.evidence: Asset class: Freehold land; Typical policy: Not depreciated.

cards.front: Capital allowances: main pool WDA rate from April 2026?
cards.evidence: main pool WDA 14% from April 2026

cards.front: Fixed assets: how is straight line depreciation calculated?
cards.back: (Cost − residual value) ÷ useful life, same every year
cards.evidence: | Straight line | (Cost − residual value) ÷ useful life, the same every year | Buildings, fixtures, most equipment |

cards.front: FRS 102 s3: going concern assessment period?
cards.back: At least 12 months from the date the accounts are approved
cards.evidence: In assessing it, the directors look at least 12 months from the date the accounts are approved (not from the year end).

cards.front: FRS 102 s3: when is the going concern basis not used?
cards.back: If management intends to liquidate or cease trading, or has no realistic alternative
cards.evidence: Accounts are prepared on a going concern basis unless management intends to liquidate the company or cease trading, or has no realistic alternative but to do so.

cards.front: Going concern: what if material uncertainties cast significant doubt?
cards.back: They must be disclosed
cards.evidence: If there are material uncertainties that may cast significant doubt on the company's ability to continue, they must be disclosed.

cards.front: Going concern: company is not a going concern - what must be disclosed?
cards.back: The basis actually used; going concern basis must not be used
cards.evidence: If the company isn't a going concern, the going concern basis must not be used, and the basis actually used must be disclosed.

cards.front: Unaudited accounts: can a client describe them as audited?
cards.back: No, never
cards.evidence: Never let a client describe unaudited accounts as audited.

cards.front: FRS 102 Section 20 leases: when must leases be reassessed under the new rules?
cards.back: For periods from 1 January 2026
cards.evidence: - Leases not reassessed under the new FRS 102 Section 20 for periods from 1 January 2026.

cards.front: FRS 102 leases: effective date of the new lessee model?
cards.back: Periods beginning on or after 1 January 2026
cards.evidence: For accounting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2026, the Periodic Review 2024 removes that distinction for lessees: most leases now go on the balance sheet as a right-of-use (ROU) asset and a lease liability, broadly aligned with IFRS 16.

cards.front: FRS 105 micro-entities: effect of the 2026 lease changes?
cards.back: None; micros keep the finance/operating lease distinction
cards.evidence: FRS 105 (micro-entities) is not changed: micros keep the finance / operating lease distinction.

cards.front: FRS 102 leases: short-term lease exemption definition?
cards.back: Lease term of 12 months or less, with no purchase option
cards.evidence: - Short-term leases: a lease term of 12 months or less (with no purchase option).

cards.front: FRS 102 leases: initial measurement of ROU asset?
cards.back: Liability + payments at/before commencement + initial direct costs + restoration costs − incentives
cards.evidence: ROU asset at commencement = the lease liability + payments made at or before commencement + initial direct costs + estimated restoration costs − lease incentives received.

cards.front: FRS 102 leases: how is the ROU asset depreciated?
cards.back: Normally straight line over the shorter of lease term and useful life
cards.evidence: - the ROU asset is depreciated, normally straight line over the shorter of the lease term and useful life.

cards.front: FRS 102 lease transition: are lessee comparatives restated?
cards.back: Generally no; leases brought on balance sheet at date of initial application
cards.evidence: On first applying the amendments, lessees generally don't restate comparatives.

cards.front: Balance sheet size limits that ROU assets could push a company over?
cards.back: £500,000 micro; £7.5m small
cards.evidence: - Size thresholds: bringing ROU assets on balance sheet increases gross assets, which could tip a company over the £500,000 micro or £7.5m small balance sheet limit.

cards.front: FRS 102 s21: three conditions to recognise a provision?
cards.back: Present obligation from past event; outflow probable; amount reliably estimable
cards.evidence: Recognise one only when all three are met:

cards.front: FRS 102: treatment of a possible (not probable) outflow?
cards.back: Disclose a contingent liability; no provision
cards.evidence: Situation: Possible obligation (outflow possible but not probable); Treatment: Disclose a contingent liability.

cards.front: FRS 102: treatment of a virtually certain inflow?
cards.back: No longer contingent: recognise the asset
cards.evidence: Situation: Inflow virtually certain; Treatment: It's no longer contingent: recognise the asset.

cards.front: FRS 102: how to measure a provision for a large population (e.g. warranties)?
cards.back: Expected value, weighting each outcome by its probability
cards.evidence: - Large population (e.g. warranties on thousands of sales): expected value, weighting each outcome by its probability.

cards.front: FRS 102 s32: adjusting vs non-adjusting events after year end?
cards.back: Adjusting: evidence of conditions at year end. Non-adjusting: conditions arising after; disclose if material
cards.evidence: Non-adjusting events reflect conditions that arose after the year end. Don't adjust; disclose if material.

cards.front: FRS 102: dividends declared after the year end - treatment?
cards.back: Not a liability at year end; disclose
cards.evidence: Dividends declared after the year end are not a liability at the year end (disclose them).

cards.front: Corporation tax: deductibility of general vs specific provisions?
cards.back: Specific provisions generally deductible if the expense is; general provisions aren't
cards.evidence: For corporation tax, specific provisions calculated in line with GAAP and with sufficient accuracy are generally deductible if the expense itself would be deductible. General provisions aren't.

cards.front: FRS 102 new Section 23 revenue: effective date?
cards.back: Periods beginning on or after 1 January 2026
cards.evidence: The FRC's Periodic Review 2024 replaced FRS 102's old revenue section with a new Section 23 'Revenue from Contracts with Customers', based on the IFRS 15 five-step model, for accounting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2026 (early adoption was allowed if all the amendments were adopted together).

cards.front: FRS 102 s23: how is the transaction price allocated to performance obligations?
cards.back: In proportion to relative standalone selling prices
cards.evidence: Step: 4. Allocate the price; Question: How much belongs to each performance obligation?; Key points: In proportion to relative standalone selling prices.

cards.front: FRS 102 s23: contract liability vs contract asset?
cards.back: Liability: paid/invoiced before performing. Asset: performed, right to payment not just time-based
cards.evidence: - Contract liability (deferred income): the customer has paid or been invoiced before the company performs.

cards.front: FRS 102 s23: what distinguishes a trade debtor from a contract asset?
cards.back: Trade debtor: unconditional right to payment (only passage of time needed)
cards.evidence: - Trade debtor: an unconditional right to payment (only the passage of time is needed).

cards.front: FRS 105 micro-entities: how is the new revenue model applied?
cards.back: Simplified version, applied prospectively to new contracts
cards.evidence: FRS 105 brings in a simplified version of the same model for micro-entities, applied prospectively to new contracts.

cards.front: MTD for Income Tax: income threshold from 6 April 2026?
cards.back: Qualifying income over £50,000 (based on 2024/25)
cards.evidence: From 6 April 2026, sole traders and landlords with qualifying income over £50,000 (based on 2024/25) must keep digital records and send quarterly updates through MTD-compatible software.

cards.front: MTD for Income Tax: later threshold reductions?
cards.back: £30,000 from April 2027; £20,000 from April 2028
cards.evidence: The threshold falls to £30,000 from April 2027 and £20,000 from April 2028.

cards.front: Sole traders: basis of assessment since 2024/25?
cards.back: Profits arising in the tax year (6 April to 5 April), whatever the accounting date
cards.evidence: Since 2024/25, sole traders and partners are taxed on the profits arising in the tax year (6 April to 5 April), whatever their accounting date.

cards.front: Sole trader tax adjustments: how are goods taken for own use treated?
cards.back: Add back at selling price (treated as a sale at market value)
cards.evidence: Item: Goods taken for own use; Adjustment: Add back at selling price; Why: Treated as a sale at market value.

cards.front: Cash basis from 2024/25: is there a turnover limit, and which purchases are excluded?
cards.back: Limit removed; capital purchases deductible except cars and land and buildings
cards.evidence: The old turnover limit was removed.

cards.front: Partnership profit sharing: usual order of allocation?
cards.back: Partners' salaries, interest on capital, then balance in profit-sharing ratio
cards.evidence: The partnership agreement sets how profit is shared, commonly in this order: partners' salaries (an allocation of profit, not an expense), interest on capital, then the balance in the profit-sharing ratio.

cards.front: FRS 102 s13: how is stock measured?
cards.back: Lower of cost and estimated selling price less costs to complete and sell, item by item
cards.evidence: Stock (inventories) is measured at the lower of cost and estimated selling price less costs to complete and sell, assessed item by item (or by groups of similar items), not in total.

cards.front: FRS 102 stock: which cost formulas are permitted?
cards.back: FIFO or weighted average (specific identification if not interchangeable); LIFO not permitted
cards.evidence: Cost formulas: FIFO or weighted average. LIFO is not permitted. Specific identification for items that aren't interchangeable (e.g. cars, bespoke jobs).

cards.front: Stock cost: how are production overheads allocated?
cards.back: On normal production capacity
cards.evidence: Include: Production overheads, allocated on normal production capacity; Exclude: Selling, distribution and general admin overheads.

cards.front: Stock cost: is carriage outwards included?
cards.back: No, it is a selling cost; carriage inwards is included
cards.evidence: Include: Import duties, carriage inwards; Exclude: Carriage outwards (a selling cost).

cards.front: Stock review: what signs suggest a write-down is needed?
cards.back: No sales in last 6–12 months; post year-end sales below cost; damaged or expired items
cards.evidence: - stock lines with no sales in the last 6–12 months;

cards.front: Service business unbilled work at year end: how is it treated?
cards.back: Revenue as service performed, shown as accrued income (contract asset), not stock at cost
cards.evidence: Service businesses (consultants, architects, accountants): unbilled work at the year end is usually revenue to be recognised as the service is performed, shown as accrued income (a contract asset), not as stock at cost.

cards.front: FRS 102 new Section 23 revenue model: when does it apply from?
cards.back: Periods beginning on or after 1 January 2026
cards.evidence: From periods beginning on or after 1 January 2026, FRS 102's new Section 23 five-step model governs this (see the revenue recognition lesson).

cards.front: Companies Act 2006: which section requires adequate accounting records?
cards.back: Section 386
cards.evidence: A company must keep accounting records that are sufficient to show and explain its transactions (Companies Act 2006 s386).

cards.front: Year-end working papers: what must a conclusion state?
cards.back: One sentence: whether the balance is fairly stated and what adjustments were made
cards.evidence: - A conclusion: one sentence saying whether the balance is fairly stated, and what adjustments you made

cards.front: Year-end: what to do with a small unexplained difference you can't resolve?
cards.back: Record it as a review point with work done; never plug it
cards.evidence: If you genuinely can't resolve a trivial difference, record it as a review point with the work you've done and let the reviewer decide.

cards.front: Year-end review points: who clears a review point?
cards.back: Only the reviewer
cards.evidence: 3. Only the reviewer clears a point.

cards.front: Year-end bank rec: why get the statement for a few weeks after year end?
cards.back: To confirm unpresented items clear as genuine timing differences
cards.evidence: Unpresented items that clear in early April confirm they were genuine timing differences.

cards.front: Loan working paper: what split must be disclosed in the accounts?
cards.back: Amounts due within one year vs after more than one year
cards.evidence: Then split it between amounts due within one year and after more than one year using the repayment schedule.

cards.front: Year-end process: which areas must be reconciled before building further?
cards.back: Bank, VAT, PAYE, loans and the director's loan account
cards.evidence: 3. Reconcile the basics: bank, VAT, PAYE, loans and the director's loan account.

cards.front: Debtor days: formula?
cards.back: Trade receivables ÷ credit sales × 365
cards.evidence: Debtor days = trade receivables ÷ credit sales × 365

cards.front: Creditor days: formula?
cards.back: Trade payables ÷ credit purchases × 365
cards.evidence: Creditor days = trade payables ÷ credit purchases × 365

cards.front: Late payment legislation: statutory interest rate on B2B debts with no contract rate?
cards.back: 8% plus the Bank of England base rate, plus fixed debt recovery costs
cards.evidence: Late payment interest: Under the late payment legislation, if a business customer pays late and the contract doesn't set a different rate, the supplier can claim statutory interest at 8% plus the Bank of England base rate for business-to-business transactions, and can also claim fixed debt recovery costs.

cards.front: Debtor/creditor days: should sales and purchases be gross or net of VAT?
cards.back: Gross (VAT-inclusive) if receivables and payables include VAT
cards.evidence: Use gross (VAT-inclusive) sales and purchases if the receivables and payables include VAT, so you're comparing like with like.

cards.front: Credit control routine: when to phone an overdue customer?
cards.back: When 14 days overdue, to find out whether there's a dispute
cards.evidence: 3. Phone call when 14 days overdue: find out whether there's a dispute.

cards.front: Aged debtors: what does a credit balance on a customer usually mean?
cards.back: Unallocated receipts, overpayments or duplicate payments; allocate or refund
cards.evidence: Signal: Credit balances on customers; What it usually means: Unallocated receipts, overpayments, duplicate payments; Action: Allocate or refund.

cards.front: Year-end debtor review: best evidence a balance is collectable?
cards.back: Receipts after the year end
cards.evidence: After-date cash is the best evidence: When reviewing debtors at a year end, tick each significant balance to receipts after the year end.

cards.front: Bank feeds: what is the first question to ask for each feed line?
cards.back: Does the other side already exist in the books?
cards.evidence: For each line, ask one question first: does the other side already exist in the books?

cards.front: Bank feeds: effect of creating a Sales receipt for an already-invoiced customer payment?
cards.back: Sale counted twice; invoice stays unpaid on aged debtors
cards.evidence: If you create a new "receive money → Sales" transaction for a customer receipt that already has an invoice, the sale is counted twice and the invoice stays unpaid on the aged debtors.

cards.front: Card processor payout: correct double entry in the bookkeeping?
cards.back: Dr Bank (net), Dr Merchant fees, Cr Clearing (gross)
cards.evidence: 2. When the payout arrives: Dr Bank (net), Dr Merchant fees, Cr Clearing (gross).

cards.front: Card processor clearing account: what should it hold at month end?
cards.back: Only payouts still in transit; reconcile to processor statement
cards.evidence: 3. At the month end the clearing account should only hold payouts still in transit. Reconcile it to the processor's statement.

cards.front: Bank rules: how often should the rules list be reviewed?
cards.back: At least quarterly, and when you take over a file
cards.evidence: Review the rules list at least quarterly and when you take over a file.

cards.front: Bank rules: which type is preferred, suggest or auto-reconcile?
cards.back: Rules that suggest a coding
cards.evidence: Prefer rules that suggest a coding over rules that auto-reconcile.

cards.front: Bank feed: how should a transfer to the business savings account be coded?
cards.back: As a transfer between the two bank accounts
cards.evidence: Feed line: Transfer to the business savings account; Other side already exists?: It will exist on the other bank account's feed; What to do: Code as a transfer between the two bank accounts.

cards.front: VAT: when can errors on earlier returns be corrected on the next return (£10,000 or less)?
cards.back: If the net value of the errors is £10,000 or less
cards.evidence: Errors on previous VAT returns can be corrected on the next return if the net value of the errors is £10,000 or less, or between £10,000 and £50,000 and no more than 1% of box 6 on the return for the period in which they're discovered.

cards.front: VAT error correction: £10,000-£50,000 net error, when can the next return be used?
cards.back: If no more than 1% of box 6 on the return for the period of discovery
cards.evidence: Errors on previous VAT returns can be corrected on the next return if the net value of the errors is £10,000 or less, or between £10,000 and £50,000 and no more than 1% of box 6 on the return for the period in which they're discovered.

cards.front: VAT (Notice 700/45): how many years can errors be corrected?
cards.back: 4 years
cards.evidence: Corrections are possible for 4 years.

cards.front: VAT errors: when must they be notified to HMRC separately?
cards.back: If over the next-return limits, or if the errors were deliberate
cards.evidence: Otherwise, or if the errors were deliberate, they must be notified to HMRC separately.

cards.front: Catch-up bookkeeping: where do unidentifiable bank items go?
cards.back: A query account (with date, amount, payee), never Sundry
cards.evidence: Anything you can't identify goes to a query account with date, amount and payee: never to Sundry.

cards.front: Catch-up: opening balances differ from last filed accounts - what is the starting point?
cards.back: The filed figures; explain the difference
cards.evidence: If the previous bookkeeper's file doesn't agree to what was filed, the filed figures are your starting point, and the difference needs explaining.

cards.front: Coding: which code for a payment of VAT to HMRC?
cards.back: VAT control (it settles the VAT liability, not an expense)
cards.evidence: Payment: VAT paid to HMRC; Why it's not an expense: Settles the VAT liability built up from sales and purchases; Code to: VAT control.

cards.front: Coding: how to code a bank loan repayment?
cards.back: Capital to the loan account; only the interest to Loan interest (expense)
cards.evidence: Payment: Loan repayment; Why it's not an expense: Capital reduces the loan; only the interest is an expense; Code to: Loan (capital) and Loan interest (interest).

cards.front: Coding: where does a director's personal spending go?
cards.back: Director's loan account
cards.evidence: Payment: Director's personal spending; Why it's not an expense: Not a business cost; Code to: Director's loan account.

cards.front: Coding: why not code PAYE payments to HMRC to Wages?
cards.back: Payroll journal already charged wages; coding to Wages doubles the cost
cards.evidence: Coding them to Wages again doubles the wage cost.

cards.front: Tax coding: client/business entertainment treatment for tax and VAT?
cards.back: Disallowable for tax; VAT is blocked
cards.evidence: Client/business entertainment: disallowable for tax, and the VAT is blocked.

cards.front: Tax coding: staff entertainment treatment for tax and VAT?
cards.back: Allowable; VAT recoverable
cards.evidence: Staff entertainment (Christmas party, team meals for employees only): allowable, VAT recoverable.

cards.front: Tax: test for an allowable expense, and HMRC manual on entertainment?
cards.back: Wholly and exclusively for trade, revenue in nature; BIM45000
cards.evidence: For tax, expenses must be wholly and exclusively for the trade and revenue (not capital) in nature, and business entertainment is specifically disallowed (BIM45000).

cards.front: Bookkeeping: entry for a credit note issued to a customer?
cards.back: Dr Sales (or Sales returns), Dr VAT control, Cr Trade receivables
cards.evidence: Event: Credit note issued to a customer; Entry: Dr Sales (or Sales returns), Dr VAT control, Cr Trade receivables; Effect: Reduces income, output VAT and what the customer owes.

cards.front: Bookkeeping: entry when refunding a customer's overpayment?
cards.back: Dr Trade receivables, Cr Bank
cards.evidence: Event: Refund paid to a customer; Entry: Dr Trade receivables, Cr Bank; Effect: Clears a credit balance on the customer's account.

cards.front: Bookkeeping: entry for a credit note received from a supplier?
cards.back: Dr Trade payables, Cr Purchases (or the expense), Cr VAT control
cards.evidence: Event: Credit note received from a supplier; Entry: Dr Trade payables, Cr Purchases (or the expense), Cr VAT control; Effect: Reduces cost, input VAT and what's owed.

cards.front: Bookkeeping: entry when a supplier refund is received in the bank?
cards.back: Dr Bank, Cr Trade payables
cards.evidence: Event: Refund received from a supplier; Entry: Dr Bank, Cr Trade payables; Effect: Clears a debit balance on the supplier's account.

cards.front: VAT: in which period is a credit note adjustment made?
cards.back: The VAT period in which the credit is given
cards.evidence: The adjustment is usually supported by a credit note showing the same kind of detail as a VAT invoice (identifying the original invoice, the reason, the VAT being credited) and is made in the VAT period in which the credit is given.

cards.front: Bookkeeping: what to do with an invoice already sent to a customer?
cards.back: Issue a credit note; don't delete or void it
cards.evidence: If an invoice has been sent to a customer, don't delete or void it to make it disappear. Issue a credit note.

cards.front: Bookkeeping: what is cut-off?
cards.back: Each transaction falls in the period the goods or services were supplied or received, regardless of invoice or payment date
cards.evidence: Cut-off means making sure each transaction falls in the period in which the goods or services were actually supplied or received, regardless of invoice or payment date.

cards.front: Goods received, supplier invoice not yet received: period-end adjustment?
cards.back: Accrue: Dr Cost, Cr Accruals
cards.evidence: Situation: Goods or services received, supplier invoice not yet received (GRNI); Risk: Cost missing from this period; Adjustment at period end: Accrue: Dr Cost, Cr Accruals.

cards.front: Customer deposit for future work posted to Sales: correcting journal?
cards.back: Dr Sales, Cr Deferred income
cards.evidence: Situation: Customer deposit for future work posted to Sales; Risk: Income recognised too early; Adjustment at period end: Dr Sales, Cr Deferred income.

cards.front: Cut-off: should accruals include VAT?
cards.back: No, accruals are net; VAT is claimed when the VAT invoice arrives and is posted
cards.evidence: Accruing VAT. Accruals are net; the VAT is claimed when the VAT invoice arrives and is posted.

cards.front: VAT on customer deposits: when is output VAT due?
cards.back: Usually when the deposit is received (tax point); defer only the net amount in the accounts
cards.evidence: Deposits and VAT. For VAT, a deposit usually creates a tax point when it's received, so output VAT is due then, even if the income is deferred in the accounts. Defer the net amount only.

cards.front: Which period-end journals should not be set to auto-reverse?
cards.back: Prepayment releases and deferred income running over several months; use a schedule
cards.evidence: Don't use reversing journals for prepayment releases or deferred income that runs over several months: use a schedule, or the balance will keep bouncing back.

cards.front: s455 tax: when is it due?
cards.back: 9 months and 1 day after the year end, with corporation tax
cards.evidence: It's due with the corporation tax, 9 months and 1 day after the year end.

cards.front: Director's loan: beneficial loan BIK threshold?
cards.back: Combined loans over £10,000 at any time in the tax year (interest below official rate)
cards.evidence: If the director's combined loans from the company exceed £10,000 at any time in the tax year and interest is charged at less than HMRC's official rate, there's a taxable benefit to report on the P11D, with Class 1A NIC for the company.

cards.front: Director's loan: bed-and-breakfasting rule thresholds?
cards.back: Repayment of £5,000+ followed within 30 days by new borrowing of £5,000+
cards.evidence: Where repayments of £5,000 or more are followed within 30 days by new borrowing of £5,000 or more, the repayment is matched against the new loan, not the old one.

cards.front: HP: at what value is the asset capitalised?
cards.back: Cash price, excluding recoverable VAT, on the date of the agreement
cards.evidence: - Capitalise the asset at its cash price (excluding recoverable VAT) on the date of the agreement, and depreciate it as normal.

cards.front: HP: when can the VAT on the goods be reclaimed?
cards.back: On the return covering the agreement date, on the full cash price
cards.evidence: - VAT: with HP, the VAT on the goods is charged up front on the full cash price, so a VAT-registered business reclaims it on the return covering the agreement date (subject to the usual blocks, e.g. on cars).

cards.front: HP: VAT treatment of the finance company's credit charges?
cards.back: Exempt from VAT
cards.evidence: The finance company's charges for the credit are exempt from VAT.

cards.front: Bank loan repayment: which element goes to profit and loss?
cards.back: Only the interest; the capital element reduces the loan liability
cards.evidence: The rule for both: keep a separate liability account for each loan or agreement, reconcile it to the lender's statement, and only the interest goes to profit and loss.

cards.front: HP instalment journal: how is each instalment recorded?
cards.back: Dr HP creditor (capital), Dr HP interest, Cr Bank
cards.evidence: - Each instalment reduces the HP creditor (capital) and charges HP interest to profit and loss.

cards.front: Loans/HP: how is the balance split at the balance sheet date?
cards.back: Capital due within one year is current; the rest is non-current
cards.evidence: At each balance sheet date, split each loan and HP balance into the capital due within one year (current liability) and the rest (non-current).

cards.front: FRS 102 leases: when do lessees put most leases on balance sheet?
cards.back: Accounting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2026
cards.evidence: Following the FRC's Periodic Review 2024, FRS 102 requires lessees to recognise most leases on the balance sheet (a right-of-use asset and a lease liability) for accounting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2026, with exemptions for short-term and low-value leases.

cards.front: Management accounts: volume effect on gross profit variance formula?
cards.back: (Actual sales − budget sales) × budget margin %
cards.evidence: Volume effect = (actual sales − budget sales) × budget margin %

cards.front: Management accounts: margin effect on gross profit variance formula?
cards.back: (Actual margin % − budget margin %) × actual sales
cards.evidence: Margin effect = (actual margin % − budget margin %) × actual sales

cards.front: Corporation tax FY2026: small profits rate and its profit limit?
cards.back: 19% on profits up to £50,000
cards.evidence: For financial year 2026 the small profits rate is 19% (profits up to £50,000) and the main rate 25% (over £250,000), with marginal relief between, and limits reduced for associated companies and short periods.

cards.front: Corporation tax FY2026: main rate and the profit level it applies above?
cards.back: 25% on profits over £250,000
cards.evidence: For financial year 2026 the small profits rate is 19% (profits up to £50,000) and the main rate 25% (over £250,000), with marginal relief between, and limits reduced for associated companies and short periods.

cards.front: Management accounts: why include a corporation tax estimate for a company?
cards.back: So reported profit and reserves available for dividends aren't overstated
cards.evidence: For a company, include an estimate of the corporation tax on the year-to-date profit so the reported profit and the reserves available for dividends aren't overstated.

cards.front: Management accounts: what should the cash section forecast include?
cards.back: VAT, PAYE, corporation tax, loan repayments
cards.evidence: Section: Cash; What it shows: Bank position, cash movement for the period, and a short forecast of upcoming commitments (VAT, PAYE, corporation tax, loan repayments).

cards.front: Month-end close: expected evidence for the VAT control account?
cards.back: Latest VAT return (unpaid) plus current period's VAT
cards.evidence: | VAT control | Latest VAT return (unpaid) plus current period's VAT |

cards.front: Month-end close: expected balance on suspense/query accounts?
cards.back: Nil
cards.evidence: | Suspense / query accounts | Should be nil |

cards.front: Month-end close: evidence for fixed assets and depreciation?
cards.back: Fixed asset register
cards.evidence: | Fixed assets and depreciation | Fixed asset register |

cards.front: Companies Act 2006 s386: what must company records be able to do?
cards.back: Show and explain transactions and disclose financial position with reasonable accuracy at any time
cards.evidence: A company's records must be sufficient to show and explain its transactions and disclose its financial position with reasonable accuracy at any time (Companies Act 2006 s386).

cards.front: Month-end close: where should corrections after the lock date be posted?
cards.back: In the current month, with a note, by someone with authority
cards.evidence: Corrections after the lock should be posted in the current month, with a note, by someone with authority to do so.

cards.front: Month-end close: evidence for the director's loan account?
cards.back: Reconciliation of movements, confirmed with the director
cards.evidence: | Director's loan account | Reconciliation of movements, confirmed with the director |

cards.front: PAYE/NIC to HMRC: monthly payer's payment deadline?
cards.back: 22nd of the next tax month (cheques by post must arrive by the 19th)
cards.evidence: Monthly payers must pay by the 22nd of the next tax month (cheques by post must arrive by the 19th).

cards.front: PAYE: when does a tax month run from and to?
cards.back: 6th to the 5th
cards.evidence: A tax month runs from the 6th to the 5th.

cards.front: Employer's Class 1 NIC 2026/27: rate and secondary threshold?
cards.back: 15% above £5,000 a year (£417 a month)
cards.evidence: Employer's Class 1 NIC is 15% on earnings above the secondary threshold of £5,000 a year (£417 a month).

cards.front: Employment Allowance 2026/27: maximum reduction in Class 1 NIC?
cards.back: Up to £10,500 for the year
cards.evidence: The Employment Allowance reduces an eligible employer's Class 1 NIC bill by up to £10,500 for the year, offset in the payroll until it's used up.

cards.front: Employment Allowance: who can't claim it?
cards.back: A company whose only employee paid above the secondary threshold is a sole director
cards.evidence: A company whose only employee paid above the secondary threshold is a sole director can't claim it.

cards.front: Payroll journal: entry to record the Employment Allowance in the books?
cards.back: Dr PAYE/NIC liability, Cr Employer's NIC
cards.evidence: In the books, the journal still shows the full employer's NIC cost, so you need a further entry to reduce the liability: Dr PAYE/NIC liability, Cr Employer's NIC

cards.front: AMAP 2026/27: car/van rate for first 10,000 business miles?
cards.back: 55p per mile
cards.evidence: | Cars and vans | 55p | 25p |

cards.front: AMAP 2026/27: car/van rate for each mile over 10,000?
cards.back: 25p per mile
cards.evidence: | Cars and vans | 55p | 25p |

cards.front: AMAP 2026/27: motorcycle mileage rate?
cards.back: 24p per mile
cards.evidence: | Motorcycles | 24p | 24p |

cards.front: AMAP 2026/27: bicycle mileage rate?
cards.back: 20p per mile
cards.evidence: | Bicycles | 20p | 20p |

cards.front: Mileage allowance: what VAT can the business reclaim?
cards.back: Only the fuel element, using advisory fuel rates, with mileage records
cards.evidence: VAT on mileage: the business can reclaim VAT only on the fuel element of a mileage allowance, using HMRC's advisory fuel rates (or AA/RAC rates), with mileage records kept.

cards.front: Petty cash VAT: when can you claim VAT on a receipt?
cards.back: Receipt shows supplier's VAT number and item is standard- or reduced-rated
cards.evidence: Only claim VAT where the receipt shows the supplier's VAT number and the purchase is standard- or reduced-rated.

cards.front: Imprest petty cash: at month end, how much is the float topped up?
cards.back: Exactly the amount spent (Dr Petty cash, Cr Bank)
cards.evidence: 4. At the month end, the vouchers are entered and the float is topped up by exactly the amount spent.

cards.front: Bookkeeping review: what if a reconciliation isn't on file?
cards.back: The balance isn't reviewed
cards.evidence: If a reconciliation isn't on file, the balance isn't reviewed.

cards.front: Proof in total: how to check output VAT?
cards.back: Standard-rated sales × 20%, compared with box 1
cards.evidence: - Output VAT: standard-rated sales × 20%, compared with box 1.

cards.front: Proof in total: how to check loan interest?
cards.back: Average loan balance × interest rate
cards.evidence: - Loan interest: average loan balance × interest rate.

cards.front: Review: what does an overdrawn director's loan account raise questions about?
cards.back: s455, benefit-in-kind and dividend questions
cards.evidence: Look for: Director's loan account overdrawn (debit); Usually means: s455, benefit-in-kind and dividend questions for the manager.

cards.front: Money laundering suspicion: who do you report to, and what must you avoid?
cards.back: Report internally to the firm's MLRO; don't tip off the client
cards.evidence: If you suspect money laundering, report it internally to your firm's MLRO and don't tip off the client.

cards.front: Trial balance: what does a debit balance on Trade payables usually mean?
cards.back: Unallocated or duplicate payments, unrecorded credit notes
cards.evidence: Look for: Debit balance on Trade payables, credit balance on Trade receivables; Usually means: Unallocated or duplicate payments, unrecorded credit notes.

cards.front: Late payment: when is a business payment late if no date is agreed?
cards.back: 30 days after the later of receipt of invoice and delivery of goods/service
cards.evidence: If no payment date is agreed, a business payment is late 30 days after the later of the customer receiving the invoice and the goods or service being delivered.

cards.front: Business-to-business payment terms: usual expected maximum?
cards.back: 60 days, unless longer terms are fair to both
cards.evidence: Business-to-business terms are usually expected to be no more than 60 days unless longer terms are fair to both.

cards.front: Purchase ledger: what date should a bill be entered with?
cards.back: The invoice date, not the payment date
cards.evidence: Enter the bill when it's received, dated with the invoice date, not when it's paid.

cards.front: Bookkeeping: how to record a deposit received with no invoice yet?
cards.back: As a credit (prepayment/overpayment) on the customer's account, allocated when invoiced
cards.evidence: Record it as a credit on the customer's account (a "prepayment" or "overpayment" in most software) and allocate it when the invoice is raised.

cards.front: Remittance advice missing for one payment covering several invoices: what to do?
cards.back: Ask, or allocate to oldest first and note the assumption
cards.evidence: Without one, ask, or allocate to the oldest first and note the assumption.

cards.front: MTD for Income Tax: qualifying income threshold from April 2026?
cards.back: Over £50,000 (based on 2024/25 income)
cards.evidence: over £50,000 in 2024/25 from April 2026, over £30,000 in 2025/26 from April 2027, and over £20,000 in 2026/27 from April 2028

cards.front: MTD for Income Tax: qualifying income threshold from April 2027?
cards.back: Over £30,000 (based on 2025/26 income)
cards.evidence: over £50,000 in 2024/25 from April 2026, over £30,000 in 2025/26 from April 2027, and over £20,000 in 2026/27 from April 2028

cards.front: MTD for Income Tax: qualifying income threshold from April 2028?
cards.back: Over £20,000 (based on 2026/27 income)
cards.evidence: over £50,000 in 2024/25 from April 2026, over £30,000 in 2025/26 from April 2027, and over £20,000 in 2026/27 from April 2028

cards.front: Bookkeeping set-up: what counts as qualifying income for MTD for Income Tax?
cards.back: Self-employment plus property income
cards.evidence: Sole traders and landlords registered for Self Assessment are brought into MTD for Income Tax in stages, based on qualifying income (self-employment plus property income): over £50,000 in 2024/25 from April 2026, over £30,000 in 2025/26 from April 2027, and over £20,000 in 2026/27 from April 2028.

cards.front: Bookkeeping set-up: where to set the lock date after opening balances agree?
cards.back: The day before the conversion date
cards.evidence: Once the opening balances agree to the last accounts, set a lock date at the day before the conversion date so nobody can post into the prior period.

cards.front: VAT coding: which boxes do zero-rated and exempt supplies appear in?
cards.back: Boxes 6 or 7 (net value included); outside-the-scope items are left out
cards.evidence: Zero-rated is not the same as no VAT: Zero-rated and exempt supplies are in box 6 or 7; outside-the-scope items are left out.

cards.front: VAT Flat Rate Scheme: input tax reclaim exception?
cards.back: A single capital asset costing £2,000 or more including VAT
cards.evidence: - Flat Rate Scheme: the client pays a fixed percentage of gross turnover and doesn't reclaim input tax (except on a single capital asset costing £2,000 or more including VAT).

cards.front: VAT cash accounting: turnover limit to join?
cards.back: Taxable turnover up to £1.35 million
cards.evidence: - Cash accounting (taxable turnover up to £1.35 million to join): VAT is accounted for when cash is received or paid, not on the invoice date.

cards.front: Domestic construction reverse charge: supplier's box 6/7 treatment?
cards.back: Net value in box 6 only, no VAT charged
cards.evidence: - The supplier invoices without charging VAT, marks the invoice as reverse charge (e.g. "customer to account to HMRC for the VAT"), and includes the net value in box 6 only.

cards.front: VAT: reverse charge on services from overseas suppliers - which boxes?
cards.back: VAT in boxes 1 and 4; value in boxes 6 and 7
cards.evidence: When a UK business buys most business services from an overseas supplier (software subscriptions, advertising, consultancy), it accounts for the VAT under the reverse charge: VAT in box 1 and box 4, and the value in both box 6 and box 7.

cards.front: VAT coding: correct code for insurance premiums?
cards.back: Exempt
cards.evidence: Transaction: Insurance premium; Common wrong code: 20%; Right code: Exempt.

cards.front: VAT coding: correct code for train and air fares?
cards.back: Zero-rated
cards.evidence: Transaction: Train and air fares; Common wrong code: 20%; Right code: Zero-rated.

cards.front: BPR/APR from 6 April 2026: allowance at 100% relief?
cards.back: £2.5 million, combined value of 100% BPR and/or APR property
cards.evidence: A new allowance of £2.5 million applies to the combined value of property qualifying for 100% BPR and/or 100% APR.

cards.front: BPR/APR: relief rate above the £2.5m allowance?
cards.back: 50% (effective IHT rate of 20% on the excess)
cards.evidence: Above £2.5 million, relief is 50% (an effective IHT rate of 20% on the excess).

cards.front: BPR/APR allowance: can a surviving spouse use unused allowance?
cards.back: Yes; transferable, so up to £5 million for a couple
cards.evidence: Unused allowance is transferable to a surviving spouse or civil partner, so a couple can pass on up to £5 million of qualifying business or farming assets, on top of their nil-rate bands (government announcements, as legislated in FA 2026).

cards.front: BPR: relief rate on AIM shares and does the £2.5m allowance apply?
cards.back: 50%; not covered by the new allowance
cards.evidence: Shares "not listed" on recognised stock exchanges, such as AIM: the rate of relief is 50%, and these shares are not covered by the new allowance.

cards.front: BPR/APR property: interest-free IHT instalment period?
cards.back: 10 equal annual instalments, interest-free
cards.evidence: Payment: the option to pay IHT by equal annual instalments over 10 years, interest-free is extended to all property that qualifies for APR or BPR.

cards.front: BPR/APR transitional rules: lifetime transfers from which date?
cards.back: On or after 30 October 2024, if donor dies on or after 6 April 2026
cards.evidence: Transitional rules apply to lifetime transfers made on or after 30 October 2024 where the donor dies on or after 6 April 2026, so check the manual for gifts and deaths close to the change.

cards.front: BADR: CGT rate for disposals on or after 6 April 2026?
cards.evidence: Disposal date: On or after 6 April 2026; BADR rate: 18%; Lifetime limit: £1 million.

cards.front: BADR: lifetime limit on qualifying gains?
cards.back: £1 million
cards.evidence: Disposal date: 6 April 2025 to 5 April 2026; BADR rate: 14%; Lifetime limit: £1 million.

cards.front: BADR: minimum ownership period for a sole trader or partner business?
cards.back: 2 years ending on the date of disposal (or cessation)
cards.evidence: the business must have been owned for 2 years ending on the date of disposal (or the cessation date, if the business has ceased and the disposal is of assets used in the business within 3 years of cessation).

cards.front: BADR: minimum shareholding for personal company shareholders?
cards.back: At least 5% of ordinary share capital, with at least 5% of voting rights
cards.evidence: the individual holds at least 5% of the ordinary share capital, and that holding gives them at least 5% of the voting rights; and

cards.front: BADR: claim deadline for a 2026/27 disposal?
cards.back: 31 January 2029
cards.evidence: For a 2026/27 disposal the deadline is 31 January 2029.

cards.front: BADR: tax treatment of gains above the lifetime limit?
cards.back: Taxed at the normal 18%/24% rates
cards.evidence: Gains above the £1 million lifetime limit are taxed at the normal 18%/24% rates.

cards.front: CGT 2026/27: individual annual exempt amount?
cards.evidence: Item: Annual exempt amount (individuals); 2026/27: £3,000.

cards.front: CGT 2026/27: rates on gains (basic-rate band vs above)?
cards.back: 18% within unused basic-rate band; 24% above it
cards.evidence: The part of the gain that fits in the unused band is taxed at 18%; the rest at 24%.

cards.front: CGT 2026/27: rate for trustees and personal representatives?
cards.evidence: Item: Trustees and personal representatives; 2026/27: 24%.

cards.front: CGT: BADR rate and lifetime limit for 2026/27?
cards.back: 18% on qualifying gains; £1 million lifetime limit
cards.evidence: Item: Business Asset Disposal Relief; 2026/27: 18% on qualifying gains (£1 million lifetime limit).

cards.front: CGT: deadline to report and pay on UK residential property disposals?
cards.back: Within 60 days
cards.evidence: but UK residential property disposals must be reported and paid within 60 days (see the next lessons).

cards.front: CGT: chattels exempt if sold for what amount or less?
cards.back: £6,000 or less
cards.evidence: - Chattels (tangible movable property) sold for £6,000 or less.

cards.front: CGT: chattel marginal relief limit on the gain?
cards.back: 5/3 of the excess over £6,000
cards.evidence: Above that, "marginal relief" limits the gain to 5/3 of the excess over £6,000.

cards.front: CGT: what date fixes the disposal of land (usually)?
cards.back: Date contracts are exchanged (unconditional), not completion
cards.evidence: It happens when the contract becomes unconditional, not at completion: for land, the date contracts are exchanged (unless conditional).

cards.front: CGT: deadline to report a capital loss to HMRC?
cards.back: Within 4 years of the end of the tax year in which it arose
cards.evidence: 4. Reporting: a loss must be reported to HMRC within 4 years of the end of the tax year in which it arose.

cards.front: CGT: how far are brought-forward losses used against gains?
cards.back: Only to reduce remaining gains to the annual exempt amount (£3,000)
cards.evidence: 2. Brought-forward losses are then used only to the extent needed to reduce the remaining gains to the annual exempt amount (£3,000).

cards.front: CGT: how are current-year losses relieved?
cards.back: Set against current-year gains in full, before the annual exempt amount
cards.evidence: 1. Current-year losses are set against current-year gains in full, before the annual exempt amount, even if this wastes the exemption.

cards.front: CGT: loss on a disposal to a connected person can be set against what?
cards.back: Only gains on disposals to the same person
cards.evidence: 5. Connected persons: a loss on a disposal to a connected person (family, trustees, some companies) can only be set against gains on disposals to the same person, not against general gains.

cards.front: CGT: treatment of disposals between spouses living together?
cards.back: No gain, no loss; recipient takes original cost and acquisition date
cards.evidence: - Disposals between spouses or civil partners living together are at no gain, no loss (TCGA 1992 s58): the receiving spouse takes the original cost and acquisition date.

cards.front: CGT: no gain/no loss period for separating spouses from 6 April 2023?
cards.back: Up to end of the third tax year after the year they stopped living together
cards.evidence: - Transfers between separating spouses are at no gain, no loss for up to the end of the third tax year after the year in which they stopped living together (or earlier if a divorce or dissolution is granted).

cards.front: CGT: transfers under a divorce agreement or court order, time limit?
cards.back: No gain/no loss with no time limit
cards.evidence: - Transfers made under a formal divorce or separation agreement or a court order can be made at no gain/no loss with no time limit.

cards.front: IHT: lifetime rate on a CLT above the nil-rate band?
cards.back: 20% (half the death rate)
cards.evidence: - The excess over the NRB is charged at the lifetime rate of 20% (half the death rate).

cards.front: IHT CLT: tax if the donor pays the lifetime tax (gross-up)?
cards.back: 25% of the net excess (20/80)
cards.evidence: - If the donor pays the tax, the transfer is grossed up: tax = 25% of the net excess (20/80).

cards.front: IHT CLT: rate on death within seven years, and when does taper apply?
cards.back: 40%; taper if death is more than three years after transfer
cards.evidence: - If the donor dies within seven years, the CLT is re-calculated at the death rate of 40%, with taper relief if death is more than three years after the transfer and credit for lifetime tax paid (there is no refund if the lifetime tax was higher).

cards.front: IHT CLT: payment date for transfers 6 April to 30 September?
cards.back: 30 April in the following year
cards.evidence: - Payment due: for transfers 6 April to 30 September, by 30 April in the following year; for transfers 1 October to 5 April, six months after the end of the month of the transfer.

cards.front: IHT CLT: payment date for transfers 1 October to 5 April?
cards.back: Six months after the end of the month of the transfer
cards.evidence: - Payment due: for transfers 6 April to 30 September, by 30 April in the following year; for transfers 1 October to 5 April, six months after the end of the month of the transfer.

cards.front: IHT: maximum ten-year anniversary charge on a relevant property trust?
cards.back: 6% of value above the available nil-rate band
cards.evidence: - A ten-year anniversary charge applies on the value of the trust at each tenth anniversary, at a maximum of 6% of the value above the nil-rate band available (the rate is 30% of the 20% lifetime rate where there are no complicating factors).

cards.front: IHT: form used to report a CLT?
cards.back: Form IHT100
cards.evidence: Reporting is on form IHT100 (see HMRC's guidance for the reporting deadline).

cards.front: IHT: when must tax on an estate be paid to avoid interest?
cards.back: By the end of the sixth month after the death
cards.evidence: Pay the IHT by the end of the sixth month after the death to avoid interest.

cards.front: IHT400: deadline to report the estate value to HMRC?
cards.back: Within one year (HMRC's guidance)
cards.evidence: Report the estate value using the IHT400 within one year (HMRC's guidance; the legislation links the date to the end of the month of death or to the executors first acting).

cards.front: IHT: time limit for loss on sale of quoted shares relief (s179)?
cards.back: Sale within 12 months of death
cards.evidence: Loss on sale of shares (s179): if the executors sell quoted shares within 12 months of death at less than the probate value, the loss can be substituted for the original value for IHT.

cards.front: IHT: loss on sale of land relief (s191) time limit?
cards.back: 4 years
cards.evidence: For land (s191) the period is 4 years.

cards.front: IHT: quick succession relief range and period (s141)?
cards.back: 100% (within 1 year) tapering to 20% (4 to 5 years)
cards.evidence: Quick succession relief (s141): if the deceased inherited property from someone who died within five years, relief is given on the IHT paid on the earlier death, tapering from 100% (within 1 year) to 20% (within 4 to 5 years).

cards.front: IHT: time limit for a deed of variation (s142 IHTA)?
cards.back: Within two years of the death
cards.evidence: Deed of variation (s142 IHTA; s62 TCGA): beneficiaries can redirect what they inherit by a written deed within two years of the death, treated for IHT (and, if the deed so states, CGT) as made by the deceased.

cards.front: IHT: gross estate limit for excepted estate with transferred NRB?
cards.evidence: Gross estate up to £650,000 where a transferred nil-rate band doubles the threshold (both bands available)

cards.front: IHT: pension funds treated as in the estate from when?
cards.back: Deaths on or after 6 April 2027
cards.evidence: For deaths before 6 April 2027 most unused pension funds are outside the estate. For deaths on or after that date they will be in the estate, with the personal representatives responsible for reporting and paying IHT.

cards.front: Rollover relief: permitted timing of the replacement asset?
cards.back: 1 year before to 3 years after the disposal
cards.evidence: replacement must be 1 year before to 3 years after the disposal.

cards.front: Incorporation relief: claim position for transfers from 6 April 2026?
cards.back: Relief requires a claim; it no longer applies automatically
cards.evidence: For transfers on or after 6 April 2026 the position is reversed: relief under s162 requires a claim (HMRC guidance, CG65735).

cards.front: IHT: residence nil-rate band (RNRB) taper threshold and rate of reduction?

cards.front: CT600 late filing: third time in a row, more than 3 months late?
cards.back: £2,000 in total (previously £1,000)
cards.evidence: Return filed…: Late for the third time in a row: more than 3 months late; Penalty: £2,000 in total; Previously: £1,000.

cards.front: CT600: tax-geared penalty if filed 24 months or more after AP end?
cards.back: Plus 20% of the tax unpaid
cards.evidence: Return filed…: 24 months or more after the end of the AP; Penalty: Plus 20% of the tax unpaid; Previously: Unchanged.

cards.front: Corporation tax: late payment interest rate?
cards.back: Bank of England base rate plus 4%
cards.evidence: Late payment interest runs from the due date to the date of payment, at the Bank of England base rate plus 4%.

cards.front: CT groups: group relief group ownership test?
cards.back: ≥75% of ordinary shares, plus ≥75% of distributable profits and of assets on a winding up
cards.evidence: Relationship: Group relief group; Test: One company holds ≥ 75% of the other's ordinary shares (directly or indirectly, multiplying through the chain), plus ≥ 75% of distributable profits and assets on a winding up; or both are 75% subsidiaries of a third company; Effect: Losses can be surrendered between members.

cards.front: CT: gains group election to reallocate a gain or loss - time limit?
cards.back: Within 2 years of the end of the accounting period
cards.evidence: Reallocation election: two members can jointly elect (within 2 years of the end of the AP) to treat a gain or loss as made by the other, so a gain in one company can be matched with a capital loss in another (TCGA 1992 s171A).

cards.front: CT gains group: degrouping charge period after a no gain/no loss transfer?
cards.back: Company leaves the group within 6 years, still owning the asset
cards.evidence: Degrouping charge: if a company leaves the group within 6 years of receiving an asset by a no gain/no loss transfer, still owning it, the deferred gain crystallises.

cards.front: CT group relief: can capital losses be surrendered?
cards.back: No, capital losses can't be group relieved
cards.evidence: Capital losses can't be group relieved (but see gains groups below).

cards.front: CT: tax treatment of payment for group relief up to the loss surrendered?
cards.back: Ignored: not taxable for receiver, not deductible for payer
cards.evidence: A payment up to the amount of the loss surrendered is ignored for CT: not taxable for the receiver, not deductible for the payer.

cards.front: CT: effective marginal rate in the marginal relief band?
cards.evidence: a small group company may have profits in the marginal band, where relief saves tax at an effective 26.5%, more than a large company paying 25%.

cards.front: CT: associated companies test and effect?
cards.back: Control (50%) or common control; divides £50k/£250k limits and instalment thresholds
cards.evidence: Relationship: Associated companies; Test: One controls the other, or both under common control ( 50%), including by individuals; Effect: Rate limits (£50k/£250k) and instalment thresholds divided.

cards.front: CT: discovery assessment time limit where no carelessness?
cards.back: 4 years from the end of the accounting period
cards.evidence: Action: HMRC discovery assessment: no carelessness; Time limit (from the end of the accounting period, unless stated): 4 years.

cards.front: CT: discovery assessment time limit for careless inaccuracy?
cards.back: 6 years from the end of the accounting period
cards.evidence: Action: Discovery: careless inaccuracy; Time limit (from the end of the accounting period, unless stated): 6 years.

cards.front: CT: discovery time limit for deliberate inaccuracy or failure to notify?
cards.back: 20 years from the end of the accounting period
cards.evidence: Action: Discovery: deliberate inaccuracy, failure to notify, or tax avoidance arrangements not notified; Time limit (from the end of the accounting period, unless stated): 20 years.

cards.front: CT: time limit for overpayment relief claim?
cards.back: 4 years from the end of the accounting period
cards.evidence: Action: Overpayment relief claim (error in a return causing tax overpaid); Time limit (from the end of the accounting period, unless stated): 4 years.

cards.front: CT: HMRC enquiry window for a standalone company filing on time?
cards.back: 12 months from the date the return was delivered
cards.evidence: Company: Single company, or member of a small group; Return filed on time: 12 months from the date the return was delivered; Return filed late: Up to the quarter day (31 January, 30 April, 31 July, 31 October) after the first anniversary of delivery.

cards.front: Inaccuracy penalty: careless, maximum and minimum if prompted?
cards.back: Max 30%; minimum 15% if prompted (0% if unprompted)
cards.evidence: Behaviour: Careless; Maximum: 30%; Minimum: unprompted disclosure: 0%; Minimum: prompted disclosure: 15%.

cards.front: Inaccuracy penalty: deliberate and concealed, max and prompted minimum?
cards.back: Max 100%; minimum 50% if prompted
cards.evidence: Behaviour: Deliberate and concealed; Maximum: 100%; Minimum: unprompted disclosure: 30%; Minimum: prompted disclosure: 50%.

cards.front: CT: how long after closure notice can the company appeal?
cards.back: 30 days
cards.evidence: The company has 30 days to appeal.

cards.front: IFA regime: fixed-rate election rate for debits?
cards.back: 4% a year of cost, straight line
cards.evidence: 2. Fixed-rate election: elect to deduct 4% a year of cost, straight line, instead.

cards.front: IFA fixed-rate 4% election: time limit to make it?
cards.back: Within 2 years of the end of the AP of creation or acquisition
cards.evidence: The election is irrevocable and must be made within 2 years of the end of the AP in which the asset was created or acquired.

cards.front: IFAs: annual relief rate on goodwill bought with qualifying IP (from 1 April 2019)?
cards.back: 6.5% a year of cost
cards.evidence: Relief is at a fixed 6.5% a year of cost, only if the goodwill is acquired as part of the acquisition of a business that includes qualifying IP (patents, registered designs, copyright and design rights, plant breeders' rights) used in the business.

cards.front: IFAs: cap on goodwill cost qualifying for 6.5% relief?
cards.back: 6 times the cost of the qualifying IP acquired
cards.evidence: The cost that qualifies is capped at 6 times the cost of the qualifying IP acquired.

cards.front: IFAs: reinvestment relief window under CTA 2009 s754?
cards.back: 1 year before to 3 years after the sale
cards.evidence: Reinvestment relief (CTA 2009 s754) lets a company defer the part of the credit that exceeds original cost if it reinvests the proceeds in other IFAs within 1 year before to 3 years after the sale, similar to rollover relief for gains.

cards.front: IFAs: relief for goodwill acquired 8 July 2015 to 31 March 2019?
cards.back: No amortisation relief at all
cards.evidence: Goodwill acquired between 8 July 2015 and 31 March 2019 got no amortisation relief at all.

cards.front: Corp tax: lease premium rule - maximum lease length for part of premium to be income?
cards.back: 50 years or less
cards.evidence: When a company landlord grants a lease of 50 years or less for a premium, part of the premium is taxed as property income in the year the lease is granted:

cards.front: Corp tax: formula for income element of a short lease premium?
cards.back: Premium − (premium × 2% × (years of lease − 1))
cards.evidence: Income element = premium − (premium × 2% × (years of lease − 1))

cards.front: Corp tax: how far can a non-trading loan relationship deficit be carried back, and against what?
cards.back: 12 months, against non-trading loan relationship credits only
cards.evidence: 3. carried back 12 months against non-trading loan relationship credits only;

cards.front: Corp tax: when does the corporate interest restriction apply to a group?
cards.back: Net interest expense of more than £2 million a year
cards.evidence: The corporate interest restriction limits net interest deductions for a group with more than £2 million of net interest expense a year.

cards.front: Corp tax: rate paid by a close investment-holding company?
cards.back: Main rate (25%) on all profits; no small profits rate or marginal relief
cards.evidence: which pays the main rate (25%) on all its profits with no small profits rate or marginal relief.

cards.front: Corp tax: tax treatment of interest on a loan to buy let property?
cards.back: Non-trading loan relationship debit, deductible in full; not a property expense
cards.evidence: It's a non-trading loan relationship debit, deductible in full.

cards.front: Corp tax: can a company carry back a UK property business loss?
cards.back: No; set against same AP total profits, excess carried forward
cards.evidence: It can't be carried back.

cards.front: Corp tax: profits threshold above which a company is 'large' (12-month AP, no associates)?
cards.back: More than £1.5m (up to £20m); very large is more than £20m
cards.evidence: Category: Large; Profits test (12-month AP, no associates): More than £1.5m (up to £20m); Instalments due: Months 7, 10, 13 and 16 from the start of the AP (on the 14th).

cards.front: Corp tax instalments: how are the thresholds adjusted for associated companies?
cards.back: Divided by 1 + number of associated companies; pro-rated for a short AP
cards.evidence: The £1.5m (and the £10m and £20m) thresholds are divided by 1 + the number of associated companies, and pro-rated for a short AP.

cards.front: Corp tax instalments: first-year exception conditions?
cards.back: Not large in previous 12 months and profits no more than £10m (both adjusted for associates)
cards.evidence: First-year exception: a company isn't required to pay instalments for an AP if it wasn't large in the previous 12 months and its profits are no more than £10m (both adjusted for associates).

cards.front: Corp tax instalments: de minimis CT liability limit?
cards.back: No instalments if CT liability for the AP is £10,000 or less
cards.evidence: De minimis: no instalments if the company's CT liability for the AP is £10,000 or less.

cards.front: Corp tax instalments: when can penalties apply?
cards.back: Only if deliberately or recklessly failing to pay; up to twice the interest
cards.evidence: Penalties apply only where a company deliberately or recklessly fails to pay instalments (up to twice the interest).

cards.front: CT: small profits rate and its upper augmented profits limit (FY2023-FY2026)?
cards.back: 19% on augmented profits of £50,000 or less
cards.evidence: Augmented profits: £50,000 or less (lower limit); Rate: Small profits rate 19%; Notes: On taxable total profits.

cards.front: CT: main rate and the profits level above which it applies in full (no associates)?
cards.back: 25% on augmented profits over £250,000
cards.evidence: Augmented profits: Over £250,000 (upper limit); Rate: Main rate 25%; Notes: No marginal relief.

cards.front: CT: effective marginal rate in the marginal relief band?
cards.evidence: Augmented profits: £50,001 to £250,000; Rate: Main rate 25% less marginal relief; Notes: Effective marginal rate of 26.5% on profits in this band.

cards.front: CT: how are 'augmented profits' (A) calculated?
cards.back: TTP plus exempt dividends from non-group companies
cards.evidence: A = augmented profits = taxable total profits + exempt distributions (dividends) received from companies outside the group

cards.front: CT: how do associated companies change the lower and upper limits?
cards.back: Divide both by (1 + number of associated companies)
cards.evidence: The lower and upper limits are divided by (1 + the number of associated companies).

cards.front: CT: how are limits adjusted for an accounting period under 12 months?
cards.back: Limit × months in AP / 12
cards.evidence: For an AP of less than 12 months, both limits are reduced proportionately: limit × months in AP / 12.

cards.front: CT: which companies are ignored when counting associated companies?
cards.back: Dormant companies and passive holding companies
cards.evidence: Dormant companies are ignored, as are passive holding companies (no assets other than shares in 51% subsidiaries, no income other than dividends passed up, no gains).

cards.front: SBA: annual rate for corporation tax (from 1 April 2020)?
cards.back: 3% a year of qualifying cost, straight line
cards.evidence: - Rate: 3% a year of the qualifying cost, straight line (2% before 1 April 2020 for CT).

cards.front: SBA: how long does the allowance period last?
cards.back: 33⅓ years
cards.evidence: - Period: 33⅓ years from the later of the date the building is first brought into non-residential qualifying use and the date the expenditure is incurred.

cards.front: SBA: which construction contracts qualify?
cards.back: Contracts entered into on or after 29 October 2018
cards.evidence: The structures and buildings allowance (SBA) changed that for construction contracts entered into on or after 29 October 2018.

cards.front: SBA: are balancing adjustments made when the building is sold?
cards.back: No; the buyer simply continues claiming
cards.evidence: - No balancing adjustments: the allowance isn't clawed back or accelerated on sale; the buyer simply continues claiming.

cards.front: SBA: how is SBA treated when a company sells the building?
cards.back: Total SBA claimed is added to disposal proceeds for chargeable gains
cards.evidence: When a company sells a building it has claimed SBA on, the total SBA claimed is added to its disposal proceeds for chargeable gains.

cards.front: SBA: what must a buyer of a used building have to claim?
cards.back: A copy of the seller's allowance statement
cards.evidence: A buyer of a used building needs a copy from the seller, and can only claim with it.

cards.front: SBA: how are integral features in a building relieved instead?
cards.back: Special rate P&M: AIA or 50% FYA
cards.evidence: Cost: Integral features (electrical, heating, lifts, air-conditioning, cold water); SBA?: No; Instead: Special rate P&M: AIA or 50% FYA.

cards.front: CT trading loss: time limit for current year s37 claim?
cards.back: Within 2 years of the end of the loss-making AP
cards.evidence: Relief: Current year (CTA 2010 s37(3)(a)); Against: Total profits of the loss-making AP (before QCDs); Claim: Within 2 years of the end of the loss-making AP.

cards.front: CT: how far back can a s37 trading loss be carried back?
cards.back: Total profits of the previous 12 months, after a current year claim
cards.evidence: Relief: Carry back (s37(3)(b)); Against: Total profits of the previous 12 months, after a current year claim; Claim: Same claim; only if the current year claim is made first.

cards.front: CT terminal loss relief (s39): carry back period?
cards.back: Final 12 months' loss against total profits of previous 3 years, latest first
cards.evidence: Relief: Terminal loss (s39); Against: Total profits of the previous 3 years, latest first; Claim: Loss of the final 12 months of trading.

cards.front: CT: corporate loss restriction deductions allowance?
cards.back: £5 million; carried-forward losses then only against 50% of profits above
cards.evidence: The corporate loss restriction caps the use of carried-forward losses: a company (or group) can use carried-forward losses in full against the first £5 million of profits a year (the deductions allowance), but only against 50% of profits above that.

cards.front: CT: how can capital losses be relieved?
cards.back: Only against chargeable gains of the same or later periods; no carry back
cards.evidence: Capital losses (losses on disposals of chargeable assets) can only be set against chargeable gains of the same or later periods.

cards.front: CT: are s37 loss claims partial or all-or-nothing?
cards.back: All or nothing; QCDs can be wasted as they can't be carried forward
cards.evidence: Each claim is all or nothing: you can't choose to relieve only part of the available profits, even if that wastes the benefit of qualifying charitable donations (which are deducted after loss relief and can't be carried forward).

cards.front: Corporation tax: maximum length of an accounting period?
cards.back: 12 months
cards.evidence: It can never exceed 12 months (CTA 2009 s10).

cards.front: CT: payment due date for a non-large company's accounting period?
cards.back: 9 months and 1 day after the end of the AP
cards.evidence: - Payment: each AP has its own due date, 9 months and 1 day after the end of that AP (for companies that are not "large").

cards.front: CT: filing date for CT600s where the period of account is up to 18 months?
cards.back: 12 months after the end of the period of account
cards.evidence: - Filing: both CT600s are due by the filing date for the period of account: normally 12 months after the end of the period of account (for periods of account up to 18 months).

cards.front: CT: deadline for a new company to tell HMRC it has become active?
