cards.back: Within 3 months of the start of its first accounting period
cards.evidence: A new company must tell HMRC it has become active for corporation tax (for example, it has started trading) within 3 months of the start of its first accounting period.

cards.front: CT: how are capital allowances dealt with in a long period of account?
cards.back: Computed separately for each AP, not time-apportioned
cards.evidence: That's wrong: compute allowances for each accounting period separately.

cards.front: CT long period of account: how is a chargeable gain allocated between APs?
cards.back: To the AP in which the disposal happens
cards.evidence: | Chargeable gains | Allocated to the AP in which the disposal happens |

cards.front: CT: do LLPs carrying on a business pay corporation tax?
cards.back: No; they are tax-transparent and the members are taxed
cards.evidence: Body: LLPs carrying on a business; Pays CT?: No; Notes: Tax-transparent: members are taxed.

cards.front: Companies House: normal accounts deadline, private company?
cards.back: 9 months after the ARD
cards.evidence: Accounts: Normal; Private company: 9 months after the ARD; Public company: 6 months after the ARD.

cards.front: Companies House: first accounts covering over 12 months, private company deadline?
cards.back: Later of 21 months from incorporation and 3 months from the ARD
cards.evidence: Accounts: First accounts covering more than 12 months; Private company: The later of 21 months from incorporation and 3 months from the ARD; Public company: The later of 18 months from incorporation and 3 months from the ARD.

cards.front: Companies House late filing penalty: private company, more than 3 but not more than 6 months late?
cards.evidence: How late the accounts are delivered: More than 3 months but not more than 6 months; Private company or LLP: £750; Public company: £3,000.

cards.front: Companies House late filing penalty: public company, more than 6 months late?
cards.evidence: How late the accounts are delivered: More than 6 months; Private company or LLP: £1,500; Public company: £7,500.

cards.front: Companies House: what happens to the penalty if accounts are late two years in a row?
cards.back: The second year's penalty is doubled
cards.evidence: If a company's accounts are filed late two years in a row, the penalty for the second year is doubled.

cards.front: First accounting reference period: permitted length?
cards.back: More than 6 months and not more than 18 months
cards.evidence: The first accounting reference period runs from incorporation to the first ARD, and must be more than 6 months and not more than 18 months.

cards.front: Companies House fee: online confirmation statement (first in payment period)?
cards.back: £50 online / software (£110 on paper)
cards.evidence: Filing: Confirmation statement (first in the payment period); Online / software: £50; Paper: £110.

cards.front: Companies House fee: standard online incorporation?
cards.back: £100 online/software (£124 paper)
cards.evidence: Filing: Incorporation; Online / software: £100; Paper: £124.

cards.front: ACSP: time limit to report changes to the ACSP's details?
cards.back: Within 14 days
cards.evidence: - Ongoing duties: report changes to the ACSP's details within 14 days, respond to information requests, and keep records of identity checks for 7 years.

cards.front: ACSP: how long must records of identity checks be kept?
cards.back: 7 years
cards.evidence: - Ongoing duties: report changes to the ACSP's details within 14 days, respond to information requests, and keep records of identity checks for 7 years.

cards.front: Companies House: when did ACSP registration open?
cards.back: 18 March 2025
cards.evidence: Authorised Corporate Service Providers (ACSPs): - ACSP registration opened on 18 March 2025.

cards.front: Companies House: earliest date agents must be ACSPs and presenters verified?
cards.back: No earlier than November 2027, with at least 6 months' notice
cards.evidence: - No earlier than November 2027: identity verification of presenters (the people who file) becomes compulsory for filing any document, and third-party agents filing for companies must be registered ACSPs. Companies House has said it will give at least 6 months' notice.

cards.front: Public company (plc): minimum allotted share capital and paid-up requirement?
cards.back: £50,000, at least a quarter paid up
cards.evidence: Minimum allotted share capital of £50,000, at least a quarter paid up.

cards.front: Private limited company: minimum directors and who can be one?
cards.back: At least one director, who must be a natural person
cards.evidence: At least one director, who must be a natural person.

cards.front: Public company (plc): minimum directors and secretary requirement?
cards.back: At least two directors and a qualified company secretary
cards.evidence: At least two directors and a qualified company secretary.

cards.front: CIC: extra report filed with its accounts?
cards.back: CIC34 report
cards.evidence: Files an extra CIC34 report with its accounts.

cards.front: LLP: minimum number of designated members?
cards.back: At least two
cards.evidence: At least two designated members.

cards.front: Company numbers: prefix for an England and Wales LLP versus a Scottish LLP?
cards.back: OC for England and Wales LLP; SO for Scottish LLP
cards.evidence: Company numbers show where the entity is registered: 8 digits for England and Wales, SC for Scotland, NI for Northern Ireland, OC for an England and Wales LLP, SO for a Scottish LLP.

cards.front: CS01: deadline for delivery after the review period ends?
cards.back: Within 14 days after the end of the review period
cards.evidence: The statement must be delivered within 14 days after the end of the review period.

cards.front: Companies House: online CS01 fee and when it is charged?
cards.back: £50, once with the first statement in each 12-month payment period
cards.evidence: Method: Online or software; Fee: £50; When charged: Once, with the first statement in each 12-month payment period.

cards.front: Companies House: paper CS01 fee?
cards.back: £110, once per 12-month payment period
cards.evidence: Method: Paper CS01; Fee: £110; When charged: Once, with the first statement in each 12-month payment period.

cards.front: CS01: how often must a company deliver a confirmation statement?
cards.back: At least once every 12 months
cards.evidence: Every company (and every LLP) must deliver a confirmation statement at least once every 12 months (Companies Act 2006 s853A).

cards.front: CS01: which statements did ECCTA add from 4 March 2024?
cards.back: Lawful purpose confirmation and an appropriate registered email address
cards.evidence: The two statements added by ECCTA (from 4 March 2024): On every confirmation statement the company must:

cards.front: CS01: can director, PSC or registered office changes be made on it?
cards.back: No; file AP01, TM01, CH01, PSC forms, AD01 first
cards.evidence: Changes to directors, secretaries, PSCs and the registered office must be filed on their own forms (AP01, TM01, CH01, PSC01 to PSC09, AD01) before the CS01, which then simply confirms the register is correct.

cards.front: CS01: what happens if a director has not verified identity?
cards.back: Companies House will not accept the statement
cards.evidence: Companies House will not accept the statement until every director has done so.

cards.front: Companies Act 2006: what is the legal test for distributable profits (ss830)?
cards.back: Accumulated realised profits less accumulated realised losses (not previously distributed, capitalised or written off)
cards.evidence: A company may only make a distribution out of profits available for the purpose: its accumulated, realised profits (so far as not previously distributed or capitalised) less its accumulated, realised losses (so far as not previously written off).

cards.front: Model articles: who decides an interim dividend versus a final dividend?
cards.back: Interim: the directors. Final: shareholders by ordinary resolution, on directors' recommendation
cards.evidence: Who decides; Interim dividend: The directors (board decision); Final dividend: Declared by the shareholders by ordinary resolution, on the directors' recommendation.

cards.front: Model articles: when does an interim dividend become a debt?
cards.back: Only when paid; the board can change its mind until then
cards.evidence: When it becomes a debt; Interim dividend: Only when paid: the board can change its mind until then; Final dividend: When declared, unless a later payment date is set.

cards.front: Dividends: what are 'relevant accounts' (s836) normally?
cards.back: The last annual accounts circulated to members
cards.evidence: Whether a distribution can be made is judged by reference to relevant accounts (s836): normally the last annual accounts circulated to members.

cards.front: Dividends: what can a company use if the last annual accounts show insufficient profit?
cards.back: Interim accounts (s838) allowing a reasonable judgement; not filed for a private company
cards.evidence: If those don't show enough profit, the company can prepare interim accounts (s838) that enable a reasonable judgement to be made.

cards.front: CA 2006 s847: when must a shareholder repay an unlawful distribution?
cards.back: If they knew, or had reasonable grounds to believe, it was unlawful when made
cards.evidence: If a distribution is made in breach of the rules and, at the time, the shareholder knows or has reasonable grounds for believing it was unlawful, they are liable to repay it (or its value).

cards.front: Dividend waiver: by when must the deed be executed to be effective?
cards.back: Before entitlement: before an interim is paid or a final is declared
cards.evidence: A shareholder can waive their right to a dividend by deed, executed before they become entitled to it (before an interim is paid, or before a final is declared).

cards.front: Which reserves are not distributable when working out dividend capacity?
cards.back: Share premium, share capital, capital redemption reserve and revaluation reserve (unrealised)
cards.evidence: Share premium, share capital and the capital redemption reserve are not distributable.

cards.front: Companies House: when is a company dormant (CA 2006 s1169)?
cards.back: No significant accounting transaction in the period
cards.evidence: A company is dormant during a period in which it has no significant accounting transaction: a transaction that must be entered in the company's accounting records.

cards.front: Companies House dormancy: which transactions are disregarded?
cards.back: Subscriber share payments, registrar fees, late filing penalties paid to Companies House

cards.front: Corporation tax: when is a company usually dormant?
cards.back: Not carrying on a business and has no income
cards.evidence: A company is usually dormant for corporation tax if it is not carrying on a business and has no income: no trade, no rents, no investment income.

cards.front: Dormant company: which corporation tax returns must it file?
cards.back: Only if HMRC has issued a notice to deliver
cards.evidence: - Corporation tax returns only if HMRC has issued a notice to deliver.

cards.front: Who can use paper form AA02 for dormant accounts?
cards.back: Only a company dormant since incorporation that has never traded
cards.evidence: The paper form AA02 is only for a company that has been dormant since incorporation and has never traded.

cards.front: Dormant company starts business: how long to tell HMRC?
cards.back: Within 3 months of starting business activity
cards.evidence: - HMRC: tell HMRC within 3 months of the company starting business activity (trading, letting property, earning income).

cards.front: Dormant company: audit exemption provision for small companies?
cards.evidence: A dormant company that qualifies as small can claim audit exemption (CA 2006 s480).

cards.front: ECCTA identity verification: start date and transition length?
cards.back: 18 November 2025; 12-month transition
cards.evidence: Identity verification became a legal requirement from 18 November 2025 for directors and people with significant control, phased in over a 12-month transition.

cards.front: Companies House personal code: how many characters?
cards.back: 11 characters
cards.evidence: On success they receive a Companies House personal code (11 characters).

cards.front: Identity verification: when must an existing director provide their personal code?
cards.back: When the company files its next confirmation statement in the 12-month transition
cards.evidence: Person: Existing director; When they must provide their personal code: When the company files its next confirmation statement during the 12-month transition.

cards.front: Identity verification: deadline for a PSC who is not a director?
cards.back: First 14 days of their birth month
cards.evidence: Person: PSC who is not a director; When they must provide their personal code: In the first 14 days of their birth month (born 22 January: 1 to 14 January).

cards.front: Identity verification: PSC who is also a director of the same company, deadline?
cards.back: 14-day period starting the day after the confirmation statement date
cards.evidence: Person: PSC who is also a director of the same company; When they must provide their personal code: In the 14-day period starting the day after the company's confirmation statement date.

cards.front: ACSP registration with Companies House: when did it open?
cards.back: 18 March 2025
cards.evidence: Registration opened on 18 March 2025, and an ACSP must be supervised for anti-money laundering purposes.

cards.front: Companies House: how many SIC codes can an incorporation application list?
cards.back: Up to four (SIC 2007) codes
cards.evidence: Item: SIC codes; What you need: Up to four Standard Industrial Classification (2007) codes describing the business; Common pitfall: Choosing 99999 (dormant) for a company that will trade.

cards.front: Companies House: registered office rule from 4 March 2024?
cards.back: Must always be an appropriate address; PO Boxes not allowed
cards.evidence: The appropriate address rule (in force from 4 March 2024): A company's registered office must at all times be an appropriate address.

cards.front: Companies House: incorporation fees (online/software, paper, same-day)?
cards.back: £100 online or software; £124 paper; £156 same-day via software
cards.evidence: From the current Companies House fees schedule: incorporation costs £100 online or by software, £124 on paper, and £156 for a same-day incorporation through software.

cards.front: Incorporation: minimum number of directors and who they must be?
cards.back: At least one director, a natural person, identity verified
cards.evidence: Item: Officers; What you need: At least one director (a natural person), each identity verified with a Companies House personal code. Secretary optional.; Common pitfall: Director hasn't verified yet, so the application can't proceed.

cards.front: Corporation tax: deadline to register a new company?
cards.back: Within 3 months of starting to trade
cards.evidence: Within the first few weeks you'll usually need to: register the company for corporation tax (within 3 months of starting to trade), consider VAT and PAYE registration, open a business bank account, issue share certificates, record the opening entries, diarise the first confirmation statement and accounts deadlines, and update your engagement letter and client due diligence for the new entity.

cards.front: New company: how is the accounting reference date set automatically?
cards.back: Last day of the month in which the incorporation anniversary falls
cards.evidence: A new company's accounting reference date (ARD) is set automatically as the last day of the month in which the anniversary of incorporation falls.

cards.front: LLP: minimum number of members and designated members?
cards.back: Two members and at least two designated members
cards.evidence: Minimum; Company: One director who's a natural person; LLP: Two members and at least two designated members.

cards.front: LLP: deadline to file LL AP01 / LL TM01 / LL CH01 for member changes?
cards.back: Within 14 days
cards.evidence: - Member changes (appointment, cessation, change of details, or change in designated status): file LL AP01 / LL TM01 / LL CH01 within 14 days.

cards.front: LLP: accounts filing deadline for a normal period?
cards.back: 9 months after the year end
cards.evidence: - Accounts: due 9 months after the year end (21 months from incorporation for a first period over 12 months), with the same late filing penalties as a private company: £150 / £375 / £750 / £1,500.

cards.front: LLP: late filing penalties for accounts (private company scale)?
cards.evidence: - Accounts: due 9 months after the year end (21 months from incorporation for a first period over 12 months), with the same late filing penalties as a private company: £150 / £375 / £750 / £1,500.

cards.front: LLP: when can a sole member become personally liable for debts?
cards.back: After carrying on business with only one member for more than 6 months
cards.evidence: If an LLP carries on business with only one member for more than 6 months, that member can become personally liable for debts incurred after the 6 months (LLPA 2000 s4A).

cards.front: LLP: what happens if designated members fall below two?
cards.back: Every member is treated as designated (LLPA 2000 s8)
cards.evidence: If the number of designated members falls below two, every member is treated as designated (LLPA 2000 s8).

cards.front: LLP PSC: ownership/voting threshold for surplus assets and votes?
cards.back: More than 25%
cards.evidence: - hold rights to more than 25% of the surplus assets on a winding up;

cards.front: Companies House: deadline to file AP01 or TM01 for a director change?
cards.back: Within 14 days
cards.evidence: Event: Appoint a director; Form: AP01 (AP02 for a corporate director); Deadline: Within 14 days; Fee: None.

cards.front: Company name change by special resolution: form and online fee?
cards.back: NM01 plus the resolution; £20 online (same-day £85)
cards.evidence: Event: Change company name by special resolution; Form: NM01 plus the resolution; Deadline: Takes effect on the new certificate; Fee: £20 online (same-day £85).

cards.front: CA 2006 s168: notice needed to remove a director by ordinary resolution?
cards.back: Special notice (28 days) to the company
cards.evidence: Special notice (28 days) of the resolution must be given to the company, and the director has the right to make written representations and be heard at the meeting.

cards.front: Registered office change: how long can documents still be served at the old address?
cards.back: 14 days after registration (CA 2006 s87)
cards.evidence: The change takes effect when Companies House registers it, but for 14 days afterwards documents can still validly be served at the old address (CA 2006 s87).

cards.front: Company minutes of directors' meetings: minimum retention period?
cards.back: At least 10 years
cards.evidence: Record: Minutes of directors' meetings; Rule: Keep for at least 10 years; Where: CA 2006 s248.

cards.front: Private company accounting records: retention under CA 2006 vs HMRC?
cards.back: 3 years under CA 2006; HMRC needs 6 years
cards.evidence: Record: Accounting records; Rule: Keep for 3 years (private company); HMRC needs 6 years; Where: CA 2006 s388.

cards.front: Name change by special resolution: what vote percentage is required?
cards.back: 75% of votes
cards.evidence: The usual route is a special resolution (75% of votes) and form NM01 with the fee.

cards.front: PSC: share/voting rights threshold for conditions 1 and 2?
cards.back: More than 25% (exactly 25% is not enough)
cards.evidence: 'More than' 25%: Exactly 25% is not enough.

cards.front: PSC: when does an individual hold an interest indirectly through a company?
cards.back: Majority stake: more than 50% of shares or votes, or right to appoint/remove majority of board, or dominant influence
cards.evidence: An individual holds an interest indirectly through a company in which they have a majority stake (more than 50% of shares or votes, or the right to appoint or remove a majority of its board, or the right to exercise dominant influence).

cards.front: PSC: time limit to tell Companies House of new PSCs or changes?
cards.back: Within 14 days of confirming the change
cards.evidence: You must tell Companies House about new PSCs and about any changes, such as a change of personal details or nature of control, within 14 days of confirming the change.

cards.front: PSC: which Companies House form notifies that someone has ceased to be a PSC?
cards.back: PSC07
cards.evidence: | PSC07 | Notify that someone has ceased to be a PSC |

cards.front: PSC: which form notifies a relevant legal entity (RLE) as a PSC?
cards.back: PSC02
cards.evidence: | PSC02 | Notify a relevant legal entity |

cards.front: PSC: when is a corporate shareholder a registrable RLE?
cards.back: If it meets a condition and is subject to its own PSC disclosure requirements
cards.evidence: A corporate shareholder that meets a condition is a relevant legal entity (RLE). It is registrable (it goes on the register instead of the people behind it) if it is subject to its own PSC disclosure requirements, for example another UK company, or one listed on certain regulated markets.

cards.front: Companies Act: deadline to file SH01 return of allotment?
cards.back: Within one month of allotment (s555); no fee
cards.evidence: After allotting, the company must deliver a return of allotment (SH01) to Companies House within one month (s555).

cards.front: Pre-emption (s561): minimum acceptance period for offer to existing shareholders?
cards.back: At least 14 days
cards.evidence: Pre-emption rights (CA 2006 s561): If a company allots equity securities for cash, it must first offer them to existing ordinary shareholders in proportion to their holdings, on the same or better terms, with at least 14 days to accept.

cards.front: Companies Act: deadline to issue share certificate after allotment?
cards.back: Within two months (s769)
cards.evidence: Also: update the register of members, issue a share certificate within two months (s769), and file any ordinary/special resolutions (s551 authority, s570 disapplication) within 15 days of passing them.

cards.front: s551 authority to allot: maximum duration?
cards.back: 5 years, stating the maximum number of shares
cards.evidence: Ordinary resolution giving authority (max 5 years, stating the maximum number of shares), then a board resolution.

cards.front: Variation of class rights: default consent needed (s630)?
cards.back: 75% of that class, if articles specify nothing else
cards.evidence: Varying the rights of an existing class needs the consent the articles require, or otherwise 75% of that class (s630).

cards.front: Variation of class rights: SH10 filing deadline?
cards.back: Within one month
cards.evidence: File an SH10 (particulars of variation of rights) within one month, and the amended articles plus the special resolution within 15 days.

cards.front: Companies Act: can shares be allotted at a discount to nominal value?
cards.evidence: Shares can't be allotted at a discount to nominal value (s580).

cards.front: Buy-back: deadline to file SH03 return of purchase at Companies House?
cards.back: Within 28 days
cards.evidence: Within 28 days: deliver the return of purchase (SH03) to Companies House (s707).

cards.front: Buy-back SH03: stamp duty rate and threshold?
cards.back: 0.5% of consideration (rounded up to £5) where consideration is over £1,000
cards.evidence: The SH03 is a stampable document: 0.5% stamp duty on the consideration (rounded up to £5) where the consideration is over £1,000, and the SH03 must be stamped by HMRC before it's sent to Companies House.

cards.front: Buy-back: deadline to file SH06 notice of cancellation?
cards.back: Within 28 days, with a statement of capital
cards.evidence: Within 28 days: deliver the notice of cancellation (SH06) with a statement of capital (s708).

cards.front: Small buy-back out of cash (s692(1ZA)): limit per financial year?
cards.back: Lower of £15,000 and 5% of share capital
cards.evidence: If the articles permit, a private company can buy back shares out of cash up to the lower of £15,000 and 5% of its share capital in a financial year, without identifying distributable profits..

cards.front: Buy-back: how long must the contract be kept at the registered office?
cards.back: 10 years
cards.evidence: Update the register of members, check PSCs (the remaining shareholders' percentages go up) and keep the contract at the registered office for 10 years.

cards.front: Buy-back capital treatment: seller's minimum ownership period?
cards.back: 5 years (3 years if inherited)
cards.evidence: the seller is UK resident and has owned the shares for 5 years (3 years if inherited, including the deceased's period of ownership);

cards.front: Buy-back capital treatment: required reduction in seller's holding?
cards.back: Holding no more than 75% of what it was before
cards.evidence: the seller's interest is substantially reduced: after the buy-back their percentage holding is no more than 75% of what it was before; and

cards.front: Reduction of capital by solvency statement: SH19 filing deadline?
cards.back: Within 15 days
cards.evidence: A private company can also reduce its share capital by special resolution supported by a directors' solvency statement (CA 2006 ss641–644), filing form SH19 with the statement and resolution within 15 days.

cards.front: Stock transfer form: rate of stamp duty on consideration?
cards.back: 0.5%, rounded up to the nearest £5
cards.evidence: Stamp duty is charged at 0.5% of the consideration (Finance Act 1999 Sch 13), rounded up to the nearest £5.

cards.front: Stamp duty on shares: when can Certificate 1 be used?
cards.back: Consideration of £1,000 or less, not part of a larger transaction over £1,000
cards.evidence: If the consideration is £1,000 or less and the transfer isn't part of a larger transaction over £1,000, complete Certificate 1 on the form: no duty, and the form doesn't need to go to HMRC.

cards.front: Share transfer: deadline to pay stamp duty and send form to HMRC?
cards.back: Within 30 days of the form being signed and dated
cards.evidence: Where duty is due, pay it and send the form to HMRC (by email to the Stamp Duty mailbox) within 30 days of the form being signed and dated.

cards.front: Directors refuse to register a share transfer: time limit for notice of refusal?
cards.back: As soon as practicable and within 2 months (CA 2006 s771)
cards.evidence: If they refuse, they must send the transferee notice of refusal with reasons as soon as practicable and within 2 months (CA 2006 s771).

cards.front: Share transfer: time limit to issue new share certificate?
cards.back: Within 2 months (s776)
cards.evidence: Cancel the old share certificate and issue a new one within 2 months (s776).

cards.front: Stamp duty: what consideration is entered for a gift of shares?
cards.back: "Nil"; no duty and no certificate needed
cards.evidence: A gift has no consideration: enter "Nil" as the consideration. No duty is due and no certificate is needed.

cards.front: CGT: gift of shares to a child (connected person)?
cards.back: Disposal at market value; holdover relief (TCGA 1992 s165) may be available for unquoted trading co shares
cards.evidence: Gifts to anyone else connected (children, siblings): a disposal at market value for CGT, even though no money changes hands. Gift holdover relief (TCGA 1992 s165) may be available for shares in an unquoted trading company.

cards.front: Strike-off (DS01): maximum distribution for capital treatment under s1030A?
cards.back: £25,000 total; if exceeded, the whole amount is income
cards.evidence: A distribution to shareholders in anticipation of a strike-off is treated as a capital distribution, rather than an income distribution, only if the total of such distributions is not more than £25,000, and the company intends to secure its debts are paid and to be struck off within two years.

cards.front: DS01: deadline to send copies to members, creditors, employees etc?
cards.back: Within 7 days of filing (s1006)
cards.evidence: 3. Within 7 days, send a copy to every member, creditor, employee, pension scheme manager or trustee and any director who didn't sign (s1006).

cards.front: DS01: earliest strike-off after the first Gazette notice if no objection?
cards.back: No earlier than 2 months after the notice
cards.evidence: 5. If no objection, the company is struck off no earlier than 2 months after the notice, and a second Gazette notice confirms dissolution.

cards.front: Voluntary strike-off: look-back period for ineligibility (trading, name change)?
cards.back: 3 months
cards.evidence: A company can't apply if, in the last 3 months, it has:

cards.front: Administrative restoration (RT01): who can apply?
cards.back: A former director or member
cards.evidence: | Who applies | A former director or member | Wide range of interested persons (e.g. former directors, members, creditors) |

cards.front: What happens to a dissolved company's remaining property?
cards.back: Passes to the Crown as bona vacantia (s1012)
cards.evidence: When a company is dissolved, any property it still owns, including cash in a bank account you forgot to close, a VAT repayment, or a debt someone owes it, passes to the Crown as bona vacantia (CA 2006 s1012).

cards.front: Settlements: minor children rule - section and de minimis limit?
cards.back: s629; parent's income unless £100 or less a year
cards.evidence: Minor children: for unmarried minor children, income from shares given by a parent is always treated as the parent's (s629), whether or not the gift is outright, unless the income is £100 or less a year.

cards.front: Dividend waiver: when must it be executed to be effective?
cards.back: By deed, before the dividend is declared (right arises); usually 12 months
cards.evidence: For a waiver to be effective it must be a deed, executed before the right to the dividend arises (before it is declared), and normally for a limited period (often 12 months).

cards.front: Dividend tax rates from 6 April 2026: basic and higher, and allowance?
cards.back: 10.75% basic, 35.75% higher; £500 allowance
cards.evidence: Keep an eye on the dividend rates (10.75% basic, 35.75% higher from 6 April 2026) and the £500 allowance

cards.front: Jones v Garnett (Arctic Systems): why did the taxpayer win?
cards.back: Outright gift exception applied: wife held an ordinary share with full rights
cards.evidence: The House of Lords agreed there was a "settlement" (the arrangement) but held the outright-gift exception applied: she had been given an ordinary share with the full rights attached, not a right to income only.

cards.front: 30-day rule: how much of the repayment is matched?
cards.back: The lower of the repayment and the new loan/benefits
cards.evidence: The repayment is then matched against the new loan. Relief under s458 is denied on the lower of the two amounts, so s455 tax is payable on that matched sum as if the original loan hadn't been repaid.

cards.front: CT600A: how to treat a matched repayment when claiming s458 relief?
cards.back: Exclude the matched amount; no s458 relief to that extent
cards.evidence: Where matching applies, the repayment gives no s458 relief to the extent matched, so the s455 tax on the original loan stays payable.

cards.front: Beneficial loans: official rate of interest for 2026/27?
cards.evidence: Official rate of interest for 2026/27: 3.75%.

cards.front: Beneficial loans: £10,000 exemption – when does it apply?
cards.back: Total loans never exceed £10,000 at any time in the tax year; if exceeded, whole loan is charged
cards.evidence: £10,000 exemption: if the total of all such loans does not exceed £10,000 at any time in the tax year, the benefit is exempt and need not be reported.

cards.front: Beneficial loan benefit: P11D filing deadline?
cards.back: 6 July
cards.evidence: Deadline; s455 charge: 9 months and 1 day after the year end; Beneficial loan benefit: P11D by 6 July; Class 1A paid by 22 July (electronic).

cards.front: s455 charge: rate for loans made from 6 April 2026?
cards.evidence: Rate; s455 charge: 35.75% for loans made from 6 April 2026; Beneficial loan benefit: 3.75% official rate × the loan, then taxed at the director's marginal rate.

cards.front: s455 charge: payment deadline after company year end?
cards.back: 9 months and 1 day after the year end
cards.evidence: Deadline; s455 charge: 9 months and 1 day after the year end; Beneficial loan benefit: P11D by 6 July; Class 1A paid by 22 July (electronic).

cards.front: Strike-off (s1030A): max total distribution with capital treatment?
cards.back: £25,000 in total; above that, taxed as a dividend
cards.evidence: Capital treatment only up to £25,000 in total (CTA 2010 s1030A); anything above is taxed as a dividend.

cards.front: BADR rate from 6 April 2026, and lifetime limit?
cards.back: 18% (14% in 2025/26); £1 million lifetime limit
cards.evidence: Business Asset Disposal Relief (BADR) taxes qualifying gains at 18% from 6 April 2026 (14% in 2025/26), up to a £1 million lifetime limit.

cards.front: BADR liquidation: time limit for distribution after cessation?
cards.back: Within 3 years after cessation
cards.evidence: The distribution must be made within 3 years after the cessation.

cards.front: MVL: declaration of solvency requires company to pay debts within what period?
cards.back: 12 months
cards.evidence: Required: directors swear the company can pay all debts within 12 months

cards.front: CGT 2026/27: rates on ordinary gains and annual exempt amount?
cards.back: 18% / 24%; annual exempt amount £3,000
cards.evidence: CGT rates for 2026/27: 18% / 24% on ordinary gains; the annual exempt amount is £3,000.

cards.front: Winding-up TAAR: condition C time period for same or similar trade?
cards.back: Within 2 years after the distribution
cards.evidence: C: within 2 years after the distribution the individual is involved in carrying on a same or similar trade or activity to that of the wound-up company.

cards.front: CA 2006: which section sets out the duty to promote the success of the company?
cards.evidence: Section: s172; Duty: Promote the success of the company; In plain English: Act in good faith for the benefit of the members as a whole, having regard to employees, suppliers, community, reputation and long-term consequences..

cards.front: CA 2006: which section covers the duty to avoid conflicts of interest?
cards.evidence: Section: s175; Duty: Avoid conflicts of interest; In plain English: Don't put yourself in a position where your interests conflict, or may conflict, with the company's, unless authorised..

cards.front: CA 2006: which section requires declaring interest in a proposed transaction?
cards.evidence: Section: s177; Duty: Declare interest in a proposed transaction; In plain English: Tell the other directors about any interest in a transaction with the company before it is entered into..

cards.front: CA 2006: what is a shadow director?
cards.back: Someone whose directions or instructions the board is accustomed to act on (not professional advisers)
cards.evidence: - Shadow directors: the board is accustomed to act on their directions or instructions (but not professional advisers acting in that capacity).

cards.front: Dividends: from what profits may a company pay a dividend, and which section makes members repay?
cards.back: Distributable profits; member who knew it was unlawful must repay (s847)
cards.evidence: A dividend may only be paid out of distributable profits (CA 2006 Part 23). Paying one that the accounts don't support is a breach of duty (s171, s174) and the member who knew it was unlawful must repay it (s847).

cards.front: Directors' duties: whose interests must be considered once insolvency is likely?
cards.back: Creditors (s172(3), BTI v Sequana [2022] UKSC 25)
cards.evidence: Once insolvency is likely, the director must have regard to the interests of creditors (s172(3), BTI v Sequana [2022] UKSC 25).

cards.front: DLA: when does a s455 charge arise on an overdrawn balance?
cards.back: If unpaid 9 months and 1 day after the year end
cards.evidence: Tax consequence: s455 charge if unpaid 9 months and 1 day after the year end; beneficial loan BIK if over £10,000..

cards.front: DLA: overdrawn balance size that triggers beneficial loan BIK?
cards.evidence: Tax consequence: s455 charge if unpaid 9 months and 1 day after the year end; beneficial loan BIK if over £10,000..

cards.front: Director's loan to company: tax deducted at source on yearly interest paid?
cards.back: 20% (basic rate), accounted for on form CT61 each quarter
cards.evidence: If it is paid, the company deducts income tax at 20% (basic rate) at source if it is yearly interest paid to an individual, accounts for it on form CT61 each quarter, and the director declares it as savings income.

cards.front: Which statute may challenge a director repaying a credit DLA when insolvent?
cards.back: Preference, Insolvency Act 1986 s239
cards.evidence: A director should never repay themselves from a credit DLA while the company is insolvent or near to it: it may be challenged as a preference (Insolvency Act 1986 s239).

cards.front: DLA: Companies Act 2006 sections requiring disclosure of director advances and credits?
cards.evidence: 5. Show the DLA balance in the accounts (Companies Act 2006 ss412–413 disclosure of advances and credits to directors).

cards.front: Dividends: legal test for paying a distribution (CA 2006 s830)?
cards.back: Only out of accumulated, realised profits less accumulated, realised losses
cards.evidence: A company may only make a distribution out of profits available for the purpose (s830): accumulated, realised profits less accumulated, realised losses.

cards.front: Dividends: when must a shareholder repay an unlawful distribution?
cards.back: If they knew, or had reasonable grounds to believe, it was unlawful (s847)
cards.evidence: A shareholder who receives a distribution knowing, or having reasonable grounds to believe, it was unlawful must repay it (s847).

cards.front: Dividend tax 2026/27: dividend allowance?
cards.back: £500 a year at 0%, and it uses up band space
cards.evidence: Band: Dividend allowance; Rate: 0%; Notes: £500 a year, uses up band space.

cards.front: Dividend tax 2026/27: basic rate on dividends?
cards.back: 10.75% (up from 8.75% from 6 April 2026)
cards.evidence: Band: Basic rate; Rate: 10.75%; Notes: Increased from 8.75% for dividends from 6 April 2026.

cards.front: Dividend tax 2026/27: higher rate on dividends?
cards.evidence: Band: Higher rate; Rate: 35.75%; Notes: Increased from 33.75%.

cards.front: Dividend tax 2026/27: additional rate on dividends?
cards.back: 39.35% (unchanged)
cards.evidence: Band: Additional rate; Rate: 39.35%; Notes: Unchanged.

cards.front: s455 charge on loans to participators from 6 April 2026: rate?
cards.evidence: HMRC may treat the payment as a loan to a participator (s455, 35.75% for loans from 6 April 2026) or as earnings (PAYE and NIC), rather than a dividend.

cards.front: Interim vs final dividend: when does each become a debt?
cards.back: Interim: when paid. Final: when members approve it or the resolution date
cards.evidence: | When it becomes a debt | When it is paid (it can be changed until then) | When the shareholders approve it, or the date specified in the resolution |

cards.front: Pensions 2026/27: standard annual allowance?
cards.evidence: The annual allowance for 2026/27 is £60,000.

cards.front: Pensions: how far back can unused annual allowance be carried forward?
cards.back: 3 tax years
cards.evidence: Limits; Employer pension contribution: Annual allowance £60,000 (carry forward 3 years); Salary: None; Dividend: Distributable reserves.

cards.front: Pensions: tapered annual allowance thresholds?
cards.back: Threshold income over £200,000 and adjusted income over £260,000
cards.evidence: Reductions: the tapered annual allowance (threshold income above £200,000 and adjusted income above £260,000) and the money purchase annual allowance (once flexible access has been taken) can restrict it.

cards.front: Employer pension contribution: when is the CT deduction given?
cards.back: In the period the contribution is actually paid
cards.evidence: The deduction is given in the period the contribution is actually paid, not when accrued or provided for.

cards.front: Pensions: normal minimum pension age from 6 April 2028?
cards.evidence: Access; Employer pension contribution: From normal minimum pension age (57 from 6 April 2028); 25% tax-free subject to the lump sum allowance; Salary: Immediate; Dividend: Immediate.

cards.front: Dividend tax rates in 2026/27 (basic/higher/additional)?
cards.evidence: Employee NIC / income tax; Employer pension contribution: None on payment; Salary: Yes; Dividend: Dividend tax 10.75% / 35.75% / 39.35%.

cards.front: Employer pension contribution above the annual allowance: consequence?
cards.back: Company deduction unaffected; director gets an annual allowance charge on the excess
cards.evidence: An employer contribution above the allowance doesn't affect the company's deduction (the test is wholly and exclusively), but the director gets an annual allowance charge on the excess.

cards.front: s455: rate for loans made on or after 6 April 2026?
cards.evidence: For loans made or benefits conferred on or after 6 April 2026 it is 35.75%.

cards.front: s455: rate for loans made 6 April 2022 to 5 April 2026?
cards.evidence: For loans made 6 April 2022 to 5 April 2026 it is 33.75%; 6 April 2016 to 5 April 2022 32.5%; before that 25%.

cards.front: s455: when is the tax due?
cards.back: 9 months and 1 day after the end of the accounting period of the loan, if still outstanding
cards.evidence: Due: with the corporation tax for the period, i.e. 9 months and 1 day after the end of the accounting period in which the loan was made, to the extent the loan is still outstanding.

cards.front: s456: small loan exception limit for employees/directors?
cards.back: £15,000 total, full-time worker with no material interest (5% or less)
cards.evidence: Exceptions: a loan of up to £15,000 in total to a full-time working director or employee who has no material interest (5% or less) is outside s455 (s456).

cards.front: s458: when is refund paid if loan repaid after the deadline?
cards.back: 9 months and 1 day after the end of the period of repayment, with no interest
cards.evidence: Repayment after the deadline: the tax paid is refunded, but only 9 months and 1 day after the end of the accounting period in which the repayment was made. HMRC pays no interest on the delay.

cards.front: Employment Allowance 2026/27: annual amount?
cards.back: £10,500 a year
cards.evidence: Item: Employment Allowance; Figure: £10,500 a year.

cards.front: Employment Allowance: when can a company NOT claim it?
cards.back: When the only employee paid above the secondary threshold is also a director
cards.evidence: A company cannot claim it if the only employee paid above the secondary threshold is also a director of the company.

cards.front: Dividend tax 2026/27: basic / higher / additional rates?
cards.evidence: Item: Dividend tax: basic / higher / additional; Figure: 10.75% / 35.75% / 39.35%.

cards.front: Dividend allowance 2026/27?
cards.evidence: Item: Dividend allowance; Figure: £500.

cards.front: NIC: lower earnings limit for a State Pension qualifying year?
cards.back: £6,708 a year (£129 a week)
cards.evidence: But if it is below the lower earnings limit (£6,708 a year, £129 a week), it does not give a qualifying year for State Pension.

cards.front: Personal pension relief with zero salary: gross limit?
cards.back: £3,600 gross
cards.evidence: A zero salary limits personal pension relief to £3,600 gross.

cards.front: Corporation tax 2026/27: rates and limits?
cards.back: 19% to £50,000; 25% above £250,000; marginal relief between
cards.evidence: Item: Corporation tax; Figure: 19% on profits to £50,000; 25% above £250,000; marginal relief between.

cards.front: Write-off of director's loan: how is the director taxed (ITTOIA 2005 ss415–416)?
cards.back: Amount released is treated as dividend income; no grossing up, no tax credit
cards.evidence: the amount released or written off is treated as dividend income, taxed at the dividend rates (for 2026/27 10.75% basic, 35.75% higher, 39.35% additional).

cards.front: Dividend tax rates 2026/27: basic, higher, additional?
cards.evidence: the amount released or written off is treated as dividend income, taxed at the dividend rates (for 2026/27 10.75% basic, 35.75% higher, 39.35% additional).

cards.front: 2026/27: dividend allowance amount?
cards.evidence: The dividend allowance (£500) can be used if available.

cards.front: Director's loan write-off: HMRC's NIC view (CTM61660)?
cards.back: Class 1 NIC (employee and secondary) due where participator is an employee/director
cards.evidence: NIC: where the participator is an employee (including a director), HMRC's view in CTM61660 is that the amount written off is "remuneration or profit derived from an employment", so Class 1 NIC (employee and secondary) is due.

cards.front: Director's loan write-off: in which period does company s458 relief arise?
cards.back: The period in which the write-off takes place
cards.evidence: For a write-off, relief arises in the period in which the write-off takes place.

cards.front: Director's loan release without distributable reserves: consequence?
cards.back: Release is unlawful; amount may have to be repaid under s847
cards.evidence: If the company doesn't have distributable reserves (CA 2006 Part 23), the release is unlawful and the amount may have to be repaid under s847.

cards.front: Insolvency Act 1986: which section lets a eve-of-insolvency loan write-off be challenged?
cards.back: s238 (transaction at an undervalue)
cards.evidence: A write-off made on the eve of insolvency can be challenged as a transaction at an undervalue (Insolvency Act 1986 s238).

cards.front: Record retention: sole traders and partners, how long?
cards.back: At least 5 years after the 31 January submission deadline of the relevant tax year
cards.evidence: - Sole traders and partners: at least 5 years after the 31 January submission deadline of the relevant tax year (gov.uk, Business records if you're self-employed).

cards.front: Companies Act 2006 s388: how long must company accounting records be kept?
cards.back: 3 years (private company); 6 years (public company)
cards.evidence: Companies Act 2006 s386 requires every company to keep adequate accounting records, and s388 says they must be preserved for 3 years from when they're made for a private company and 6 years for a public company.

cards.front: Corporation tax: how long must HMRC records be kept?
cards.back: 6 years from the end of the accounting period (longer if enquiry open or return late)
cards.evidence: - Companies, for corporation tax: HMRC requires records to be kept for 6 years from the end of the accounting period (longer if an enquiry is still open or a return was late), so in practice keep company records for at least 6 years.

cards.front: Accounting equation (basic form)?
cards.back: Assets = Capital + Liabilities
cards.evidence: Assets = Capital + Liabilities

cards.front: Accounting: how are drawings treated?
cards.back: They reduce capital directly, not an expense, so they don't reduce taxable profit
cards.evidence: Drawings reduce capital directly. They never go through the income statement, so they don't reduce taxable profit.

cards.front: Accounting: why is capital also called net assets?
cards.back: Capital = Assets − Liabilities
cards.evidence: Rearranged, it's how you find a missing figure. For example Capital = Assets − Liabilities, which is why capital is also called net assets.

cards.front: Accruals: year-end journal for an accrued expense?
cards.back: Dr Expense, Cr Accruals (current liability)
cards.evidence: Adjustment: Accrued expense (accrual); What it means: Cost incurred this year, not yet invoiced or recorded; Journal: Dr Expense, Cr Accruals; Balance sheet: Current liability.

cards.front: Prepayments: year-end journal for a prepaid expense?
cards.back: Dr Prepayments, Cr Expense (current asset)
cards.evidence: Adjustment: Prepaid expense (prepayment); What it means: Cost paid/recorded this year that relates to next year; Journal: Dr Prepayments, Cr Expense; Balance sheet: Current asset.

cards.front: Accruals: journal and balance sheet treatment of deferred income?
cards.back: Dr Sales, Cr Deferred income; current liability
cards.evidence: Adjustment: Deferred income; What it means: Income invoiced/received this year for work next year; Journal: Dr Sales, Cr Deferred income; Balance sheet: Current liability.

cards.front: Accruals: formula for a prepayment?
cards.back: Amount paid × months after year end ÷ months covered
cards.evidence: Prepayment = amount paid × months after the year end ÷ months covered

cards.front: Accruals: formula for expense for the year from the ledger?
cards.back: Opening prepayment − opening accrual + paid in year − closing prepayment + closing accrual
cards.evidence: Expense for the year = opening prepayment − opening accrual + amount paid/invoiced in year − closing prepayment + closing accrual

cards.front: Accruals: when are year-end adjustments reversed?
cards.back: On the first day of the next period
cards.evidence: Year-end adjustments are reversed on the first day of the next period.

cards.front: Accruals and VAT: what amount is accrued for a VAT-registered client?
cards.back: The net cost, as no invoice exists so no input tax to claim
cards.evidence: An accrual is the net cost if the client is VAT registered and can recover the VAT: no invoice exists yet, so there's no input tax to claim.

cards.front: Bank rec: two-step method, what is Step 1?
cards.back: Update the cash book for items the bank knows about and correct errors, giving the adjusted cash book balance
cards.evidence: Step 1: update the cash book. Post everything the bank knows about that the books don't, and correct any errors in the books. This gives the adjusted cash book balance, which is the figure that goes in the trial balance and the accounts.

cards.front: Bank rec: how to get from statement balance to adjusted cash book balance?
cards.back: Statement − unpresented payments + outstanding lodgements ± bank errors
cards.evidence:
Balance per bank statement
 − unpresented payments
 + outstanding lodgements
 ± bank errors
 = adjusted cash book balance

cards.front: Bank rec: journal to post a dishonoured customer cheque?
cards.back: Dr Trade receivables, Cr Bank
cards.evidence:
Dr Trade receivables £740
Cr Bank £740

cards.front: Bank rec: do unpresented cheques and outstanding lodgements need posting?
cards.back: No, they are timing differences and reconciling items only
cards.evidence: Items 4 and 5 are timing differences: they'll clear in September with no further entries.

cards.front: Bank statement: how is an overdraft shown in the client's books?
cards.back: A credit balance on Bank (a debit balance on the statement)
cards.evidence: An overdrawn statement shows a debit balance; in the books an overdraft is a credit balance on Bank.

cards.front: Bank rec: what to do with a cheque unpresented for six months or more?
cards.back: Find out why; it may need writing back
cards.evidence: A cheque unpresented for six months or more probably won't clear. Find out why; it may need writing back.

cards.front: Cloud software: does ticking 'reconciled' on feed lines prove the bank balance?
cards.back: No; check the software balance to the actual statement closing balance at period end
cards.evidence: It doesn't prove the balance. Always check the balance per the software against the closing balance on the actual bank statement (or the bank's own app) at the period end.

cards.front: Companies Act 2006 s386: what must accounting records be?
cards.back: Sufficient to show and explain the company's transactions, disclosing financial position with reasonable accuracy at any time
cards.evidence: A company must keep accounting records that are "sufficient to show and explain the company's transactions" and that disclose its financial position with reasonable accuracy at any time (Companies Act 2006 s386).

cards.front: Bookkeeping: what is a book of prime entry?
cards.back: A list where similar transactions are first recorded, one line each, with totals added up (book of original entry)
cards.evidence: Books of prime entry (also called books of original entry). Lists where similar transactions are first recorded, one line each, with the totals added up.

cards.front: Sales ledger total should equal which nominal ledger account?
cards.back: Trade receivables control account
cards.evidence: Sales ledger (receivables ledger). One account per customer, showing what each owes. Its total should equal the Trade receivables control account in the nominal ledger.

cards.front: Purchase ledger total should equal which nominal ledger account?
cards.back: Trade payables control account
cards.evidence: Purchase ledger (payables ledger). One account per supplier. Its total should equal the Trade payables control account.

cards.front: What goes through the journal as a book of prime entry?
cards.back: Entries not from a day book or bank: depreciation, accruals, corrections, payroll, opening balances
cards.evidence: Book of prime entry: The journal; Source document: Journal vouchers, workings, payroll reports; What it records: Anything that doesn't belong in another book: depreciation, accruals, corrections, payroll, opening balances.

cards.front: Double entry for a customer receipt of money against an invoice?
cards.back: Dr Bank, Cr Trade receivables control (not Sales)
cards.evidence: The receipt of £600 came through the cash book (Dr Bank, Cr Trade receivables control), not the sales day book.

cards.front: Why is posting a supplier invoice as a 'spend money' bank payment wrong?
cards.back: Supplier ledger never shows it, so creditors are wrong and the payment may later be coded twice
cards.evidence: If the invoice is entered as a "spend money" transaction on the day it's received, the supplier ledger never shows it, so the creditors figure is wrong and the payment later gets coded twice.

cards.front: Tax: AIA relief rate and annual limit for most plant and machinery?
cards.back: 100% relief up to £1 million a year
cards.evidence: For most plant and machinery the Annual Investment Allowance (AIA) gives 100% relief up to £1 million a year, but it doesn't cover cars, which get writing down allowances instead.

cards.front: Capital allowances: how are cars treated regarding AIA?
cards.back: Not covered by AIA; they get writing down allowances
cards.evidence: For most plant and machinery the Annual Investment Allowance (AIA) gives 100% relief up to £1 million a year, but it doesn't cover cars, which get writing down allowances instead.

cards.front: Capital allowances: do structures and buildings qualify for AIA?
cards.back: No, they don't qualify for AIA at all
cards.evidence: Structures and buildings, for example, don't qualify for AIA at all.

cards.front: FRS 102 s17: is recoverable VAT part of an asset's cost?
cards.back: No, recoverable VAT is not part of cost
cards.evidence: Recoverable VAT is not part of cost.

cards.front: Capital vs revenue: replacing a whole machine or van, or part of a larger asset?
cards.back: Whole separate asset is capital; part of a larger asset is normally a repair
cards.evidence: Replacing an entire separate asset (a whole machine, a whole van) is capital; replacing a part of a larger asset (the roof of a building, a van's engine) is normally a repair.

cards.front: Capital vs revenue: treatment of a maintenance contract or extended warranty?
cards.back: Revenue (prepay any part for future years)
cards.evidence: Cost: Maintenance contract or extended warranty; Treatment: Revenue (prepay any part for future years); Why: Running cost.

cards.front: Capital vs revenue: staff training on a new machine?
cards.back: Revenue, as it relates to staff, not the asset's condition
cards.evidence: Cost: Staff training on the new machine; Treatment: Revenue; Why: Relates to staff, not to the asset's condition.

cards.front: Control accounts: what is a contra entry between ledgers?
cards.back: Dr Trade payables control, Cr Trade receivables control; both individual accounts also updated
cards.evidence: A contra happens when a business both buys from and sells to the same party and the two agree to set off balances: Dr Trade payables control, Cr Trade receivables control, and both individual accounts are updated.

cards.front: Control accounts: do cash sales go through receivables control?
cards.back: No - no customer or supplier balance is created
cards.evidence: Cash sales and cash purchases never go through the control accounts, because no customer or supplier balance was created.

cards.front: Control account reconciliation: effect of an entry missed from the books entirely?
cards.back: Affects both sides, so it shows no difference
cards.evidence: - An entry missed out of the books entirely affects both and won't show up as a difference at all.

cards.front: Reconciliation: error in a day-book total or its nominal ledger posting affects what?
cards.back: The control account only
cards.evidence: - An error in a day-book total or a posting from it to the nominal ledger affects the control account only.

cards.front: VAT control: what should the balance equal after each return is filed?
cards.back: Liability (or repayment) on the latest return plus any earlier unpaid returns
cards.evidence: - VAT control: after each return is filed, the balance should equal the liability (or repayment) on the latest return, plus any earlier unpaid returns.

cards.front: Xero/QuickBooks: why can aged debtors differ from receivables control?
cards.back: Manual journal to the control account, or payment received but not allocated to an invoice
cards.evidence: They can still differ if someone posts a manual journal directly to the control account, or if a payment is received but not allocated to an invoice.

cards.front: What should a convincing control account reconciliation show?
cards.back: Both balances, each adjustment with one-line reason, agreed figure, aged report attached, dated and initialled
cards.evidence: Show the balance per the control account, the balance per the listing, each adjustment to either side with a one-line reason, and the agreed figure. Attach the aged report. Date it and initial it.

cards.front: FRS 102 s17: what is the depreciable amount of an asset?
cards.back: Cost less residual value
cards.evidence: Under FRS 102 section 17 the depreciable amount of an asset (cost less residual value) is allocated on a systematic basis over its useful life.

cards.front: Straight-line depreciation: formula?
cards.back: (Cost − residual value) ÷ useful life
cards.evidence: Method: Straight line; Formula: (Cost − residual value) ÷ useful life; Typical use: Buildings, fixtures, office equipment, computers; Pattern: Same charge every year.

cards.front: Reducing balance depreciation: formula?
cards.back: Net book value (NBV) at start of year × %
cards.evidence: Method: Reducing balance; Formula: Net book value (NBV) at start of year × %; Typical use: Vehicles, plant; Pattern: Higher charges early on, falling each year.

cards.front: Disposal account: what does a debit balance mean?
cards.back: A loss on disposal (credit balance = profit)
cards.evidence: 4. Balance on the disposal account: a debit balance is a loss, a credit balance is a profit

cards.front: Part-exchange: how is the trade-in allowance posted?
cards.back: Cr Disposals (trade-in allowance)
cards.evidence: Part-exchange: the trade-in value is the disposal proceeds of the old asset and part of the payment for the new one: Dr New asset – cost (full price), Cr Disposals (trade-in allowance), Cr Bank/creditor (the balance paid).

cards.front: Depreciation and disposal profits/losses: tax treatment?
cards.back: Not allowable or taxable; added back/deducted, capital allowances given instead
cards.evidence: Depreciation and profits or losses on disposal are not allowable or taxable for income tax or corporation tax.

cards.front: VAT: standard rate fraction of a gross (VAT-inclusive) figure that is VAT?
cards.back: 1/6 of the gross (net is 5/6)
cards.evidence: The standard rate is 20%. If you're given a VAT-inclusive (gross) figure at the standard rate, the VAT is 1/6 of the gross (because 20/120 = 1/6), and the net is 5/6.

cards.front: Double entry: which account types increase with a debit (DEAD)?
cards.back: Expenses, Assets, Drawings
cards.evidence:
| Expenses | Liabilities |
| Assets | Income |
| Drawings | Capital |

cards.front: Bookkeeping: journal to record a credit sale with VAT?
cards.back: Dr Trade receivables (gross); Cr Sales (net); Cr VAT control (VAT)
cards.evidence:
Dr Trade receivables (debtors) £1,200
Cr Sales £1,000
Cr VAT control £200

cards.front: Bookkeeping: journal for VAT on a credit purchase (input tax)?
cards.back: Dr VAT control; it reduces what's owed to HMRC
cards.evidence: The input tax is a debit to VAT control because it reduces what's owed to HMRC.

cards.front: Bank statement says 'credit': what is it in the client's books?
cards.back: Money in: a debit to Bank
cards.evidence: When a client's statement says "credit", money has come in, which in the client's books is a debit to Bank.

cards.front: Double entry: how should owner's drawings be posted?
cards.back: Dr Drawings, Cr Bank; never to Wages or Sundry expenses
cards.evidence: Drawings are not an expense. Post them to Drawings, never to Wages or Sundry expenses.

cards.front: Incomplete records: definition of mark-up?
cards.back: Gross profit as a percentage of cost
cards.evidence: - Mark-up is gross profit as a percentage of cost.

cards.front: Incomplete records: definition of margin?
cards.back: Gross profit as a percentage of sales
cards.evidence: - Margin is gross profit as a percentage of sales.

cards.front: Incomplete records: formula to convert mark-up to margin?
cards.back: Margin = mark-up ÷ (1 + mark-up)
cards.evidence: Converting between them: Margin = mark-up ÷ (1 + mark-up). Mark-up = margin ÷ (1 − margin).

cards.front: Incomplete records: what does a 25% margin equal as a mark-up?
cards.back: 33⅓% mark-up
cards.evidence: So 50% mark-up = 33⅓% margin; 25% margin = 33⅓% mark-up.

cards.front: Incomplete records: net assets formula for profit?
cards.back: Closing net assets − opening net assets + drawings − capital introduced
cards.evidence: Profit = closing net assets − opening net assets + drawings − capital introduced

cards.front: Self-employed record keeping: minimum retention period?
cards.back: At least 5 years after the 31 January submission deadline for the tax year
cards.evidence: Self-employed people must keep records of all sales and income and all business expenses, and keep them for at least 5 years after the 31 January submission deadline for the tax year.

cards.front: Incomplete records: formula for credit purchases?
cards.back: Payments to suppliers + closing payables − opening payables (+ discounts received)
cards.evidence: Credit purchases = payments to suppliers + closing payables − opening payables (+ discounts received)

cards.front: Corporation tax FY2026: main rate and small profits rate?
cards.back: Main rate 25% (profits over £250,000); small profits rate 19% (up to £50,000)
cards.evidence: For the financial year 2026 (starting 1 April 2026) the main rate is 25% for profits over £250,000 and the small profits rate is 19% for profits up to £50,000, with marginal relief in between.

cards.front: Private company: deadline to file accounts at Companies House?
cards.back: 9 months after the year end
cards.evidence: - Accounts to Companies House: 9 months after the year end for a private company (first accounts: 21 months from incorporation, or 3 months from the accounting reference date if later).

cards.front: Corporation tax payment deadline for most small companies?
cards.back: 9 months and 1 day after the end of the accounting period
cards.evidence: - Corporation tax payment: for most small companies, 9 months and 1 day after the end of the accounting period.

cards.front: CT600 company tax return: filing deadline?
cards.back: 12 months after the end of the accounting period
cards.evidence: - Company tax return (CT600): 12 months after the end of the accounting period.

cards.front: Company size: micro-entity thresholds (meet 2 of 3)?
cards.back: Turnover ≤ £1m; balance sheet total ≤ £500,000; ≤ 10 employees
cards.evidence: Size: Micro-entity; Must meet at least 2 of: Turnover ≤ £1m; balance sheet total ≤ £500,000; ≤ 10 employees; Usual framework: FRS 105 (very limited disclosures).

cards.front: Company size: small company thresholds (meet 2 of 3)?
cards.back: Turnover ≤ £15m; balance sheet total ≤ £7.5m; ≤ 50 employees
cards.evidence: Size: Small; Must meet at least 2 of: Turnover ≤ £15m; balance sheet total ≤ £7.5m; ≤ 50 employees; Usual framework: FRS 102 section 1A.

cards.front: Companies Act 2006 s830: what can dividends be paid out of?
cards.back: Accumulated realised profits less accumulated realised losses
cards.evidence: A company may only make a distribution (such as a dividend) out of profits available for the purpose (Companies Act 2006 s830): broadly, accumulated realised profits less accumulated realised losses.

cards.front: FRS 102 s13: how are inventories measured?
cards.back: At the lower of cost and net realisable value (NRV)
cards.evidence: Under FRS 102 section 13, inventories are measured at the lower of cost and estimated selling price less costs to complete and sell (net realisable value, NRV).

cards.front: Inventory: which cost-flow methods are permitted, and which is not?
cards.back: FIFO and weighted average permitted; LIFO not permitted
cards.evidence: LIFO is not permitted; FIFO and weighted average are.

cards.front: Inventory valuation: at what level is the cost vs NRV comparison made?
cards.back: Item by item (or groups of similar items), not stock as a whole
cards.evidence: The comparison is made item by item (or for groups of similar items), not for the stock as a whole.

cards.front: Cost of sales formula?
cards.back: Opening inventory + purchases − closing inventory
cards.evidence: Cost of sales = opening inventory + purchases − closing inventory

cards.front: Inventory cost: are carriage inwards and carriage outwards included?
cards.back: Carriage inwards yes; carriage outwards no (a selling cost)
cards.evidence: Cost: Carriage outwards (delivery to customers); Include?: No; Why: A selling cost.

cards.front: Inventory cost: is recoverable VAT included?
cards.back: No; it is reclaimed from HMRC
cards.evidence: Cost: Recoverable VAT; Include?: No; Why: Reclaimed from HMRC.

cards.front: FIFO: how is closing stock valued?
cards.back: At the most recent prices
cards.evidence: FIFO (first in, first out): the oldest stock is assumed to be sold first, so closing stock is valued at the most recent prices.

cards.front: VAT bad debt relief: where is the claim made on the VAT return?
cards.back: Box 4, for the period in which the conditions are first met
cards.evidence: The relief is claimed by including the VAT in box 4 of the return for the period in which the conditions are first met.

cards.front: VAT bad debt relief: can a cash accounting scheme client claim it?
cards.back: No - no output VAT was ever paid on the unpaid invoice
cards.evidence: Clients on the cash accounting scheme never paid the output VAT on an unpaid invoice, so there is no bad debt relief to claim.

cards.front: Income tax: is a general provision (e.g. 2% of all debtors) deductible?
cards.back: No - HMRC does not allow general provisions (BIM42701)
cards.evidence: HMRC does not allow a general provision (such as 2% of all debtors) that ignores the circumstances of particular debtors (BIM42701).

cards.front: Accounting entry for an increase in the allowance for doubtful debts?
cards.back: Dr Irrecoverable debts expense, Cr Allowance for doubtful debts
cards.evidence: - Increase in the allowance: Dr Irrecoverable debts expense, Cr Allowance for doubtful debts

cards.front: Debt recovered after VAT bad debt relief claimed: VAT treatment?
cards.back: Repay the corresponding VAT to HMRC as output tax
cards.evidence: If VAT bad debt relief was claimed, the corresponding VAT must be repaid to HMRC as output tax.

cards.front: Partnership Act 1890 s24: default profit and loss sharing?
cards.back: Equally between partners (and losses contributed equally)
cards.evidence: Partners share capital and profits equally, and contribute equally to losses.

cards.front: Partnership Act 1890 s24: default interest on a partner's advance beyond agreed capital?
cards.back: 5% a year
cards.evidence: A partner who advances money beyond their agreed capital is entitled to interest at 5% a year on it.

cards.front: Partnership Act 1890 s24: default interest on capital and partner salary?
cards.back: No interest on capital; no salary
cards.evidence: No interest on capital.

cards.front: Partnership: how is a partner's 'salary' treated in the accounts?
cards.back: Allocation of profit in the appropriation account, not an expense or payroll
cards.evidence: It goes in the appropriation account, never the income statement, and never through payroll.

cards.front: Partnership: how are monthly payments to a partner treated?
cards.back: As drawings
cards.evidence: If a partner is paid monthly, the payments are drawings.

cards.front: Partnership: how is interest on a partner's loan to the firm treated?
cards.back: Normally an expense in arriving at profit
cards.evidence: Interest on a partner's loan to the firm (as opposed to their capital) is normally treated as an expense in arriving at profit.

cards.front: Partnership: formula for a partner's total profit share?
cards.back: Salary + interest on capital + share of residual − interest on drawings
cards.evidence: A partner's total share = salary + interest on capital + share of residual − interest on drawings.

cards.front: Partnership: what does a debit balance on a current account mean?
cards.back: The partner has drawn more than their share
cards.evidence: Credit; a debit balance means the partner has drawn more than their share.

cards.front: Sole trader accounts: cost of sales formula?
cards.back: Opening inventory + purchases + carriage inwards − closing inventory
cards.evidence: Line: Cost of sales; How it's made up: Opening inventory + purchases + carriage inwards − closing inventory.

cards.front: Sole trader: capital account reconciliation formula?
cards.back: Opening capital + capital introduced + net profit − drawings = closing capital (equals net assets)
cards.evidence: Section: Capital; Includes: Opening capital + capital introduced + net profit − drawings = closing capital (equals net assets).

cards.front: Are drawings an expense in a sole trader's income statement?
cards.back: No; they reduce capital in the balance sheet
cards.evidence: Drawings are never an expense. They reduce capital in the balance sheet.

cards.front: Sole trader: how to record goods taken for own use?
cards.back: At cost: Dr Drawings, Cr Purchases
cards.evidence: Goods taken for own use are drawings at cost: Dr Drawings, Cr Purchases.

cards.front: Accounts adjustment: effect of a prepayment?
cards.back: Reduces expense in the income statement; current asset in the balance sheet
cards.evidence: | Prepayment | Reduces expense | Current asset |

cards.front: Accounts adjustment: effect of an accrual?
cards.back: Increases expense; current liability in the balance sheet
cards.evidence: | Accrual | Increases expense | Current liability |

cards.front: Sole trader: who uses the cash basis as standard since 2024/25?
cards.back: Sole traders and partnerships without corporate partners, unless they opt out for accruals
cards.evidence: Since 2024/25 the cash basis is the standard method for sole traders and partnerships without corporate partners, unless they opt out and use the accruals basis.

cards.front: Sole trader: private use of a business cost, accounting entry?
cards.back: Reduce expenses and increase drawings
cards.evidence: | Private use of a business cost | Reduces expense | Increases drawings |

cards.front: Suspense account: which side if debits exceed credits on the TB?
cards.back: Credit (e.g. £1,190 credit if debits exceed credits by £1,190)
cards.evidence: If debits exceed credits by £1,190, suspense is a credit of £1,190.

cards.front: Correcting errors: does an error of principle go through suspense?
cards.back: No, the TB is unaffected so suspense isn't used
cards.evidence: Original error: Omission, commission, principle, original entry, complete reversal, compensating; TB affected?: No; Suspense in correction?: No.

cards.front: Correcting journal: how to correct a single-sided entry?
cards.back: Yes, the correction goes through suspense
cards.evidence: Original error: Single-sided entry; TB affected?: Yes; Suspense in correction?: Yes.

cards.front: Correcting a complete reversal: what amount is the correcting journal?
cards.back: Double the original amount
cards.evidence: - Correction: Dr Insurance £1,200, Cr Bank £1,200 (double the amount: once to cancel, once to post correctly).

cards.front: Which corrections change profit?
cards.back: Only those touching an income or expense account
cards.evidence: Only corrections that touch an income or expense account change profit:

cards.front: Can you clear a small residual suspense balance to sundry expenses?
cards.back: No; if unexplained, agree treatment with manager and record why
cards.evidence: Never write off suspense: Clearing a residual suspense balance to sundry expenses "because it's small" hides errors that might be much bigger and offsetting.

cards.front: FRS 102 s10: how are material prior period errors corrected?
cards.back: Retrospectively, by restating comparatives
cards.evidence: Under FRS 102 section 10, material prior period errors are corrected retrospectively by restating comparatives.

cards.front: Trial balance: what does a balanced TB prove?
cards.back: Only that total debits equal total credits
cards.evidence: What a balanced trial balance proves: Only that total debits equal total credits.

cards.front: TB difference: what does a difference divisible by 9 suggest?
cards.back: A transposition or a misplaced decimal point
cards.evidence: 3. Divide by 9. If the difference divides exactly by 9, look for a transposition (digits swapped: 780 written as 870 gives 90) or a misplaced decimal point (£250 typed as £25 gives £225).

cards.front: TB difference: what quick test spots an item in the wrong column?
cards.back: Halve the difference
cards.evidence: 2. Halve it. If a £310 item was put in the wrong column, the difference is £620.

cards.front: Where is a TB difference put while you investigate it?
cards.back: A suspense account (temporarily)
cards.evidence: When the TB doesn't balance, the difference is put to a suspense account temporarily while you investigate.

cards.front: Error of principle: definition?
cards.back: Wrong type of account used (e.g. van repair posted to an asset)
cards.evidence: Error: Principle; What happened: Wrong type of account; Example: Van repair posted to Motor vehicles – cost (an asset).

cards.front: Error of commission: definition?
cards.back: Right type of account, but the wrong account
cards.evidence: Error: Commission; What happened: Right type of account, wrong account; Example: Sale to J Smyth posted to J Smith's account.

cards.front: Which six errors do NOT stop a TB balancing?
cards.back: Omission, commission, principle, original entry, complete reversal, compensating
cards.evidence: Error: Omission; What happened: Transaction not recorded at all; Example: A supplier invoice left in a drawer.

cards.front: IR35: employer NIC rate and threshold since April 2025?
cards.back: 15% from a £5,000 threshold
cards.evidence: The rate changes since April 2025 (employer NIC at 15% from a £5,000 threshold, and dividend rates up by 2 percentage points from April 2026) have reduced, but not removed, the advantage of working outside IR35 through a company.

cards.front: Dividend rates change from April 2026?
cards.back: Up by 2 percentage points
cards.evidence: The rate changes since April 2025 (employer NIC at 15% from a £5,000 threshold, and dividend rates up by 2 percentage points from April 2026) have reduced, but not removed, the advantage of working outside IR35 through a company.

cards.front: IR35 contractor advice: what are the four parts of a sound answer?
cards.back: Status analysis, numbers per structure, genuine options, written record of advice
cards.evidence: A sound answer has four parts: (1) the status analysis, (2) the numbers under each structure, (3) practical options that are genuine, and (4) a written record of the advice.

cards.front: IR35: if the contractor disputes an SDS, which process can they use?
cards.back: The 45-day process
cards.evidence: If he disagrees, he can use the 45-day process, but the facts favour Tallis.

cards.front: IR35: options if an engagement is inside IR35?
cards.back: Accept it, renegotiate the rate, move to an umbrella, or end the engagement

cards.front: IR35 Ch8 deemed payment: step 1 flat allowance for PSC running costs?

cards.front: Employment status: Ready Mixed Concrete – what are the three stages of the test?
