cards.front: Employment status: are personal service, control and mutuality enough to make someone an employee?
cards.back: No – necessary but not sufficient; stage 3 is an overall assessment of all the facts
cards.evidence: Stages 1 and 2 (together with mutuality of obligation: an obligation to provide work and an obligation to do it) are necessary but not sufficient. If they're met, stage 3 is an overall assessment of all the facts.

cards.front: Autoclenz v Belcher [2011] UKSC 41: what principle does it establish?
cards.back: Courts find the true agreement where written terms don't reflect reality, considering relative bargaining power
cards.evidence: In Autoclenz Ltd v Belcher [2011] UKSC 41 the Supreme Court said that where the written terms don't reflect what the parties actually agreed and did, the court should find the true agreement, taking account of the relative bargaining power of the parties.

cards.front: PGMOL v HMRC [2024] UKSC 29: what did the Supreme Court hold on mutuality and control?
cards.back: Both present in each match engagement, but necessary not sufficient; sent back to FTT for overall assessment
cards.evidence: The Supreme Court held that mutuality of obligation and control were present in each individual match engagement: the framework of obligations, code of conduct, assessments and sanctions gave sufficient control, even though PGMOL did not tell referees how to apply the laws of the game.

cards.front: Atholl House [2022] EWCA Civ 501: was there a presumption of employment once control and mutuality were found?
cards.back: No – the assessment is wide and multi-factorial; HMRC lost on its main ground
cards.evidence: The Court of Appeal rejected that approach: the assessment is a wide, multi-factorial one, and a person who is genuinely in business on their own account (the Hall v Lorimer idea) can fall outside employment even where there is personal service and some control.

cards.front: Employment status: what are the three different 'status' questions?

cards.front: IR35 Ch10: who is the fee-payer in a client → agency → PSC chain?
cards.back: The agency (the party closest to and paying the intermediary)

cards.front: IR35 Ch10: how must the fee-payer flag the worker on RTI?

cards.front: IR35 Ch10: which NIC earnings period applies to a director-worker?

cards.back: April 2017 (public sector); April 2021 (private sector)
cards.evidence: Since April 2017 (public sector) and April 2021 (private sector), the off-payroll working rules have moved the responsibility for deciding status to the client in many cases.

cards.front: IR35 Chapter 8: allowance in the deemed payment calculation?
cards.back: 5% allowance on the PSC's receipts, plus deductions
cards.evidence: Amount charged; Chapter 8 (intermediaries legislation, 'IR35'): A deemed payment calculated on the PSC's receipts with a 5% allowance and deductions; Chapter 10 (off-payroll working rules): The fee-payer's payment to the PSC, less VAT and (in some cases) expenses.

cards.front: IR35 Chapter 8: when does the PSC account for the deemed employment payment?
cards.back: At 5 April
cards.evidence: Who accounts for tax and NIC; Chapter 8 (intermediaries legislation, 'IR35'): The PSC, through a deemed employment payment at 5 April; Chapter 10 (off-payroll working rules): The fee-payer (client or agency), through deemed direct payments each time the worker is paid.

cards.front: MSC: how many s61B(1) conditions must be met for a company to be an MSC?

cards.front: MSC rules: which ITEPA 2003 provisions contain them?
cards.back: ITEPA 2003 Part 2 Chapter 9 (ss61A–61J)

cards.back: Agency or end client, jointly and severally with the umbrella

cards.back: The end client
cards.evidence: If no agency is involved, the end client is liable.

cards.back: £50,270 a year (0% employer NIC up to it, 15% above)

cards.front: NIC category letter for an apprentice under 25 on an approved apprenticeship?
cards.back: H
cards.evidence: Letter: H; Who: Apprentice under 25 on an approved apprenticeship; Employee NIC: Same as A; Employer NIC: 0% up to the AUST (£50,270), 15% above.

cards.front: NIC category V: who qualifies and for how long?
cards.back: Veteran in first 12 months of civilian employment
cards.evidence: Letter: V; Who: Veteran in their first 12 months of civilian employment since leaving the armed forces; Employee NIC: Same as A; Employer NIC: 0% up to the VUST (£50,270), 15% above.

cards.front: NIC category C: employee and employer NIC treatment?
cards.back: Over State Pension age: no employee NIC; employer 15% above ST
cards.evidence: Letter: C; Who: Over State Pension age; Employee NIC: None; Employer NIC: 15% above ST, as for A.

cards.front: Employment Allowance: how is it claimed?
cards.back: On the EPS, setting the Employment Allowance indicator to "Yes"
cards.evidence: Claiming: Claim on the EPS by setting the Employment Allowance indicator to "Yes".

cards.front: Employment Allowance: how many years back can past claims go?
cards.back: Up to 4 years
cards.evidence: Claims for previous years (up to 4 years back) involve a state aid declaration, because for earlier years EA counted as de minimis state aid for some sectors.

cards.front: Freeport categories F, I, L, S: employer NIC treatment?
cards.back: 0% up to £25,000 (FUST), 15% above
cards.evidence: Letter: F, I, L, S; Who: Freeport employees (eligible employer, special tax site); Employee NIC: Varies by letter; Employer NIC: 0% up to the FUST (£25,000), 15% above.

cards.front: RTI: when must the FPS be sent?
cards.back: On or before the date employees are paid (contractual payday)
cards.evidence: Send the FPS on or before the date employees are paid, the contractual payday, not the date the software is run.

cards.front: RTI: EPS deadline to affect that month's PAYE bill?
cards.back: By the 19th of the following tax month
cards.evidence: What goes on an EPS (send by the 19th of the following tax month to affect that month's bill)

cards.front: PAYE: monthly payment deadline if paying electronically?
cards.back: 22nd after the end of the tax month (19th if by cheque)
cards.evidence: - Monthly: by the 22nd after the end of the tax month if paying electronically (e.g. 22 June for tax month 2, 6 May to 5 June); by the 19th if paying by cheque through the post.

cards.front: PAYE: when can an employer pay quarterly?
cards.back: Average monthly payments reasonably expected under £1,500
cards.evidence: - Quarterly: allowed if the employer reasonably expects its average monthly payments to be under £1,500.

cards.front: PAYE: late payment penalty rates by number of defaults?
cards.back: 1-3: 1%; 4-6: 2%; 7-9: 3%; 10+: 4% (first late payment not a default)
cards.evidence: The first late payment doesn't count as a default. Then the penalty is 1% of the late amounts for 1–3 defaults, 2% for 4–6, 3% for 7–9 and 4% for 10 or more.

cards.front: RTI: FPS deadline for casual staff under £96 a week with no P45?
cards.back: Within 7 days of paying
cards.evidence: - Pay that genuinely can't be calculated in advance (e.g. piecework) and casual staff paid under £96 a week with no P45: within 7 days of paying.

cards.front: PAYE: how early can you register before you first pay staff?
cards.back: No more than 2 months before you start paying people
cards.evidence: - You cannot register more than 2 months before you start paying people.

cards.front: Employer NIC 2026/27: rate and secondary threshold?
cards.back: 15% above £5,000 a year (£417 a month)
cards.evidence: - Employer (secondary) Class 1 NIC at 15% on earnings above the secondary threshold of £5,000 a year (£417 a month) for 2026/27.

cards.front: Auto-enrolment: minimum employer contribution and qualifying earnings band?
cards.back: 3% of earnings between £6,240 and £50,270 a year
cards.evidence: - Employer pension contribution — at least 3% of qualifying earnings (earnings between £6,240 and £50,270 a year) for an auto-enrolled worker.

cards.front: Employment Allowance 2026/27: maximum annual amount?
cards.back: Up to £10,500 a year
cards.evidence: The Employment Allowance (up to £10,500 a year for 2026/27) can wipe out employer NIC for many small employers — but not for a company whose only employee is a sole director.

cards.front: PAYE: late-reporting reason if paid before the PAYE reference arrives?
cards.back: Reason G
cards.evidence: If staff have to be paid before the PAYE reference comes through, run the payroll as normal, store the FPS, and send it as soon as the reference arrives, using late-reporting reason G.

cards.front: Payroll: starter checklist statement A gives which starting code?
cards.back: 1257L, cumulative
cards.evidence: Statement: A; The employee says…: This is my first job since 6 April. I've not had taxable Jobseeker's Allowance, ESA, Incapacity Benefit, or a state or occupational pension; Starting code: 1257L, cumulative.

cards.front: Payroll: starter checklist statement B gives which starting code?
cards.back: 1257L week 1/month 1
cards.evidence: Statement: B; The employee says…: This is now my only job, but since 6 April I've had another job or one of those benefits. I don't receive a state or occupational pension; Starting code: 1257L week 1/month 1.

cards.front: Payroll: starter checklist statement C gives which starting code?
cards.back: BR, cumulative
cards.evidence: Statement: C; The employee says…: I have another job, or I receive a state or occupational pension; Starting code: BR, cumulative.

cards.front: Payroll: starting code if no starter statement is ticked or form not returned?
cards.back: 0T week 1/month 1
cards.evidence: Statement: No statement ticked / form not returned; The employee says…: ; Starting code: 0T week 1/month 1.

cards.front: Payroll: maximum tax deducted under a K code in a pay period?
cards.back: 50% of the employee's pay for that period
cards.evidence: Overriding limit: tax deducted under a K code in any pay period can't exceed 50% of the employee's pay for that period.

cards.front: Payroll: how long to keep starter checklist or P45 records?
cards.back: Current tax year plus 3 more tax years
cards.evidence: Keep the starter checklist or P45 with the payroll records for the current year plus 3 more tax years.

cards.front: Payroll: Scottish flat-rate codes SBR, SD0, SD1, SD2, SD3 rates for 2026/27?
cards.evidence: Scottish flat-rate codes are SBR (20%), SD0 (21%), SD1 (42%), SD2 (45%) and SD3 (48%).

cards.front: SSP: maximum period payable in a linked period?
cards.back: 28 weeks
cards.evidence: Rule: Maximum; Before 6 April 2026: 28 weeks; From 6 April 2026: 28 weeks.

cards.front: SSP: when do two periods of sickness link?
cards.back: If they are 8 weeks or less apart
cards.evidence: Two periods of sickness link if they're 8 weeks or less apart.

cards.front: SSP: how long must employers keep SSP records and evidence?
cards.back: 3 years after the tax year
cards.evidence: Keep records of SSP paid and the evidence for 3 years after the tax year.

cards.front: SSP1: when must it be issued if SSP is going to run out?
cards.back: By the beginning of the 23rd week
cards.evidence: If an employee doesn't qualify, or their SSP will end while they're still sick, the employer gives them form SSP1: within 7 days of the first day off sick if they don't qualify, or by the beginning of the 23rd week if SSP is going to run out.

cards.front: SSP from April 2026: waiting days and earnings test?
cards.back: No waiting days; no lower earnings limit test
cards.evidence: If you learned SSP before then, unlearn two things: there are no waiting days, and there's no lower earnings limit test.

cards.front: Student loan 2026/27: Plan 5 monthly threshold and rate?
cards.evidence: Plan: Plan 5; Who typically has it: English students starting from Aug 2023 (repayments from April 2026); Annual: £25,000; Monthly: £2,083.33; Weekly: £480.76; Rate: 9%.

cards.front: Postgraduate loan 2026/27: annual threshold and deduction rate?
cards.evidence: Plan: Postgraduate loan (PGL); Who typically has it: Master's or doctoral loans (England and Wales); Annual: £21,000; Monthly: £1,750.00; Weekly: £403.84; Rate: 6%.

cards.front: Student loan 2026/27: Plan 4 monthly threshold and who has it?
cards.back: £2,816.25 a month (£33,795 a year); Scottish students
cards.evidence: Plan: Plan 4; Who typically has it: Scottish students; Annual: £33,795; Monthly: £2,816.25; Weekly: £649.90; Rate: 9%.

cards.front: Student loan: how is the calculated deduction rounded?
cards.back: Round down to the whole pound
cards.evidence: 4. Round down to the whole pound.

cards.front: Student loan: when can an employer stop deductions?
cards.back: Only on HMRC stop notice (SL2 or PGL2), or when the employee leaves
cards.evidence: Stop deductions only when HMRC sends a stop notice (SL2 or PGL2), or the employee leaves.

cards.front: Student loan: how are two student loan plans deducted?
cards.back: One 9% deduction using the lowest threshold of the plans
cards.evidence: Two student loan plans (e.g. Plan 1 and Plan 2): the employer deducts one 9% deduction using the lowest threshold of the plans, and the SLC allocates it between the loans.

cards.front: Termination payments: Class 1A NIC rate and base?
cards.back: 15% on the s401 excess over £30,000
cards.evidence: 5. Class 1A NIC at 15% on the s401 excess over £30,000, reported through RTI and paid with the PAYE for the month in which the termination payment was made, not on the P11D(b) in July.

cards.front: Termination payments: how and when is Class 1A paid?
cards.back: Via RTI, with PAYE for the month of payment, not on the P11D(b)
cards.evidence: 5. Class 1A NIC at 15% on the s401 excess over £30,000, reported through RTI and paid with the PAYE for the month in which the termination payment was made, not on the P11D(b) in July.

cards.front: PENP formula (ITEPA 2003 s402D)?
cards.back: PENP = (BP × D ÷ P) − T
cards.evidence: The PENP formula (ITEPA 2003 s402D): PENP = (BP × D ÷ P) − T

cards.front: Termination payment made after the P45 is issued: how is tax operated?
cards.back: Tax with 0T on week 1/month 1 basis; FPS with original leaving date; no new P45
cards.evidence: Paid after the P45 is issued: tax with 0T on a week 1/month 1 basis, report on an FPS with the original leaving date, and don't issue another P45.

cards.front: PENP: what happens if the formula gives a negative result?
cards.back: PENP is nil
cards.evidence: If the formula gives a negative result, PENP is nil, and it can't exceed the total relevant termination award.

cards.front: Annual allowance: standard amount for 2026/27?
Annual allowance: how many previous years can be carried forward?
cards.back: Three tax years (must have been a member of a registered scheme in each)
cards.evidence: An individual can use unused annual allowance from the previous three tax years, provided they were a member of a registered pension scheme in each year they carry forward from.

cards.front: Carry forward: which year is used first after the current year?
cards.back: The earliest of the three years, then the next, then the latest
cards.evidence: Then carry forward from the earliest of the three years first, then the next, then the latest.

cards.front: Annual allowance: when must the pension savings statement be sent?
cards.back: By 6 October following the end of the tax year
cards.evidence: Schemes must send a pension savings statement by 6 October following the end of the tax year to anyone whose inputs exceed the annual allowance.

cards.front: Scheme pays: charge threshold for the member to request it?
cards.back: Charge exceeds £2,000 (and inputs to that scheme exceed the AA)
cards.evidence: The member can ask the scheme to pay it (scheme pays), in return for a reduction in benefits, if the charge exceeds £2,000 and the inputs to that scheme exceed the AA.

cards.front: Pension tax relief: limit on personal contributions relief by earnings?
cards.back: Higher of £3,600 and 100% of relevant earnings
cards.evidence: Relevant earnings still limit personal contributions: the director can only get tax relief on personal contributions up to the higher of £3,600 and 100% of relevant earnings, but employer contributions (which aren't limited by earnings) can use carry forward in full.

cards.front: Annual allowance: how are DB scheme inputs measured?
cards.back: Increase in value of benefits over the year, using a factor of 16 (with adjustments)
cards.evidence: Defined benefit (DB) schemes: the increase in the value of the member's benefits over the year (using a factor of 16, with adjustments).

cards.front: AE 2026/27: annual earnings trigger for automatic enrolment?
cards.back: £10,000 a year (£833 monthly, £192 weekly)
cards.evidence: Measure: Earnings trigger (auto-enrolment); Annual: £10,000; Monthly: £833; Weekly: £192.

cards.front: AE 2026/27: qualifying earnings band annual lower limit?
cards.back: £6,240 a year (£520 monthly, £120 weekly)
cards.evidence: Measure: Lower limit of qualifying earnings band; Annual: £6,240; Monthly: £520; Weekly: £120.

cards.front: AE 2026/27: qualifying earnings band annual upper limit?
cards.back: £50,270 a year (£4,189 monthly, £967 weekly)
cards.evidence: Measure: Upper limit of qualifying earnings band; Annual: £50,270; Monthly: £4,189; Weekly: £967.

cards.front: AE: employer duty for an entitled worker, and their earnings and age?
cards.back: Aged 16–74, earning £6,240 or less: must let them join, no need to contribute
cards.evidence: | Entitled worker | 16–74 | At or below £6,240 | Must let them join a scheme but need not contribute |

cards.front: AE: maximum postponement period for assessment?
cards.back: Up to three months
cards.evidence: Postponement: An employer may postpone assessment for up to three months from the duties start date (or from the date a new worker starts, or when a worker first meets the criteria).

cards.front: AE: deadline to give a postponement notice to the worker?
cards.back: Within six weeks of the postponement start date
cards.evidence: The employer must give the worker a written postponement notice within six weeks of the postponement start date.

cards.front: AE: time employer has to complete enrolment after the enrolment date?
cards.back: Six weeks from the enrolment date
cards.evidence: The employer then has six weeks from that date to complete the process (joining the worker to the scheme and giving the written information), but the worker is treated as an active member from the enrolment date.

cards.front: Auto-enrolment: deadline to submit declaration of compliance to TPR?
cards.back: Within 5 months of the duties start date
cards.evidence: Step: 7. Declare compliance; What to do: Submit the online declaration of compliance to TPR; Timing: Within 5 months of the duties start date.

cards.front: Auto-enrolment: deadline to write to workers after duties start or enrolment date?
cards.back: Within 6 weeks
cards.evidence: Step: 5. Write to workers; What to do: Tell each worker what has happened and their rights; Timing: Within 6 weeks of the duties start date or enrolment date.

cards.front: Auto-enrolment: contributions payment deadline to the scheme?
cards.back: 22nd of following month (19th if by cheque), unless scheme sets earlier
cards.evidence: Timing: By the 22nd of the month following deduction (19th if paying by cheque), unless the scheme sets an earlier date.

cards.front: Auto-enrolment: how often must an employer re-enrol eligible jobholders?
cards.back: Every 3 years, with re-declaration within 5 months
cards.evidence: Step: 8. Re-enrol and re-declare; What to do: Re-enrol eligible jobholders who have opted out or stopped, every 3 years; Timing: Re-enrolment date every 3 years; re-declaration within 5 months of it.

cards.front: Auto-enrolment: when is a director a 'worker'?
cards.back: Has an employment contract and at least one other person also has one with the company
cards.evidence: A director is a "worker" only if they have a contract of employment with the company and at least one other person (who may be another director) also has a contract of employment with it.

cards.front: Auto-enrolment: minimum total contribution and employer/employee split?
cards.back: 8% total: employer 3%, employee 5% of qualifying earnings
cards.evidence: Minimum % of qualifying earnings; Employer: 3%; Employee: 5%; Total: 8%.

cards.front: Auto-enrolment: how long is the opt-out window and when does it start?
cards.back: One month, from the later of becoming an active member and receiving enrolment information
cards.evidence: A worker who has been automatically enrolled (or re-enrolled) has a one-month opt-out period, starting on the later of the date they become an active member and the date they receive the enrolment information.

cards.front: Auto-enrolment: where must a worker get the opt-out notice from?
cards.back: The pension provider, not the employer
cards.evidence: To opt out the worker must give a valid opt-out notice obtained from the pension provider, not from the employer; an employer can't supply a form of its own for this purpose.

cards.front: Auto-enrolment: what happens to contributions if a worker opts out within the window?
cards.back: Treated as never joined; employee refunded (normally within one month), employer's contributions returned
cards.evidence: If the worker opts out within the window, they are treated as if they had never joined: the employee's contributions are refunded (normally within one month) and the employer's contributions are returned to the employer.

cards.front: Auto-enrolment: earnings range for a non-eligible jobholder who can opt in?
cards.back: Between £6,240 and £10,000 (employer must pay the 3% minimum)
cards.evidence: A non-eligible jobholder (16–21, or State Pension age to 74, or earning between £6,240 and £10,000) can give an opt-in notice; the employer must enrol them and pay the 3% minimum.

cards.front: Auto-enrolment: entitled worker earnings level and employer contribution duty?
cards.back: Earnings £6,240 or less; employer must provide a scheme but needn't contribute
cards.evidence: An entitled worker (earnings £6,240 or less) can ask to join; the employer must put them in a scheme but doesn't have to contribute.

cards.front: Pensions 2026/27: lump sum allowance (LSA) amount?
cards.evidence: Allowance: Lump sum allowance (LSA); Amount: £268,275; What it limits: Total tax-free lump sums a person can take from all schemes in their lifetime (mainly the 25% pension commencement lump sum and the tax-free part of UFPLS).

cards.front: Pensions 2026/27: lump sum and death benefit allowance (LSDBA) amount?
cards.evidence: Allowance: Lump sum and death benefit allowance (LSDBA); Amount: £1,073,100; What it limits: Total tax-free lump sums taken during life plus tax-free lump sum death benefits paid to beneficiaries.

cards.front: Pensions: overseas transfer allowance (OTA) amount and what it covers?
cards.back: £1,073,100; transfers to QROPS free of overseas transfer charge
cards.evidence: Allowance: Overseas transfer allowance (OTA); Amount: £1,073,100; What it limits: Transfers to qualifying recognised overseas pension schemes (QROPS) free of the overseas transfer charge.

cards.front: Pensions: how is a UFPLS taxed?
cards.back: 25% tax-free (subject to LSA); 75% taxed as pension income at marginal rate
cards.evidence: - An uncrystallised funds pension lump sum (UFPLS) is paid with 25% tax-free (subject to the LSA) and 75% taxable as pension income at the person's marginal rate.

cards.front: Pensions: death before 75, lump sum tax-free if paid within what time?
cards.back: Within two years of the administrator being told of the death, up to the LSDBA
cards.evidence: - Before age 75: a lump sum death benefit paid within two years of the scheme administrator being told of the death is normally tax-free, up to the LSDBA (less lump sums already used).

cards.front: Pensions: which flexible access triggers the MPAA, and what is its amount?
cards.back: UFPLS or flexi-access drawdown income; £10,000
cards.evidence: A UFPLS or flexi-access drawdown income triggers the MPAA (£10,000).

cards.front: Pensions: HMRC repayment forms for tax overpaid on first withdrawal?
cards.back: P55, P53Z or P50Z (or online claim)
cards.evidence: A first taxable withdrawal is often taxed on a month 1 basis, so the client may be over-taxed and have to reclaim through the relevant HMRC repayment form (P55, P53Z or P50Z) or the online claim.

cards.front: Pension tax relief: limit on personal contributions getting relief?
cards.back: Higher of 100% of relevant UK earnings and £3,600 gross (£2,880 net)
cards.evidence: Personal (employee) contributions get tax relief up to the higher of 100% of relevant UK earnings for the year and £3,600 gross (£2,880 net) if the individual has little or no earnings.

cards.front: Pensions: annual allowance for 2026/27?
cards.evidence: Employer contributions aren't limited by earnings but by the annual allowance (£60,000 for 2026/27, see later lessons).

cards.front: Relief at source: how much does the employee pay and what does the provider claim?
cards.back: Employee pays 80% of gross; provider claims 20% from HMRC
cards.evidence: Relief at source (RAS): Employee pays 80% of the gross contribution from net pay; the provider claims 20% from HMRC.

cards.front: Net pay arrangement: how is the contribution deducted in payroll?
cards.back: From gross pay before calculating PAYE
cards.evidence: How it works; Net pay arrangement: Employer deducts the contribution from gross pay before calculating PAYE;

cards.front: RAS: extra relief a higher-rate (40%) and additional-rate (45%) taxpayer must claim?
cards.back: 20% more at 40%; 25% more at 45%
cards.evidence: A higher-rate taxpayer must claim the additional relief (20% more at 40%, 25% more at 45%) by Self Assessment (box on the return) or by asking HMRC to adjust the tax code.

cards.front: IHT & pensions: date from which unused pension funds fall into the estate?
cards.back: Deaths on or after 6 April 2027
cards.evidence: From deaths on or after 6 April 2027 most unused pension funds and death benefits fall into the estate for inheritance tax.

cards.front: IHT: rate charged on taxable estate above NRB and RNRB?
cards.evidence: - IHT is charged at 40% on the part of the taxable estate above the available nil-rate band and residence nil-rate band (and the RNRB taper for estates over £2 million, which now catches pension funds too).

cards.front: IHT: RNRB taper applies to estates over what value?
cards.back: £2 million
cards.evidence: - IHT is charged at 40% on the part of the taxable estate above the available nil-rate band and residence nil-rate band (and the RNRB taper for estates over £2 million, which now catches pension funds too).

cards.front: Do BPR and APR apply to pension funds in the estate?
cards.back: No, neither applies
cards.evidence: - Business Property Relief and Agricultural Property Relief do not apply to pension funds.

cards.front: Pensions: LSDBA amount?
cards.evidence: The LSDBA (£1,073,100) governs the income tax treatment of lump sum death benefits (tax-free to a point for deaths before 75).

cards.front: Pensions 2026/27: annual allowance?
cards.back: £60,000 (plus carry forward)
cards.evidence: Limit for tax relief; Employer contribution: Annual allowance (£60,000 in 2026/27, plus carry forward); deduction subject to wholly and exclusively; Personal contribution: Higher of 100% of relevant UK earnings and £3,600 gross, and within the annual allowance.

cards.front: Pensions: which income is not relevant UK earnings?
cards.back: Dividends, interest and rental income
cards.evidence: Dividends, interest and rental income are not relevant earnings.

cards.front: Employer v personal pension contribution: corporation tax relief?
cards.back: Employer: yes, on the company. Personal: no.
cards.evidence: Corporation tax relief; Employer contribution: Yes, on the company; Personal contribution: No.

cards.front: Pensions: what happens if inputs exceed the annual allowance with no carry forward?
cards.back: An annual allowance charge arises on the member
cards.evidence: If total inputs (personal + employer) exceed the annual allowance and no carry forward is available, an annual allowance charge arises on the member.

cards.front: Auto-enrolment: duties for a sole director?
cards.back: None; a sole director never has AE duties
cards.evidence: A sole director never has AE duties.

cards.front: Employer pension for a family member: when is it likely disallowed?
cards.back: When the family member does little or no work (salary too)
cards.evidence: A pension paid for a family member who does little or no work is likely to be disallowed (and the salary too).

cards.front: Salary sacrifice pension: NIC cap from 6 April 2029?
cards.back: Only the first £2,000 a year is NIC-exempt (employee and employer)
cards.evidence: From 6 April 2029 only the first £2,000 a year of employee pension contributions made through salary sacrifice will be exempt from NIC (employee and employer).

cards.front: Salary sacrifice: income tax relief on contributions above the £2,000 cap from 2029?
cards.back: Still get income tax relief, but NIC is due
cards.evidence: Contributions above £2,000 will be treated for NIC like ordinary employee contributions (NIC still due), though they will still get income tax relief.

cards.front: Auto-enrolment: minimum total contribution and minimum employer share?
cards.back: Total at least 8%, employer at least 3%
cards.evidence: The employer must meet the minimum contribution requirement (the total must be at least 8% with the employer paying at least 3%) based on the scheme's earnings definition, and records must show how.

cards.front: Auto-enrolment: earnings trigger relevant after salary sacrifice?
cards.evidence: A worker could drop below the £10,000 trigger or the qualifying band after sacrifice.

cards.front: Pensions annual allowance for 2026/27?
cards.evidence: Employer contributions are subject to the annual allowance (£60,000 for 2026/27) like any other pension input.

cards.front: Salary sacrifice: income levels where reduced adjusted net income matters?
cards.evidence: Student loan repayments and Child Benefit High Income Charge/personal allowance taper are based on income after the sacrifice, which can be a benefit: sacrificing salary can reduce adjusted net income (relevant at £60,000 and £100,000).

cards.front: Salary sacrifice: what if the arrangement is not valid?
cards.back: Tax and NIC due on full original pay; treated as employee contribution
cards.evidence: If the arrangement is not valid, tax and NIC are due on the full original pay and the contribution is treated as an employee contribution.

cards.front: Pension annual allowance taper 2026/27: two income tests?
cards.back: Threshold income over £200,000 and adjusted income over £260,000
cards.evidence:
1. Threshold income is over £200,000, and
2. Adjusted income is over £260,000.

cards.front: Tapered annual allowance 2026/27: rate of reduction?
cards.back: £1 for every £2 of adjusted income over £260,000
cards.evidence: For every £2 by which adjusted income exceeds £260,000, the annual allowance falls by £1, down to a minimum of £10,000 (reached at adjusted income of £360,000 or more).

cards.front: Tapered annual allowance 2026/27: minimum and the income at which it is reached?
cards.back: £10,000, at adjusted income of £360,000 or more
cards.evidence: For every £2 by which adjusted income exceeds £260,000, the annual allowance falls by £1, down to a minimum of £10,000 (reached at adjusted income of £360,000 or more).

cards.front: Money purchase annual allowance (MPAA) 2026/27: amount?
cards.evidence: The MPAA is £10,000 for 2026/27.

cards.front: MPAA: deadline to tell other schemes after flexible access statement?
cards.back: Within 91 days of receiving the statement
cards.evidence: The member must tell every other scheme they are contributing to within 91 days of receiving the flexible access statement from the provider.

cards.front: MPAA triggered: alternative annual allowance for DB inputs?
cards.evidence: DB inputs have a separate alternative annual allowance (£50,000);

cards.front: Can unused MPAA be carried forward, or carry forward cover an MPAA excess?
cards.back: No to both
cards.evidence: Unused MPAA cannot be carried forward, and carry forward cannot be used to cover an MPAA excess;

cards.front: Auto-enrolment: amount of TPR fixed penalty notice (FPN)?
cards.evidence: Step: Fixed penalty notice (FPN); What it is: A £400 fine; Typical trigger: Failure to comply with a compliance or unpaid contributions notice, or other breach.

cards.front: TPR escalating penalty: daily rate for 50–249 workers?
cards.back: £2,500 per day

cards.front: TPR escalating penalty: daily rate for 250–499 workers?
cards.back: £5,000 per day

cards.front: TPR escalating penalty: daily rate for 500 or more workers?
cards.back: £10,000 per day

cards.front: Which tribunal hears appeals against TPR notices after review?
cards.back: First-tier Tribunal (General Regulatory Chamber)
cards.evidence: An employer can apply for a review of a notice by TPR within the time limit stated in the notice, and then appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (General Regulatory Chamber) if the review doesn't resolve it.

cards.front: TPR notice under review or appeal: does it stay in force?
cards.back: Yes, unless TPR suspends it
cards.evidence: A notice stays in force while the review or appeal is under way, unless TPR suspends it.

cards.front: SA: deadline for taxpayer to amend a return?
cards.back: 12 months after the 31 January filing deadline
cards.evidence: Action: Taxpayer amends the return; Time limit: 12 months after the 31 January filing deadline; For 2025/26: 31 January 2028.

cards.front: SA: overpayment relief claim time limit?
cards.back: 4 years after the end of the tax year
cards.evidence: Action: Overpayment relief claim; Time limit: 4 years after the end of the tax year; For 2025/26: 5 April 2030.

cards.front: SA: HMRC enquiry window for an on-time return?
cards.back: 12 months after the date the return was filed
cards.evidence: Action: HMRC opens an enquiry into an on-time return; Time limit: 12 months after the date the return was filed; For 2025/26: e.g. filed 10 December 2026, so 10 December 2027.

cards.front: SA: each payment on account is what share of prior-year liability?
cards.evidence: Payments on account (POAs) for 2026/27 are each 50% of the 2025/26 SA liability (income tax and Class 4, less tax deducted at source).

cards.front: SA: penalty range for careless inaccuracy, unprompted?
cards.back: 0% to 30% of potential lost revenue
cards.evidence: | Careless | 0% to 30% | 15% to 30% |

cards.front: SA: how long to appeal an HMRC closure notice?
cards.back: 30 days
cards.evidence: The taxpayer has 30 days to appeal, and can then ask for a statutory review or go to the First-tier Tribunal.

cards.front: SA: max period HMRC can suspend a careless penalty?
cards.back: Up to 2 years
cards.evidence: HMRC can suspend a careless penalty for up to 2 years if the taxpayer agrees to conditions that will improve their record keeping.

cards.front: Class 2 NIC: small profits threshold for 2026/27?
cards.evidence: - Profits at or above the small profits threshold (£7,105 for 2026/27): Class 2 is treated as paid, so the year counts towards state pension and contributory benefits without any payment.

cards.front: Voluntary Class 2 NIC: weekly rate for 2026/27?
cards.back: £3.65 a week (£189.80 for a full 52-week year)
cards.evidence: - Profits below £7,105: no liability, but the person can pay voluntary Class 2 at £3.65 a week for 2026/27 (£189.80 for a full 52-week year) to protect their NI record.

cards.front: Class 4 NIC 2026/27: 6% main rate band?
cards.back: Profits between £12,570 and £50,270
cards.evidence: Profits: £12,570 – £50,270 (upper profits limit); Rate: 6%.

cards.front: Class 4 NIC 2026/27: rate on profits above upper profits limit?
cards.back: 2% on profits over £50,270
cards.evidence: Profits: Over £50,270; Rate: 2%.

cards.front: Class 4 NIC: when is a person exempt due to age?
cards.back: Reached state pension age before 6 April, the start of the tax year
cards.evidence: Exemptions: No Class 4 is due if the person has reached state pension age before the start of the tax year (6 April).

cards.front: Class 4 NIC: do landlords with property income pay it?
cards.back: No, unless the activity is a genuine trade
cards.evidence: Profits from a property business aren't trading profits, so landlords don't pay Class 4 (unless the activity is a genuine trade).

cards.front: Class 4 NIC: how are partners charged?
cards.back: Each partner pays on their own share of the profit
cards.evidence: For partners, each partner pays Class 4 on their own share of the profit.

cards.front: Employee expenses: statutory test for deductibility (ITEPA s336)?
cards.back: Obliged to incur and pay it, and wholly, exclusively and necessarily in performing the duties
cards.evidence: An employee can deduct an expense only if they're obliged to incur and pay it as holder of the employment and the amount is incurred wholly, exclusively and necessarily in the performance of the duties.

cards.front: AMAP: car/van mileage rates for business miles?
cards.back: 45p/mile for first 10,000 miles, then 25p
cards.evidence: The approved mileage allowance payment (AMAP) rates for cars and vans are 45p per mile for the first 10,000 business miles in the tax year and 25p thereafter.

cards.front: Employment: deduction for unreimbursed homeworking costs from 6 April 2026?
cards.back: Removed; no deduction, though employers can still reimburse tax-free
cards.evidence: Expense: Additional costs of working from home; Deductible?: No, from 6 April 2026; Notes: The deduction for unreimbursed homeworking costs was removed. Employers can still reimburse tax-free where conditions are met.

cards.front: P11D: date by which employee should receive it?
cards.back: By 6 July after the tax year
cards.evidence: Document: P11D (or payrolled benefits on payslips); What it gives you: Cash equivalents of benefits in kind and expenses not payrolled; When the employee should have it: By 6 July after the tax year.

cards.front: P60: date by which employee should receive it?
cards.back: By 31 May after the tax year
cards.evidence: Document: P60; What it gives you: Pay and tax deducted for the tax year from that employer; When the employee should have it: By 31 May after the tax year.

cards.front: Benefits in kind: loans taxable if over what amount?
cards.back: Beneficial loans over £10,000
cards.evidence: beneficial loans over £10,000

cards.front: FIG regime: who qualifies?
cards.back: UK resident in first 4 tax years of residence, after at least 10 consecutive tax years of non-UK residence
cards.evidence: Who qualifies: an individual who is UK resident under the SRT for a tax year that falls within their first 4 tax years of UK residence after at least 10 consecutive tax years of non-UK residence.

cards.front: FIG regime: time limit to make a claim?
cards.back: Within 12 months of the 31 January filing date (2026/27: 31 January 2029)
cards.evidence: Time limit: the claim must be made within 12 months of the 31 January filing date. For 2026/27 that's by 31 January 2029.

cards.front: FIG regime: what allowances are lost on a claim?
cards.back: Personal allowance, CGT annual exempt amount, blind person's allowance, marriage allowance
cards.evidence: the person loses their personal allowance and the CGT annual exempt amount for that year, along with blind person's allowance and marriage allowance,

cards.front: Foreign tax credit relief: how is the amount calculated?
cards.back: Lower of the foreign tax paid and the UK tax on that income
cards.evidence: FTCR = the lower of the foreign tax paid and the UK tax on that income

cards.front: TRF charge rates on designated pre-6 April 2025 foreign income and gains?
cards.evidence: The charge is 12% for designations in 2025/26 and 2026/27, and 15% in 2027/28, the final year.

cards.front: FIG regime: is foreign tax credit relief available on relieved income?
cards.back: No, as there is no UK tax to credit against
cards.evidence: foreign tax credit relief isn't available on relieved income, since there's no UK tax to credit against.

cards.front: HICBC: ANI level where the charge starts (2024/25 onwards)?
cards.evidence: - ANI of £60,000 or less: no charge.

cards.front: HICBC: how is the charge calculated between £60,000 and £80,000 ANI?
cards.back: 1% of Child Benefit for each complete £200 of ANI above £60,000
cards.evidence: - ANI between £60,000 and £80,000: charge = 1% of the Child Benefit for each complete £200 of ANI above £60,000.

cards.front: HICBC: charge when ANI is £80,000 or more?
cards.back: 100% of the Child Benefit
cards.evidence: - ANI of £80,000 or more: charge = 100% of the Child Benefit.

cards.front: Child Benefit 2026/27: weekly rates?
cards.back: £27.05 eldest or only child; £17.90 each additional child
cards.evidence: For 2026/27 the weekly rates are £27.05 for the eldest or only child and £17.90 for each additional child.

cards.front: HICBC: who is liable to pay the charge?
cards.back: The partner with the higher ANI, even if the other receives the benefit
cards.evidence: The person liable is whichever of the two partners has the higher ANI, even if it's the other partner who receives the Child Benefit.

cards.front: HICBC: registration deadline for Self Assessment if not already registered?
cards.back: 5 October after the tax year
cards.evidence: A person liable to the charge who isn't otherwise in Self Assessment must register (by 5 October after the tax year), unless they pay through PAYE.

cards.front: HICBC: what was the pre-2024/25 threshold and rate?
cards.back: £50,000 threshold; 1% for each £100
cards.evidence: (Before 2024/25 the threshold was £50,000 and the rate was 1% for each £100. Use the old rules for earlier years' returns.)

cards.front: Income tax 2026/27 (non-Scottish): basic rate band size and rate?
cards.back: £37,700 of taxable income at 20%
cards.evidence: Band: Basic rate; Taxable income: £0 – £37,700 of taxable income; Rate: 20%.

cards.front: Income tax 2026/27: higher rate band and rate?
cards.evidence: Band: Higher rate; Taxable income: £37,701 – £125,140; Rate: 40%.

cards.front: Income tax 2026/27: additional rate threshold and rate?
cards.evidence: Band: Additional rate; Taxable income: Over £125,140; Rate: 45%.

cards.front: Personal allowance taper: when does it start and how does it reduce?
cards.back: ANI over £100,000; reduced £1 for every £2 of excess
cards.evidence: If adjusted net income exceeds £100,000, the personal allowance is reduced by £1 for every £2 of the excess.

cards.front: Personal allowance taper: income level at which allowance is fully lost?
cards.evidence: It's fully lost at £125,140.

cards.front: Income tax: gross income at which higher rate starts with full personal allowance?
cards.evidence: With a full allowance, the higher rate starts at gross income of £12,570 + £37,700 = £50,270.

cards.front: Income tax: how is adjusted net income calculated?
cards.back: Net income less gross relief-at-source pension contributions and gross Gift Aid
cards.evidence: Adjusted net income = net income, less the gross amount of personal pension contributions paid net (relief at source) and gross Gift Aid donations.

cards.front: Marriage allowance: how far can a claim be backdated?
cards.back: Up to 4 years
cards.evidence: Claims can be backdated up to 4 years if the conditions were met in those years.

cards.front: Gift Aid: how do you gross up a net donation on the return?
cards.evidence: Gross up the donation: net × 100/80.

cards.front: Gift Aid: deadline for carrying a donation back to the previous tax year?
cards.back: Election on the previous year's return, filed on or before 31 January
cards.evidence: Carry-back: donations made in the current tax year can be treated as made in the previous tax year, if the election is made on that year's return when it's filed on or before 31 January.

cards.front: Pension tax relief: limit on relievable gross personal contributions?
cards.back: 100% of relevant UK earnings, or £3,600 gross if earnings are lower
cards.evidence: Limits: relief is available on gross contributions up to 100% of relevant UK earnings (or £3,600 gross if earnings are lower), and contributions above the annual allowance (£60,000, or less if tapered or after flexible access) trigger an annual allowance charge.

cards.front: Pensions: standard annual allowance before tapering?
cards.evidence: Limits: relief is available on gross contributions up to 100% of relevant UK earnings (or £3,600 gross if earnings are lower), and contributions above the annual allowance (£60,000, or less if tapered or after flexible access) trigger an annual allowance charge.

cards.front: Personal allowance taper: ANI range and effective marginal rate?
cards.back: Effective 60% between £100,000 and £125,140
cards.evidence: the personal allowance taper above £100,000 (an effective 60% marginal rate between £100,000 and £125,140),

cards.front: High Income Child Benefit Charge: ANI range?
cards.back: Between £60,000 and £80,000
cards.evidence: the High Income Child Benefit Charge between £60,000 and £80,000.

cards.front: MTD for Income Tax: qualifying income threshold for 6 April 2026 start?
cards.back: Over £50,000 (2024/25 qualifying income)
cards.evidence: Qualifying income in tax year…: 2024/25; is more than…: £50,000; MTD starts from: 6 April 2026.

cards.front: MTD for Income Tax: threshold and start date based on 2025/26 income?
cards.back: Over £30,000; MTD from 6 April 2027
cards.evidence: Qualifying income in tax year…: 2025/26; is more than…: £30,000; MTD starts from: 6 April 2027.

cards.front: MTD for Income Tax: threshold and start date based on 2026/27 income?
cards.back: Over £20,000; MTD from 6 April 2028
cards.evidence: Qualifying income in tax year…: 2026/27; is more than…: £20,000; MTD starts from: 6 April 2028.

cards.front: MTD ITSA: standard quarterly update period 6 April to 5 July, deadline?
cards.back: 7 August
cards.evidence: Update period: 6 April to 5 July; Deadline: 7 August.

cards.front: MTD ITSA: deadline for the update covering 6 April to 5 January?
cards.back: 7 February
cards.evidence: Update period: 6 April to 5 January; Deadline: 7 February.

cards.front: MTD ITSA: late payment penalty rates in 2026/27?
cards.back: 3% at day 15, another 3% at day 30, 10% a year from day 31
cards.evidence: Late payment penalties follow the VAT-style regime: 3% of tax unpaid at day 15, another 3% at day 30, and 10% a year from day 31.

cards.front: Partnership SA800: online filing deadline?
cards.back: 31 January (31 October after the tax year on paper)
cards.evidence: - SA800 deadline: 31 October after the tax year on paper, or 31 January online, the same as for individuals.

cards.front: Partnership return: initial late filing penalty per partner?
cards.back: £100 per partner who was a partner in the period
cards.evidence: - Late filing: each partner who was a partner during the period is charged a £100 initial penalty, followed by daily penalties and further penalties if the return is still outstanding.

cards.front: Partnership profits: are partner salaries and interest on capital deductible expenses?
cards.back: No. They are profit-sharing only; add back and allocate first
cards.evidence: Salaries and interest on capital are not expenses: A partner's "salary" and "interest on capital" are not deductible expenses of the partnership.

cards.front: Partnership profit allocation: balance after salaries and interest is split how?
cards.back: In the profit-sharing ratio (the balance can be negative)
cards.evidence: Step: 4; What to do: Split the balance (which can be negative) in the profit-sharing ratio.

cards.front: Partnership: how is a new or leaving partner treated for tax?
cards.back: New partner starts a trade on joining; leaver ceases on leaving
cards.evidence: A new partner is treated as starting a trade on the day they join, and a leaving partner as ceasing on the day they leave, while the partnership itself carries on.

cards.front: Partnership: notional loss for a partner when the firm has an overall profit?
cards.back: Set it to nil and reallocate to the other partners in proportion
cards.evidence: Set the notional figure to nil and reallocate it to the other partners in proportion to their shares, so the partners are taxed on the firm's actual total.

cards.front: MTD for Income Tax: does partnership income count towards qualifying income?
cards.back: No; and HMRC has set no date for partnerships to join
cards.evidence: - MTD for Income Tax: partnership income doesn't count towards a partner's MTD qualifying income, and HMRC hasn't set a date for partnerships to join.

cards.front: Property income: property allowance amount and effect?
cards.back: £1,000: no need to report if gross income is £1,000 or less; above that, can deduct flat £1,000 instead of expenses
cards.evidence: Property allowance: an individual with gross property income of £1,000 or less in the tax year doesn't need to report it. Above £1,000, they can deduct a flat £1,000 instead of actual expenses if that's better.

cards.front: Rent-a-room relief: annual tax-free limit?
cards.back: £7,500 a year (£3,750 each if income is shared)
cards.evidence: Rent-a-room relief: letting furnished accommodation in the individual's own home is tax-free up to £7,500 a year (£3,750 each if the income is shared).

cards.front: Section 24: rate of tax reduction for residential finance costs?
cards.back: 20% (basic rate) tax reduction; finance costs not deducted
cards.evidence: Instead, the landlord gets a basic rate (20%) tax reduction on the lowest of (ITTOIA 2005 ss274A–274C; PIM2058):

cards.front: Property income: cash basis default threshold for individuals?
cards.back: Property receipts of £150,000 or less (unless they elect for accruals)
cards.evidence: the cash basis is the default for individuals whose property receipts are £150,000 or less, unless they elect for accruals,

cards.front: Joint property income: how are spouses taxed, and Form 17 time limit?
cards.back: 50:50; Form 17 election for actual shares within 60 days
cards.evidence: Spouses and civil partners living together are taxed 50:50 on jointly held property income, whatever their actual shares. If they own the property in unequal beneficial shares, they can elect to be taxed on those actual shares by both signing Form 17 and sending it to HMRC within 60 days, with evidence of the unequal ownership.

cards.front: MTD for Income Tax: qualifying income thresholds?
cards.back: Over £50,000 from April 2026; over £30,000 from April 2027
cards.evidence: Gross rents count towards qualifying income for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax (more than £50,000 from April 2026, more than £30,000 from April 2027).

cards.front: SA: POAs not required if previous year's SA liability was below what?
cards.back: Less than £1,000
cards.evidence: - the previous year's SA liability was less than £1,000, or

cards.front: SA: POAs not required if what share of prior year's tax was collected at source?
cards.back: More than 80%
cards.evidence: - more than 80% of the previous year's total income tax and Class 4 was collected at source (PAYE, tax deducted on interest, etc.).

cards.front: SA: how much is each payment on account normally?
cards.back: 50% of the previous year's relevant amount
cards.evidence: POAs are two advance instalments towards the current year's tax, each normally 50% of the previous year's "relevant amount" — the income tax and Class 4 NIC that was payable through SA (i.e. after tax deducted at source such as PAYE).

cards.front: SA: late filing penalty if return is 1 day late?
cards.back: £100 fixed penalty, even if no tax is due
cards.evidence: How late: 1 day; Penalty: £100 fixed penalty (even if no tax is due).

cards.front: SA: daily late filing penalty after 3 months, and its maximum?
cards.back: £10 per day for up to 90 days, max £900
cards.evidence: How late: 3 months; Penalty: £10 per day for up to 90 days (maximum £900).

cards.front: SA: latest online filing date for 2026/27 to collect an underpayment via tax code?
cards.back: 30 December 2027 (underpayment under £3,000)
cards.evidence: Date: 30 December 2027; What happens: Online filing deadline if the client wants an underpayment (under £3,000) collected through their tax code.

cards.front: SA: Self Serve Time to Pay is available for debts up to what amount?
cards.evidence: Self Serve Time to Pay is available online for SA debts up to £30,000 (subject to conditions).

cards.front: SA: time limit to appeal a penalty on reasonable excuse grounds?
cards.back: 30 days
cards.evidence: Appeal within 30 days.

cards.front: Dividend tax 2026/27: ordinary and upper rates?
cards.back: 10.75% ordinary; 35.75% upper
cards.evidence: Budget 2025 increased the dividend ordinary rate from 8.75% to 10.75% and the upper rate from 33.75% to 35.75% from 6 April 2026.

cards.front: Savings income: starting rate for savings (SRS) amount and condition?
cards.back: Up to £5,000 at 0%, reduced £1 for each £1 of taxable non-savings income
cards.evidence: Starting rate for savings (SRS): up to £5,000 at 0%. Available only to the extent that taxable non-savings income is below £5,000. Each £1 of taxable non-savings income reduces the £5,000 by £1.

cards.front: Personal savings allowance (PSA): amount by taxpayer type?
cards.back: £1,000 basic; £500 higher; nil additional
cards.evidence: Personal savings allowance (PSA): £1,000 for a basic rate taxpayer, £500 for a higher rate taxpayer, nil for an additional rate taxpayer.

cards.front: Savings rates from 6 April 2027 (Budget 2025)?
cards.evidence: Budget 2025 also announced that savings (and property) income rates will rise by 2 percentage points to 22% / 42% / 47% from 6 April 2027.

cards.front: Do SRS, PSA and dividend allowance use up the basic rate band?
cards.back: Yes; they are taxed at 0%, not deducted, so they use up the band
cards.evidence: Income covered by the SRS, PSA or dividend allowance is still taxable income taxed at 0%. It still uses up the basic rate band.

cards.front: Self-employment: flat trading allowance amount?
cards.back: £1,000 instead of deducting actual expenses
cards.evidence: Individuals with trading income can deduct a flat £1,000 trading allowance instead of actual expenses.

cards.front: Trading allowance: when is gross income fully covered and not reportable?
cards.back: Gross trading income of £1,000 or less
cards.evidence: If gross trading income is £1,000 or less, it's fully covered and doesn't need to be reported.

cards.front: Self-employment: cash basis status from 2024/25?
cards.back: Default for sole traders and individual partnerships; old turnover limits removed
cards.evidence: From 2024/25 the cash basis became the default for sole traders and partnerships of individuals, and the old turnover limits were removed.

cards.front: Cash basis: main equipment exception still getting capital allowances?
cards.back: Cars
cards.evidence: Under the cash basis most equipment is simply deducted when paid for (cars are the main exception — they still get capital allowances).

cards.front: Simplified expenses: vehicle mileage rates per business mile?
cards.evidence: Sole traders can use flat rates for some costs: vehicle mileage at 45p/25p per business mile instead of actual motor costs (you can't claim capital allowances on that vehicle then), a flat monthly amount for working from home based on hours, and a flat private-use adjustment for living in business premises.

cards.front: Transition profits from 2023/24: over how many years are they spread?
cards.back: Five years (2023/24 to 2027/28) unless accelerated
cards.evidence: Transition profits are spread over five years (2023/24 to 2027/28) unless the client elected to accelerate them, so you may still see a fifth of a transition profit on 2026/27 returns.

cards.front: Tax year basis: which year end is treated as equivalent to 5 April?
cards.back: 31 March
cards.evidence: A 31 March year end is treated as equivalent to 5 April.

cards.front: SRT: second automatic overseas test for an arriver?
cards.back: Resident in none of previous 3 years and fewer than 46 days in the UK
cards.evidence: Test: Second; Conditions: UK resident in none of the previous 3 tax years, and fewer than 46 days in the UK.

cards.front: SRT: first automatic UK test?
cards.back: 183 days or more in the UK in the tax year
cards.evidence: Test: First; Conditions: 183 days or more in the UK in the tax year.

cards.front: SRT: how many days in the UK may be ignored for exceptional circumstances?
cards.back: Up to 60 days a year
cards.evidence: Up to 60 days a year can be ignored if the person was here only because of exceptional circumstances beyond their control, such as sudden serious illness or a national emergency, and intended to leave.

cards.front: SRT: what is the work tie?
cards.back: Working in the UK (more than 3 hours a day) on at least 40 days in the year
cards.evidence: | Work | They work in the UK (more than 3 hours a day) on at least 40 days in the year |

cards.front: SRT: ties needed for a leaver with 46 to 90 UK days?
cards.back: 3 or more ties
cards.evidence: Days in the UK: 46 to 90; Leaver (resident in 1+ of previous 3 years): 3 or more ties; Arriver (resident in none of previous 3 years): All 4 ties.

cards.front: SRT: ties needed for an arriver with 91 to 120 UK days?
cards.back: 3 or more ties
cards.evidence: Days in the UK: 91 to 120; Leaver (resident in 1+ of previous 3 years): 2 or more ties; Arriver (resident in none of previous 3 years): 3 or more ties.

cards.front: SA: deadline to notify HMRC of chargeability for 2026/27?
cards.back: 5 October 2027
cards.evidence: For 2026/27 (ending 5 April 2027) that's 5 October 2027.

cards.front: SA: trading income level that triggers a sole trader return?
cards.back: Gross trading income over £1,000
cards.evidence: Trigger: Self-employed sole trader with gross trading income over £1,000; Notes: The £1,000 trading allowance covers very small side-income (see the self-employment lesson)..

cards.front: SA: how long is a UTR?
cards.back: 10 digits
cards.evidence: HMRC issues a Unique Taxpayer Reference (UTR), a 10-digit number, usually by post within a couple of weeks (longer at peak).

cards.front: SA: which supplementary page is used for UK property income?
cards.back: SA105
cards.evidence: Page: SA105; Use for: UK property.

cards.front: SA: which supplementary page is used for capital gains?
cards.back: SA108
cards.evidence: Page: SA108; Use for: Capital gains.

cards.front: SA: failure to notify penalty is based on what?
cards.back: Potential lost revenue: tax unpaid at 31 January
cards.evidence: Failure to notify carries a penalty based on the "potential lost revenue" — the tax unpaid at 31 January — with the percentage depending on behaviour (non-deliberate, deliberate, deliberate and concealed) and reduced for disclosure.

cards.front: SA: form used to register as a partner?
cards.back: SA401 (the partnership itself uses SA400)
cards.evidence: Partners: register as a partner (SA401). The partnership itself is registered with SA400.

cards.front: AML: how many HM Treasury-appointed supervisors are there in the UK?
cards.back: 25: three statutory and 22 professional body supervisors
cards.evidence: There are 25 in the UK, including three statutory supervisors (HMRC, the FCA and the Gambling Commission) and 22 professional body supervisors (such as ICAEW, ACCA, AAT, CIOT and ATT for their members).

cards.front: AML: what must a practice do if no professional body supervises it?
cards.back: Register with HMRC as an accountancy service provider
cards.evidence: A practice must be supervised: if it is not supervised by a professional body, it must register with HMRC as an accountancy service provider.

cards.front: MLR 2017: which regulation requires the firm-wide risk assessment?
cards.back: Regulation 18
cards.evidence: The firm-wide risk assessment (MLR 2017 reg 18)

cards.front: MLR 2017: which regulation covers policies, controls and procedures?
cards.back: Regulation 19
cards.evidence: Policies, controls and procedures (reg 19)

cards.front: AML: how long must CDD and transaction records be kept?
cards.back: Five years after the end of the business relationship or completion of the transaction
cards.evidence: Keep CDD records and transaction records for five years after the end of the business relationship (or completion of the transaction).

cards.front: POCA 2002: which sections create the main money laundering offences?
cards.evidence: Creates the money laundering offences (concealing, arranging, acquiring, using or possessing criminal property: ss327–329), the failure to disclose offence for the regulated sector (s330) and tipping off (s333A)

cards.front: POCA 2002: which section is the regulated-sector failure to disclose offence?
cards.evidence: Creates the money laundering offences (concealing, arranging, acquiring, using or possessing criminal property: ss327–329), the failure to disclose offence for the regulated sector (s330) and tipping off (s333A)

cards.front: MLR 2017: beneficial owner threshold for a non-listed company?
cards.back: Individual owning or controlling more than 25% of shares or voting rights, or otherwise exercising control
cards.evidence: Any individual who ultimately owns or controls more than 25% of the shares or voting rights, or who otherwise exercises control (for example by appointing a majority of directors).

cards.front: CDD: what must you do if you can't complete it?
cards.back: Don't transact or establish/continue the relationship; consider making a suspicious activity report
cards.evidence: If you can't complete CDD, you must not carry out a transaction or establish or continue the relationship, and should consider whether to make a suspicious activity report.

cards.front: CDD: beneficial owners of a trust?
cards.back: Settlor, trustees, protector, beneficiaries (or class) and anyone else exercising ultimate control
cards.evidence: The settlor, the trustees, the protector (if any), the beneficiaries (or class of beneficiaries) and any other individual exercising ultimate control.

cards.front: CDD: who is the beneficial owner if no individual can be identified?
cards.back: The senior managing official; record why no beneficial owner was identified
cards.evidence: The senior managing official: record why no beneficial owner could be identified.

cards.front: What does enhanced due diligence (EDD) involve?
cards.back: Source of funds and wealth information, senior management approval, enhanced ongoing monitoring
cards.evidence: EDD means more information (source of funds and source of wealth), senior management approval, and enhanced ongoing monitoring.

cards.front: CDD: what must you do on a material discrepancy with the Companies House register?
cards.back: Report it to Companies House
cards.evidence: Discrepancies: if you find a material discrepancy between the information you hold and the Companies House register, you must report it to Companies House (in the manner required by the regulations).

cards.front: CDD: does Companies House director/PSC ID verification replace your own CDD?
cards.back: No; it applies from 18 November 2025 but doesn't replace your CDD
cards.evidence: Companies House identity verification for directors and PSCs (from 18 November 2025) does not replace your own CDD.

cards.front: AML records: how long must they be kept after the client relationship ends?
cards.back: Five years from the end of the relationship
cards.evidence: Keep your own working papers, AML records (five years from the end of the relationship) and the disengagement correspondence.

cards.front: Professional clearance: what if the client refuses permission to contact the previous accountant?
cards.back: Treat as a warning sign and consider declining
cards.evidence: If the client refuses permission, treat that as a warning sign and consider declining.

cards.front: Professional clearance: what if the previous accountant does not reply?
cards.back: Proceed with caution after a reasonable time; record steps taken
cards.evidence: If there is no reply after a reasonable time, you may proceed with caution, and record the steps taken.

cards.front: Work outside the engagement letter: what should you confirm in writing?
cards.back: The scope, the fee and the deadline
cards.evidence: When the client asks for something outside the letter (a new VAT registration, a one-off CGT computation), confirm in writing: the scope, the fee and the deadline, preferably via a variation letter or email recorded on the file.

cards.front: Disengagement: what must be done about HMRC authority?
cards.back: Cancel the agent authorisation and agent services account link

cards.front: Disengaging because of an AML issue: what must you avoid in giving reasons?
cards.back: Reasons that tip off the client; follow the MLRO's advice
cards.evidence: If you withdraw because of an AML issue, don't give reasons that tip off the client (see the SAR lesson); follow the MLRO's advice.

cards.front: Professional ethics: what are the five fundamental principles?
cards.back: Integrity, objectivity, professional competence and due care, confidentiality, professional behaviour
cards.evidence: Principle: Integrity; What it means: Be straightforward and honest in all professional and business relationships; Practice example: Don't sign off a return you know contains a false figure.

cards.evidence: If you find an error in a client's affairs, you must advise the client to correct it.

cards.front: Ethics: what are the steps for managing a conflict of interest?
cards.back: Identify, assess, disclose and get consent, safeguards, decline or withdraw, document

cards.front: Failure to prevent fraud (ECCTA): when did the offence come into force?
cards.back: 1 September 2025
cards.evidence: It came into force on 1 September 2025.

cards.front: Failure to prevent fraud: penalty on conviction of an organisation?
cards.back: An unlimited fine
cards.evidence: The penalty is an unlimited fine.

cards.front: Failure to prevent fraud: how many principles for reasonable procedures, and what are they?
cards.back: Six: top-level commitment, risk assessment, proportionate procedures, due diligence, training, monitoring

cards.front: Failure to prevent fraud: who is an 'associated person'?
cards.back: Employee, agent, subsidiary or anyone performing services for or on behalf of the organisation
cards.evidence: A person associated with the organisation (an employee, agent, subsidiary or any person who performs services for or on behalf of the organisation) commits a base fraud offence.

cards.front: Companies House ID verification: start date for new directors and PSCs?
cards.back: 18 November 2025
cards.evidence: from 18 November 2025 new directors and PSCs must verify their identity; existing directors have a 12-month transition, confirming verification with their next confirmation statement.

cards.front: Companies House ID verification: transition period for existing directors?
cards.back: 12 months, confirmed with next confirmation statement
cards.evidence: from 18 November 2025 new directors and PSCs must verify their identity; existing directors have a 12-month transition, confirming verification with their next confirmation statement.

cards.front: UK GDPR: deadline to respond to a subject access request?
cards.back: Without undue delay and within one month of receipt
cards.evidence: Respond without undue delay and within one month of receipt (extendable by up to two further months for complex or numerous requests, with notice).

cards.front: UK GDPR: maximum extension for complex or numerous DSARs?
cards.back: Up to two further months, with notice
cards.evidence: Respond without undue delay and within one month of receipt (extendable by up to two further months for complex or numerous requests, with notice).

cards.front: UK GDPR: time limit to notify the ICO of a reportable breach?
cards.back: Without undue delay and within 72 hours of becoming aware
cards.evidence: If the breach is likely to result in a risk to individuals' rights and freedoms, notify the ICO without undue delay and within 72 hours of becoming aware.

cards.front: UK GDPR breach: when must affected individuals also be told?
cards.back: If there is a high risk, without undue delay
cards.evidence: If there is a high risk, also tell the individuals affected without undue delay.

cards.front: Data protection: how long are AML records kept?
cards.back: Five years after the end of the relationship
cards.evidence: AML records are kept five years after the end of the relationship; tax and accounting files are commonly kept for the period in which HMRC can challenge a return (generally up to 6 years, longer if deliberate behaviour is suspected), and for any longer period needed to defend a claim.

cards.front: Data protection: usual retention for tax and accounting files?
cards.back: Generally up to 6 years; longer if deliberate behaviour is suspected
cards.evidence: AML records are kept five years after the end of the relationship; tax and accounting files are commonly kept for the period in which HMRC can challenge a return (generally up to 6 years, longer if deliberate behaviour is suspected), and for any longer period needed to defend a claim.

cards.front: UK GDPR: practice's role when running payroll on client's instructions?
cards.back: Processor (client is controller); written contract needed
cards.evidence: Activity: Running payroll for a client under the client's instructions; Typical role of the practice: Processor for the client's employee data (the client is controller); Why: The practice acts on the client's instructions, so a written contract (data processing terms) is needed.
