cards.front: HMRC agent authorisation: what is the Agent Services Account (ASA)?
cards.back: Secure HMRC account to manage client authorisations and access digital tax services
cards.evidence: Create an Agent Services Account (ASA): the secure HMRC account used to manage client authorisations and access digital tax services.

cards.front: Agent authorisation: how does the digital handshake work?
cards.back: Agent sends invitation link via ASA; client signs in to HMRC and accepts
cards.evidence: The agent sends an invitation link; the client signs in to HMRC and accepts; this replaces the 64-8 for the services that support it

cards.front: Form 64-8: does a Self Assessment authorisation cover VAT?
cards.back: No, not unless the VAT boxes are completed
cards.evidence: Authorisation covers the wrong tax: a 64-8 for Self Assessment doesn't cover VAT unless the VAT boxes are completed.

cards.front: Company Tax Return: HMRC enquiry window?
cards.back: 12 months after the date the return was delivered
cards.evidence: Company Tax Returns: an enquiry window of 12 months after the date the return was delivered (FA 1998 Sch 18 para 24), with similar rules for late filing.

cards.front: Discovery assessment: time limit for ordinary behaviour?
cards.back: 4 years
cards.evidence: | Ordinary (no careless or deliberate error) | 4 years |

cards.front: Discovery assessment: time limit where behaviour is careless?
cards.back: 6 years
cards.evidence: | Careless | 6 years |

cards.front: Discovery assessment: time limit where behaviour is deliberate?
cards.back: 20 years
cards.evidence: | Deliberate | 20 years |

cards.front: Schedule 36 information notice: penalty for failing to comply?
cards.back: Initial £300, then up to £60 per day while failure continues
cards.evidence: Penalties: failing to comply attracts an initial penalty of £300, and a further penalty of up to £60 per day while the failure continues (after a penalty has been imposed).

cards.front: Schedule 36 taxpayer notice: time to appeal against it?
cards.back: 30 days (except for statutory records)
cards.evidence: The taxpayer can appeal against a notice (other than for statutory records) within 30 days.

cards.front: PCRT: which date did the new version take effect?
cards.back: 1 January 2026
cards.evidence: A new version took effect on 1 January 2026, published on 1 October 2025, to align with the IESBA's international standard on tax planning and related services.

cards.front: GAAR: test for whether an arrangement is abusive?
cards.back: Cannot reasonably be regarded as a reasonable course of action (double reasonableness test)
cards.evidence: An arrangement is abusive if entering into or carrying it out cannot reasonably be regarded as a reasonable course of action having regard to all the circumstances (the "double reasonableness" test).

cards.front: DOTAS: does a scheme reference number (SRN) mean HMRC approval?
cards.back: No; it only shows the scheme was disclosed, not that it works
cards.evidence: A scheme with an SRN isn't thereby approved by HMRC. Disclosure doesn't mean it works.

cards.front: PCRT: what if a client refuses to correct an error in their return?
cards.back: Consider ceasing to act; don't perpetuate the error; consider an AML report
cards.evidence: If the client refuses, you should consider ceasing to act. You can't then act in a way that perpetuates the error, and you should consider whether an AML report is required.

cards.front: Tax evasion vs mitigation: how does each differ?
cards.back: Evasion is illegal deliberate deception of HMRC; mitigation uses reliefs as Parliament intended
cards.evidence: Term: Tax evasion; Meaning: Illegal: deliberately deceiving HMRC (hiding income, false claims, false records); Treatment: Crime. Never assist. A report to the MLRO may be required.

cards.front: MTD for IT: penalty points threshold for quarterly submitters, and penalty?
cards.back: 4 points; £200 penalty, then £200 per further missed deadline
cards.evidence: - At 4 points (the threshold for quarterly submitters) a £200 penalty is charged, and £200 for each further missed deadline.

cards.front: VAT late submission: points threshold for annual, quarterly and monthly returns?
cards.back: 2 annual, 4 quarterly, 5 monthly; £200 penalty at threshold
cards.evidence: - Late submission: a points system. A point is added for each late return; at the threshold (2 for annual, 4 for quarterly, 5 for monthly returns) a £200 penalty is charged, and £200 for each further late return while at the threshold. Points reset after a compliant period.

cards.front: VAT late payment penalty (tax due on or after 31 May 2025)?
cards.back: 3% at day 15, a further 3% at day 30, then 10% annual rate charged daily from day 31
cards.evidence: - Late payment (periods where the tax is due on or after 31 May 2025): 3% of the tax outstanding at day 15, plus a further 3% of the tax outstanding at day 30, then a second penalty at an annual rate of 10% on the outstanding balance, charged daily from day 31.

cards.front: Self Assessment: daily late filing penalty after 3 months, and its cap?
cards.back: £10 a day for up to 90 days (max £900)
cards.evidence: Time after the deadline: 3 months; Late filing: £10 a day for up to 90 days (max £900); Late payment (of unpaid tax): .

cards.front: Self Assessment: late filing penalty at 6 months?
cards.back: 5% of the tax due or £300, whichever is greater
cards.evidence: Time after the deadline: 6 months; Late filing: 5% of the tax due or £300, whichever is greater; Late payment (of unpaid tax): A further 5% of unpaid tax.

cards.front: HMRC penalty appeal: time limit and method?
cards.back: In writing within 30 days of the penalty notice
cards.evidence: - Appeal in writing within 30 days of the penalty notice; HMRC can review, and the First-tier Tribunal hears appeals.

cards.front: POCA DAML: length of the moratorium period after a refusal?
cards.back: 31 calendar days from the day you receive the refusal
cards.evidence: - If refused, a moratorium period of 31 calendar days starts on the day you receive the refusal.

cards.front: DAML moratorium: maximum Crown Court extension?
cards.back: Periods of up to 31 days, to a maximum of 186 days beyond the initial 31 days
cards.evidence: The moratorium can be extended by the Crown Court in periods of up to 31 days, to a maximum of 186 days beyond the initial 31 days (Criminal Finances Act 2017).

cards.front: AML: how long must the firm keep internal reports, MLRO decisions and SARs?
cards.back: Five years
cards.evidence: 5. The firm keeps records of internal reports, the MLRO's decision and any SAR for five years.

cards.front: POCA 2002: which section creates the tipping off offence?
cards.back: s333A
cards.evidence: Section: s333A; Offence: Tipping off; In plain English: Disclosing that a report has been made (or an investigation is under way) where that is likely to prejudice an investigation.

cards.front: POCA 2002: which section covers failure to disclose in the regulated sector?
cards.evidence: Section: s330; Offence: Failure to disclose (regulated sector); In plain English: Failing to report knowledge or suspicion, or reasonable grounds for suspicion, as soon as practicable, where the information came in the course of regulated sector business.

cards.front: HMRC dispute: normal time limit to appeal to HMRC against a decision?
cards.back: 30 days from the decision notice
cards.evidence: Stage: Appeal to HMRC; What happens: Written notice of appeal to HMRC, giving grounds; Time limit: Normally 30 days from the decision notice.

cards.front: HMRC statutory review: request deadline and HMRC's target to conclude?
cards.back: Request within 30 days; HMRC aims to conclude within 45 days
cards.evidence: Time limit: Review request within 30 days; HMRC aims to conclude within 45 days (or as agreed).

cards.front: Upper Tribunal: time limit to apply for permission to appeal from the FTT?
cards.back: 56 days of the FTT's decision
cards.evidence: Time limit: Application for permission within 56 days of the FTT's decision.

cards.front: FTT: test applied for late appeals?
cards.back: Martland v HMRC: length of delay, reason for it, all circumstances
cards.evidence: the tribunal can allow a late appeal, applying the test in Martland v HMRC (the length of the delay, the reason for it and all the circumstances), but it should not be relied upon.

cards.front: PII: how long should run-off cover normally last when a firm closes?
cards.back: Normally six years or longer
cards.evidence: Run-off cover: when the firm closes, merges or retires, arrange run-off (extended reporting) cover, normally for six years or longer, because claims can arise years after the work.

cards.front: Hot review vs cold review: what is the difference?
cards.back: Hot: experienced reviewer before sign-off. Cold: independent, after completion, on a sample of files.
cards.evidence: Hot review: by an experienced reviewer before sign-off, checking technical accuracy, completeness and key judgements.

cards.front: R&D claim notification: deadline for notifying HMRC?
cards.back: Within 6 months after the end of the period of account
cards.evidence: A company must notify HMRC that it intends to claim, through the online service, within the claim notification period: from the first day of the period of account to which the claim relates, ending 6 months after the end of that period of account.

cards.front: R&D claim notification: when is a company exempt from notifying?
cards.back: It made an R&D claim in the 3 years ending on the last day of the notification period
cards.evidence: it has made an R&D claim in the 3 years ending on the last day of the notification period; or

cards.front: R&D: what if a required claim notification was missed?
cards.back: No claim can be made for that period
cards.evidence: If notification was required and missed, no claim can be made for that period.

cards.front: R&D: order of filing the AIF and the CT600?
cards.back: AIF first (before or same day as CT600); otherwise HMRC removes the R&D claim
cards.evidence: Every R&D claim needs an Additional Information Form, submitted online before or on the same day as the CT600. If both go on the same day, the AIF must go first. If the CT600 is filed first, HMRC removes the R&D claim from the return.

cards.front: R&D AIF: how many projects must be described if 4 or more?
cards.back: At least 3, together at least 50% of qualifying expenditure
cards.evidence: Number of projects in the claim: 4 or more; Describe: At least 3, which together account for at least 50% of the qualifying expenditure.

cards.front: R&D: which CT600 boxes are ticked for notification and AIF?
cards.back: Box 656 (notification made or exempt) and box 657 (AIF submitted)
cards.evidence: tick box 656 (claim notification made, or exempt) and box 657 (AIF submitted)

cards.front: R&D claims: Sch 24 FA 2007 maximum penalty for careless inaccuracy?
cards.back: Up to 30% of potential lost revenue
cards.evidence: - careless: up to 30%;

cards.front: R&D claims: Sch 24 FA 2007 maximum penalty for deliberate inaccuracy?
cards.back: Up to 70% of potential lost revenue
cards.evidence: - deliberate: up to 70%;

cards.front: R&D claims: Sch 24 maximum penalty for deliberate and concealed inaccuracy?
cards.back: Up to 100% of potential lost revenue
cards.evidence: - deliberate and concealed: up to 100%.

cards.front: R&D claims: minimum period to keep supporting records?
cards.back: At least 6 years from the end of the accounting period; longer if an enquiry is open
cards.evidence: Keep records for at least 6 years from the end of the accounting period (the normal CT record-keeping period), and longer if an enquiry is open.

cards.front: R&D claims: which sectors does HMRC highlight as higher-risk?
cards.back: Education, arts and recreation, and construction
cards.evidence: - the sector is one where genuine R&D is rare (HMRC highlights education, arts and recreation, and construction as higher-risk);

cards.front: PCRT: date the revised version applies from?
cards.back: 1 January 2026
cards.evidence: PCRT (Professional Conduct in Relation to Taxation), issued jointly by ICAEW, ACCA, CIOT, ATT, AAT, ICAS and STEP, is mandatory for members of those bodies; a revised version applies from 1 January 2026.

cards.front: Merged RDEC: rate of credit on qualifying expenditure?
cards.back: 20% of qualifying expenditure (taxable trading income)
cards.evidence: The credit is 20% of qualifying expenditure (ring-fence trades have different rates).

cards.front: Merged RDEC: accounting periods to which it applies?
cards.back: Periods beginning on or after 1 April 2024
cards.evidence: The merged RDEC applies to accounting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2024.

cards.front: Merged RDEC step 2: notional tax rate, main rate vs small profits?
cards.back: 25% if profits at main rate (incl. marginal relief); otherwise 19% (incl. loss-makers)
cards.evidence: The rate is the main rate (25%) if the company's profits are chargeable at the main rate (including where marginal relief applies), otherwise the small profits rate (19%), which includes loss-makers.

cards.front: Merged RDEC step 3: PAYE/NIC cap formula?
cards.back: £20,000 + 300% of relevant PAYE and NIC liabilities for the period
cards.evidence: Step 3 – the PAYE cap: £20,000 + 300% of the company's relevant PAYE and NIC liabilities for the period (unless exempt).

cards.front: Merged RDEC: what happens to excess over the PAYE cap?
cards.back: Carried forward as credit for the next period
cards.evidence: Any excess is carried forward as credit for the next period.

cards.front: Merged RDEC PAYE cap exemption: Condition B limit on connected subcontractor/EPW spend?
cards.back: No more than 15% of qualifying expenditure
cards.evidence: A company is exempt from the cap if its employees create or manage the IP from the R&D (Condition A) and its spend on connected subcontractors and connected EPWs is no more than 15% of its qualifying expenditure (Condition B).

cards.front: Merged RDEC step 7: conditions for cash payment to company?
cards.back: Going concern, no open enquiry, PAYE and VAT up to date
cards.evidence: Step 7 – pay the balance to the company, if it's a going concern and there's no open enquiry and its PAYE and VAT are up to date.

cards.front: R&D: from when must software, consumables, data and cloud costs be paid to qualify?
cards.back: Accounting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2023
cards.evidence: For accounting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2023, software, consumables, data licences and cloud costs (like staffing costs and EPWs) must actually have been paid to qualify.

cards.front: R&D: capital expenditure on plant and machinery - what relief applies?
cards.back: R&D allowances at 100% in year of spend, not an R&D credit
cards.evidence: Instead it may qualify for research and development allowances (RDAs) at 100% in the year of spend (CAA 2001 Part 6).

cards.front: R&D: what % of externally provided worker payments qualifies (unconnected)?
cards.back: 65% of staff provider payments
cards.evidence: Category: Externally provided workers; What qualifies: 65% (unconnected) of staff provider payments; Key restriction: UK PAYE condition.

cards.front: ERIS: R&D intensity threshold for periods beginning on or after 1 April 2024?
cards.back: Relevant R&D expenditure at least 30% of total relevant expenditure
cards.evidence: 3. be R&D intensive: its relevant R&D expenditure is at least 30% of its total relevant expenditure, including that of companies connected to it on at least one day in the period (CTA 2009 s1045ZA).

cards.front: ERIS: rate of additional deduction on qualifying expenditure?
cards.back: 86% (186% total deduction)
cards.evidence: Element: Additional deduction; Rate: 86% of qualifying expenditure (186% total deduction).

cards.front: ERIS: payable credit rate?
cards.back: 14.5% of the loss surrendered (not taxable)
cards.evidence: Element: Payable credit; Rate: 14.5% of the loss surrendered (not taxable).

cards.front: ERIS: surrenderable loss is the lower of what?
cards.back: Unrelieved trading loss and 186% of qualifying expenditure
cards.evidence: Element: Surrenderable loss; Rate: Lower of the unrelieved trading loss and 186% of the qualifying expenditure.

cards.front: ERIS: PAYE cap on the payable credit?
cards.back: £20,000 + 300% of relevant PAYE and NIC; claim above is invalid
cards.evidence: Element: PAYE cap; Rate: £20,000 + 300% of relevant PAYE and NIC (unless exempt); a claim above the cap is invalid, so claim only up to it.

cards.front: ERIS: grace rule if intensity falls below 30%?
cards.back: Met intensity in last 12-month period and made a valid ERIS (or old SME) claim for it
cards.evidence: Grace rule: a company that falls below 30% can still qualify if it met the intensity condition in its last 12-month accounting period and made a valid ERIS (or old SME scheme) claim for it.

cards.front: Merged RDEC for a loss-maker: cash rate now after notional tax?
cards.back: 16.2% (20% credit less 19% notional tax)
cards.evidence: Merged RDEC: 20% credit, net of 19% notional tax = 16.2% in cash now (subject to the PAYE cap), with the 3.8% withheld carried forward against future CT, and the remaining trading loss (reduced by the taxable credit) carried forward.

cards.front: Old SME R&D scheme: additional deduction for spend on or after 1 April 2023?
cards.evidence: Expenditure incurred: On or after 1 April 2023; Additional deduction: 86% (186% total); Payable credit on surrendered loss: 10%, or 14.5% if the company is R&D intensive (relevant R&D expenditure at least 40% of total relevant expenditure, including connected persons); Surrenderable loss cap: Lower of unrelieved loss and 186% of qualifying expenditure.

cards.front: Old SME scheme: additional deduction and payable credit rate for spend before 1 April 2023?
cards.back: 130% additional deduction (230% total); 14.5% payable credit
cards.evidence: Expenditure incurred: Before 1 April 2023; Additional deduction: 130% (230% total); Payable credit on surrendered loss: 14.5%; Surrenderable loss cap: Lower of unrelieved loss and 230% of qualifying expenditure.

cards.front: Old SME scheme: R&D intensity test for the 14.5% payable credit?
cards.back: Relevant R&D expenditure at least 40% of total relevant expenditure
cards.evidence: Payable credit on surrendered loss: 10%, or 14.5% if the company is R&D intensive (relevant R&D expenditure at least 40% of total relevant expenditure, including connected persons)

cards.front: Old RDEC: rates for accounting periods beginning before 1 April 2024?
cards.back: 13% for spend before 1 April 2023; 20% from 1 April 2023
cards.evidence: For accounting periods beginning before 1 April 2024, the old RDEC rate was 13% for expenditure before 1 April 2023 and 20% from 1 April 2023, with its own payment steps (notional tax at the main rate) and a PAYE/NIC cap.

cards.front: Old SME scheme: PAYE cap on payable credit (periods from 1 April 2021)?
cards.back: £20,000 plus 300% of relevant PAYE and NIC
cards.evidence: PAYE cap: for accounting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2021, the payable credit was capped at £20,000 plus 300% of relevant PAYE and NIC, with an exemption broadly similar to today's.

cards.front: Old SME scheme: subcontracted R&D to unconnected subcontractors claimable at what %?
cards.back: 65% of payments, wherever the work was done
cards.evidence: Subcontracted R&D: an SME could claim 65% of payments to unconnected subcontractors (or the connected-party rule), wherever the work was done.

cards.front: Old SME scheme: claim notification deadline?
cards.back: 6 months after the period of account
cards.evidence: was a claim notification made (deadline 6 months after the period of account)

cards.front: R&D: time limit for paying accrued staffing costs (e.g. bonuses) to count in the period?
cards.back: Within 9 months after the end of the period
cards.evidence: Staffing costs that are accrued at the period end (most often bonuses) only count for that period if they're paid within 9 months after the end of the period.

cards.front: R&D EPWs: qualifying amount for an unconnected staff provider?
cards.back: 65% of the staff provision payment (for the R&D share of time)
cards.evidence: Relationship: Unconnected staff provider (normal agency); Qualifying amount: 65% of the staff provision payment (for the R&D share of the worker's time).

cards.front: R&D EPWs: qualifying amount for a connected staff provider?
cards.back: Lower of the payment and the provider's own relevant staffing costs, if accounted for under GAAP
cards.evidence: Relationship: Connected staff provider (e.g. a group payroll company); Qualifying amount: The lower of the payment and the staff provider's own relevant staffing costs for the worker(s), provided it's accounted for under GAAP.

cards.front: Merged RDEC/ERIS: UK PAYE condition for EPW costs - which periods and what test?
cards.back: Periods beginning on/after 1 April 2024; worker's earnings wholly or partly subject to UK PAYE
cards.evidence: The UK PAYE condition (accounting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2024): Under the merged RDEC and ERIS, EPW costs only qualify if the worker's earnings are subject (wholly or partly) to UK PAYE.

cards.front: R&D staffing costs: which items are excluded?
cards.back: Benefits in kind, dividends, Class 1A NIC, recruitment fees
cards.evidence: They don't include benefits in kind (company cars, private medical insurance), dividends, Class 1A NIC, or recruitment fees.

cards.front: R&D staffing costs: which employer costs are included alongside earnings?
cards.back: Employer (secondary) Class 1 NIC, employer pension contributions, reimbursed business expenses
cards.evidence: - employer's (secondary) Class 1 NIC;

cards.front: R&D relief: when does R&D end under DSIT Guidelines para 34?
cards.back: When knowledge is codified in usable form, or a fully functional prototype or pilot plant is produced
cards.evidence: Para 34: R&D ends when knowledge is codified in a form a competent professional can use, or when a prototype or pilot plant with all the functional characteristics of the final product or process is produced.

cards.front: R&D relief: when does R&D begin and end under para 33?
cards.back: Begins when work on the uncertainty starts; ends when it is resolved or work to resolve it stops
cards.evidence: Para 33: R&D begins when work to resolve the scientific or technological uncertainty starts, and ends when that uncertainty is resolved or work to resolve it stops.

cards.front: R&D relief: which para covers qualifying indirect activities (QIAs)?
cards.back: Para 31 of the DSIT Guidelines
cards.evidence: Qualifying indirect activities (QIAs) listed in para 31.

cards.front: R&D relief: do finance and HR admin costs qualify?
cards.back: Only insofar as undertaken for the R&D; general corporate HR or finance doesn't qualify
cards.evidence: QIAs include finance, HR and admin activity only insofar as it's undertaken for the R&D.

cards.front: R&D relief: does an abandoned or failed project still qualify?
cards.back: Yes, if it sought an advance and the work tried to resolve the uncertainty (paras 10 and 38)
cards.evidence: A project that fails is still R&D if it sought an advance and the work tried to resolve the uncertainty (paras 10 and 38).

cards.front: R&D relief: which HMRC manual covers staffing costs?
cards.back: CIRD133000
cards.evidence: HMRC's guidance on staffing costs (CIRD133000) makes the same point: the costs of corporate HR or finance departments supporting the whole business don't qualify.

cards.front: R&D relief: which date decides the scheme that applies?
cards.back: The start date of the accounting period; on or after 1 April 2024 means merged RDEC or ERIS
cards.evidence: The test is the start date of the accounting period: - Accounting period beginning on or after 1 April 2024: merged RDEC or ERIS.

cards.front: Merged RDEC: rate of credit on qualifying expenditure?
cards.back: 20% of qualifying expenditure (taxable credit)
cards.evidence: Scheme: Merged RDEC (APs from 1 April 2024); Who: Any trading company in the CT charge; Mechanism: Taxable credit, recognised above the line; Rate: 20% of qualifying expenditure.

cards.front: ERIS: who qualifies and what are the rates?
cards.back: Loss-making SME, R&D intensity at least 30%; 86% additional deduction; 14.5% credit
cards.evidence: Scheme: ERIS (APs from 1 April 2024); Who: Loss-making SME with R&D intensity of at least 30%; Mechanism: Additional deduction, then optional payable credit on the surrenderable loss; Rate: 86% additional deduction (186% total); credit 14.5%.

cards.front: Old SME R&D scheme: additional deduction for spend before 1 April 2023?
cards.back: 130% additional (230% total); credit 14.5%
cards.evidence: Scheme: Old SME scheme, expenditure before 1 April 2023; Who: SMEs; Mechanism: Additional deduction and optional payable credit; Rate: 130% additional (230% total); credit 14.5%.

cards.front: Old SME scheme, spend from 1 April 2023: additional deduction and credit rates?
cards.back: 86% additional; credit 10%, or 14.5% if R&D intensive at 40%
cards.evidence: Scheme: Old SME scheme, expenditure from 1 April 2023 (APs before 1 April 2024); Who: SMEs; Mechanism: Additional deduction and optional payable credit; Rate: 86% additional; credit 10%, or 14.5% if R&D intensive at 40%.

cards.front: Old RDEC: rate from 1 April 2023 and the rate immediately before?
cards.back: 20% from 1 April 2023; 13% immediately before
cards.evidence: Scheme: Old RDEC (APs before 1 April 2024); Who: Large companies, and SMEs for some expenditure; Mechanism: Taxable credit; Rate: 20% from 1 April 2023; 13% immediately before.

cards.front: R&D relief: SME definition for ERIS and old SME scheme?
cards.back: Under 500 staff, and turnover ≤€100m or balance sheet ≤€86m, including linked/partner enterprises
cards.evidence: ERIS (like the old SME scheme) is only for SMEs: broadly fewer than 500 staff, and either turnover of no more than €100m or a balance sheet total of no more than €86m, with linked and partner enterprises included.

cards.front: Merged RDEC: qualifying amount of payment to an unconnected contractor?
cards.back: 65% of the payment relating to UK R&D (or qualifying overseas R&D)
cards.evidence: Relationship: Unconnected contractor; Qualifying amount: 65% of the payment relating to UK R&D (or qualifying overseas R&D); Legislation: CTA 2009 s1136.

cards.front: Merged RDEC: qualifying amount for a connected contractor payment?
cards.back: Lower of the payment and the contractor's own relevant expenditure on the work, accounted for under GAAP
cards.evidence: Relationship: Connected contractor; Qualifying amount: The lower of the payment and the contractor's own relevant expenditure (staffing, EPWs, consumables, software, cloud, data) on the work, provided the contractor accounts for it under GAAP; Legislation: CTA 2009 s1134.

cards.front: R&D contracting: deadline for joint election to treat unconnected parties as connected?
cards.back: In writing within 2 years of end of the AP of contract; irrevocable
cards.evidence: Relationship: Unconnected, jointly elected to be treated as connected; Qualifying amount: As for connected; election is irrevocable, made in writing within 2 years of the end of the AP in which the contract was entered into; Legislation: CTA 2009 s1135.

cards.front: R&D contracted out: who claims, customer or contractor?
cards.back: The customer (decision-maker) claims; the contractor can't for that work
cards.evidence: For accounting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2024, the merged scheme and ERIS use one approach: the company that decides to undertake the R&D is the one that claims.

cards.front: R&D overseas restriction: how are EPW payments restricted (APs from 1 April 2024)?
cards.back: Only where the workers' earnings are subject to UK PAYE
cards.evidence: EPW payments: only where the workers' earnings are subject to UK PAYE (see the staffing lesson).

cards.front: Overseas R&D exception (s1138A): are cost and worker availability relevant?
cards.back: No, both are disregarded
cards.evidence: Cost and the availability of workers are disregarded: "it's cheaper in India" or "we couldn't recruit developers in the UK" never qualifies.

cards.front: Connected contractor: do its own subcontractor payments count in relevant expenditure?
cards.back: No, they are excluded and don't flow to the customer's claim
cards.evidence: Sub-subcontracting: For a connected contractor, its payments to its own subcontractors aren't part of its relevant expenditure, so they don't flow through to the customer's claim.

cards.front: R&D tax relief: what is the core DSIT Guidelines test for R&D?
cards.back: Project seeks an advance in science or technology by resolving scientific or technological uncertainty
cards.evidence: R&D for tax purposes takes place when a project seeks to achieve an advance in science or technology.

cards.front: R&D tax relief: statutory definition of R&D (CTA 2010)?
cards.back: CTA 2010 s1138 (ITA 2007 s1006): activities treated as R&D under GAAP, as modified by DSIT Guidelines
cards.evidence: The statutory definition: CTA 2010 s1138 (and the parallel ITA 2007 s1006) say R&D means activities that fall to be treated as R&D under GAAP, as modified by the guidelines issued by the Secretary of State (the DSIT Guidelines).

cards.front: R&D tax relief: is a project that fails to achieve its advance still R&D?
cards.back: Yes (para 10)
cards.evidence: Two points often missed: work can still be an advance if a competitor has achieved it but keeps the method a trade secret (paras 11 and 21), and a project that fails to achieve its advance is still R&D (para 10).

cards.front: R&D tax relief: what is an 'advance' measured against?
cards.back: Baseline of knowledge in the field when project started, not just the company's own knowledge (para 20)
cards.evidence: An advance is measured against the baseline of knowledge and capability in the field at the time the project started: what is publicly available or readily deducible by a competent professional (para 20).

cards.front: R&D tax relief: when is mathematics treated as science?
cards.back: Mathematical advances count as science from April 2023
cards.evidence: Mathematical advances count as science from April 2023.

cards.front: R&D tax relief: what is system uncertainty?
cards.back: Components well understood, but how to combine them into a working system isn't readily deducible
cards.evidence: That includes system uncertainty: where each component is well understood but how to combine them into a working system isn't readily deducible.

cards.front: VAT cash accounting: max expected turnover to join?
cards.back: £1.35 million or less (VAT-exclusive taxable turnover, next 12 months)
cards.evidence: Scheme: Cash accounting; Join if expected turnover in the next 12 months is: £1.35 million or less; Must leave if turnover exceeds: £1.6 million (measured over the 12 months to the end of a VAT period).

cards.front: VAT cash accounting: turnover level at which you must leave?
cards.back: Over £1.6 million
cards.evidence: Scheme: Cash accounting; Join if expected turnover in the next 12 months is: £1.35 million or less; Must leave if turnover exceeds: £1.6 million (measured over the 12 months to the end of a VAT period).

cards.front: VAT cash accounting: which invoices are excluded by payment terms?
cards.back: Invoices not payable in full within 6 months
cards.evidence: What cash accounting can't be used for: lease purchase, hire purchase, conditional sale and credit sale agreements; imports; invoices issued before the goods or services are supplied; invoices not payable in full within 6 months; and certain domestic reverse charge supplies.

cards.front: VAT annual accounting: quarterly interim payments?
cards.back: 3 payments of 25% of estimated liability, end of months 4, 7 and 10
cards.evidence: | Quarterly | 3 payments, each 25% of the estimated liability | End of months 4, 7 and 10 |

cards.front: VAT annual accounting: deadline for balancing payment and return?
cards.back: Within 2 months of the year end
cards.evidence: | Balancing payment and return | Actual liability less the interim payments | Within 2 months of the year end |

cards.front: VAT bad debt relief: time limit for making the claim?
cards.back: Within 4 years and 6 months of the later of due date and supply date
cards.evidence: 5. The claim is made within 4 years and 6 months of that later date.

cards.front: VAT bad debt relief: minimum age of debt before claiming?
cards.back: 6 months from the later of payment due date and date of supply
cards.evidence: 2. At least 6 months have passed since the later of the date payment was due and the date of supply.

cards.front: VAT bad debt relief: which box is the claim made in?
cards.back: Box 4, as extra input tax (not by reducing box 1)
cards.evidence: The VAT is claimed in box 4 (as extra input tax), not by reducing box 1.

cards.front: VAT: gifts to one person - output tax arises above what value?
cards.back: Over £50 in 12 months to the same person
cards.evidence: Input tax on business gifts is claimable; output tax arises only if gifts to the same person exceed £50 in 12 months.

cards.front: VAT reverse charge: which return boxes are used for overseas B2B services?
cards.back: Box 1 and Box 4 (VAT at 20%); Boxes 6 and 7 (net value)
cards.evidence:
- Box 1: the VAT your client calculates at 20% on the net value
- Box 4: the same amount reclaimed (subject to the normal recovery rules)
- Box 6 and Box 7: the net value of the service

cards.front: VAT: how are off-street car parks treated?
cards.back: Standard-rated, so VAT is recoverable
cards.evidence: Purchase: Off-street car park (private or council); Usual VAT position: Recoverable; Why: Off-street parking is a standard-rated supply.

cards.front: VAT: on-street parking meters, parking fines, congestion charge?
cards.back: Outside the scope; no VAT to claim
cards.evidence: Purchase: On-street parking meter, parking fine, congestion charge; Usual VAT position: No VAT to claim; Why: Outside the scope: statutory charges and penalties.

cards.front: VAT: can you claim on a taxi fare?
cards.back: Only if the receipt shows a VAT number
cards.evidence: Purchase: Taxi fare; Usual VAT position: Claim only if the receipt shows a VAT number; Why: Taxis are standard-rated, but many drivers are below the registration threshold.

cards.front: VAT: passenger transport zero-rated for vehicles with how many seats?
cards.back: 10 or more seats
cards.evidence: Why: Passenger transport in vehicles with 10+ seats is zero-rated.

cards.front: VAT: Royal Mail stamps - VAT treatment?
cards.back: Exempt; no VAT to claim
cards.evidence: Purchase: Royal Mail stamps; Usual VAT position: No VAT to claim; Why: Universal postal service is exempt.

cards.front: VAT DRC construction: start date of the reverse charge?
cards.back: 1 March 2021
cards.evidence: The domestic reverse charge (DRC) for building and construction services started on 1 March 2021 (VATA 1994 s55A).

cards.front: VAT DRC: can it apply to zero-rated construction work?
cards.back: No. Only standard- or reduced-rated supplies are within the DRC
cards.evidence: 2. It's standard-rated or reduced-rated. Zero-rated work, such as building new houses, is outside the DRC.

cards.front: VAT DRC: consequence if customer fails to notify end user/intermediary status?
cards.back: Customer becomes liable for the VAT that should have been accounted for under the reverse charge
cards.evidence: If the customer fails to notify, the customer becomes liable for the VAT that should have been accounted for under the reverse charge.

cards.front: VAT DRC: what is the 5% disregard?
cards.back: If reverse charge element is 5% or less of total value, whole supply can be treated under normal VAT rules
cards.evidence: If a supply mixes reverse charge services with other items, and the reverse charge element is 5% or less of the total value, the whole supply can be treated under normal VAT rules.

cards.front: VAT DRC: who is an end user?
cards.back: A VAT- and CIS-registered business that doesn't sell the construction services on
cards.evidence: an end user: a VAT- and CIS-registered business that doesn't sell the construction services on (for example, a property developer or a business having its own premises refitted), or

cards.front: VAT DRC: how must a supplier's invoice show the VAT?
cards.back: State reverse charge applies; show VAT rate and amount, but don't add it to the amount payable
cards.evidence: show the VAT rate and the amount of VAT that the customer must account for, but not add it to the amount payable.

cards.front: VAT DRC: treatment of reverse charge sales for Flat Rate Scheme users?
cards.back: Excluded from flat rate turnover
cards.evidence: Flat Rate Scheme users have to exclude reverse charge sales from flat rate turnover, so the scheme rarely makes sense for them.

cards.front: VAT errors: time limit for correcting errors, and for deliberate errors?
cards.back: 4 years; HMRC can assess deliberate errors for up to 20 years
cards.evidence: The 4-year limit doesn't protect deliberate errors: HMRC can assess those for up to 20 years (VATA 1994 s77).

cards.front: VAT points: compliance period to reset to zero for quarterly returns?
cards.back: 12 months (4 returns on time)
cards.evidence: | Quarterly | 4 | 12 months (4 returns on time) |

cards.front: VAT late payment: first penalty if unpaid at day 16 to 30?
cards.back: 3% of the VAT still unpaid at day 15
cards.evidence: | 16 to 30 | First penalty: 3% of the VAT still unpaid at day 15 |

cards.front: VAT late payment interest rate (from 6 April 2025)?
cards.back: Bank of England base rate plus 4%
cards.evidence: Late payment interest also runs from the day after the due date until payment, at Bank of England base rate plus 4% (from 6 April 2025).

cards.front: VAT inaccuracy penalty range: careless error, unprompted disclosure?
cards.evidence: | Careless | 0% to 30% | 15% to 30% |

cards.front: FRS: maximum expected taxable turnover to join?
cards.back: £150,000 or less (excluding VAT) in the next 12 months
cards.evidence: Rule: Join if expected taxable turnover (excluding VAT) in the next 12 months is; Figure: £150,000 or less.

cards.front: FRS: VAT-inclusive income level that forces you to leave?
cards.back: Over £230,000 in the year to anniversary
cards.evidence: Rule: Must leave if total VAT-inclusive income in the year to the scheme anniversary exceeds; Figure: £230,000 (or is expected to exceed £230,000 in the next 30 days alone).

cards.front: FRS: first-year discount?
cards.back: 1% off the flat rate for first 12 months of VAT registration
cards.evidence: Rule: First-year discount; Figure: 1% off the flat rate for the first 12 months of VAT registration.

cards.front: FRS: capital asset input tax reclaim threshold?
cards.back: Single capital purchase costing £2,000 or more including VAT
cards.evidence: Rule: Capital assets; Figure: VAT reclaimable outside the scheme on a single purchase of capital goods costing £2,000 or more including VAT.

cards.front: FRS: limited cost business rate?
cards.back: 16.5%, whatever the trade sector
cards.evidence: Rule: Limited cost business rate; Figure: 16.5%, whatever the trade sector.

cards.front: FRS: limited cost trader test for relevant goods spend?
cards.back: Under 2% of turnover, or over 2% but under £1,000 a year (£250 quarterly)
cards.evidence: - more than 2% but less than £1,000 a year (£250 for a quarterly return).

cards.front: FRS: how soon can a business rejoin after leaving?
cards.back: Not within 12 months of leaving
cards.evidence: Rule: Rejoining; Figure: Not within 12 months of leaving.

cards.front: FRS: flat rate for accountancy or book-keeping?
cards.evidence: Trade sector: Accountancy or book-keeping; Flat rate: 14.5%.

cards.front: VAT: how to extract VAT from a standard-rated gross figure?
cards.back: Gross × 20/120 (= gross × 1/6)
cards.evidence: - Standard rate 20%: VAT = gross × 20/120 = gross × 1/6

cards.front: VAT: how to extract VAT from a reduced-rated gross figure?
cards.back: Gross × 5/105 (= gross × 1/21)
cards.evidence: - Reduced rate 5%: VAT = gross × 5/105 = gross × 1/21

cards.front: VAT: key difference between zero-rated and exempt supplies?
cards.back: Zero-rated is taxable at 0%, so input tax is recoverable; exempt is not taxable, so input tax is generally stuck
cards.evidence: A zero-rated supply is a taxable supply at 0%, so the business can recover the VAT on its costs. An exempt supply is not taxable, so the VAT on related costs is generally stuck with the business.

cards.front: VAT: do exempt supplies count towards the registration threshold?
cards.back: No (and input tax is not recoverable, subject to partial exemption)
cards.evidence: Category: Exempt; Rate: No VAT; Does it count towards the registration threshold?: No; Can the supplier recover related input tax?: No (subject to partial exemption); Examples: Insurance, finance, residential rent, most education and health.

cards.front: VAT: what should the control account balance at quarter end equal?
cards.back: Box 5 of the VAT return
cards.evidence: - The balance at the end of a VAT quarter should equal box 5 of the VAT return. When the business pays HMRC, debit the control account and credit the bank.

cards.front: VAT: how are output tax and input tax posted to the control account?
cards.back: Output tax credited; input tax debited
cards.evidence: - Output tax on sales is credited to it (it's a liability to HMRC).

cards.front: VAT: what is the reduced rate and an example of a supply at it?
cards.back: 5%, e.g. domestic gas, children's car seats
cards.evidence: Category: Reduced-rated; Rate: 5%; Does it count towards the registration threshold?: Yes; Can the supplier recover related input tax?: Yes; Examples: Domestic gas, children's car seats, residential conversions.

cards.front: VAT input tax: time limit to make a claim (condition 4)?
cards.back: Within 4 years, with valid evidence (normally a VAT invoice)
cards.evidence: 4. There's evidence, normally a valid VAT invoice, and the claim is made within 4 years.

cards.front: VAT: input tax on leasing a car with some private use?
cards.back: 50% of the VAT on the lease charge is blocked
cards.evidence: Cost: Leasing a car with some private use; Treatment: 50% of the VAT on the lease charge is blocked; Where the rule is: Input Tax Order art 7(2E).

cards.front: VAT: input tax on entertaining UK clients or suppliers?
cards.back: Blocked (VAT (Input Tax) Order 1992 art 5)
cards.evidence: Cost: Entertaining UK clients, suppliers or other non-employees; Treatment: Blocked; Where the rule is: VAT (Input Tax) Order 1992 art 5.

cards.front: VAT pre-registration: how far back can goods VAT be claimed?
cards.back: Goods bought in the 4 years before registration, if still held
cards.evidence: - Goods bought in the 4 years before registration, if they're still held at registration (stock and equipment, but not goods already used up or sold).

cards.front: VAT pre-registration: how far back can services VAT be claimed?
cards.back: Services received in the 6 months before registration
cards.evidence: - Services received in the 6 months before registration.

cards.front: VAT: maximum value of a simplified invoice for retail sales?
cards.back: Up to £250 including VAT
cards.evidence: - A simplified invoice is allowed for retail sales up to £250 including VAT.

cards.front: VAT Flat Rate Scheme: capital asset exception to no input tax claims?
cards.back: Single capital asset costing £2,000 or more including VAT
cards.evidence: The only exception is a single capital asset costing £2,000 or more including VAT.

cards.front: VAT exports: time limit to export and obtain evidence for zero-rating?
cards.back: Within 3 months of the time of supply
cards.evidence: - the goods are exported within 3 months of the time of supply, and

cards.front: VAT exports: how long must export evidence be kept?
cards.back: 6 years
cards.evidence: Exports go in box 6 (net value) with nothing in box 1. Keep the evidence for 6 years.

cards.front: VAT: UK VAT fraction if export evidence is missed and price was fixed?
cards.back: 1/6 of the price
cards.evidence: If the evidence isn't obtained in time, the supplier must account for UK VAT, and if the price was fixed, that VAT comes out of the price (1/6 of it).

cards.front: VAT: short-term hire of means of transport time limits?
cards.back: Up to 30 days (90 days for vessels)
cards.evidence: - Short-term hire of means of transport (up to 30 days, or 90 days for vessels): where the vehicle is put at the customer's disposal.

cards.front: VAT: PVA entries on return for imports (boxes 1, 4, 7)?
cards.back: Box 1 import VAT; box 4 same amount; box 7 value of imports excl. VAT
cards.evidence:
- Box 1: import VAT from the statement
- Box 4: the same amount, as input tax (subject to the normal rules)
- Box 7: the value of the imports, excluding VAT

cards.front: VAT: evidence to reclaim import VAT if PVA is not used?
cards.back: C79 import VAT certificate, not the agent's invoice
cards.evidence: If the business doesn't use PVA, the VAT is paid at import (often by the freight agent), and the evidence for reclaiming it is the C79 import VAT certificate, not the agent's invoice.

cards.front: VAT: B2B services to overseas customer, place of supply and UK VAT?
cards.back: Where the customer belongs; outside the scope of UK VAT
cards.evidence: Customer: Business (B2B); General rule: Where the customer belongs; UK supplier to an overseas customer: Outside the scope of UK VAT. No UK VAT charged.; Overseas supplier to a UK customer: UK customer applies the reverse charge.

cards.front: VAT option to tax: deadline to notify HMRC of the decision?
cards.back: Within 30 days of the decision, normally on form VAT1614A
cards.evidence: - Notification: notify HMRC in writing within 30 days of the decision, normally on form VAT1614A.

cards.front: VAT option to tax: when is HMRC permission needed?
cards.back: If exempt supplies of the property were made in the previous 10 years (form VAT1614H), unless automatic permission applies
cards.evidence: - Permission: if the owner has made exempt supplies of the property in the previous 10 years, it needs HMRC's permission (form VAT1614H), unless one of the automatic permission conditions applies.

cards.front: VAT option to tax: ways it can be revoked?
cards.back: 6-month cooling-off period; automatically after 6 years with no interest; or after 20 years if conditions met
cards.evidence: - Revocation: within a 6-month cooling-off period if nothing has happened since; automatically after 6 years without any interest in the property; or after 20 years, if the conditions are met.

cards.front: VAT: liability of freehold sale of a new commercial building?
cards.back: Standard-rated (compulsory) if less than 3 years from completion
cards.evidence: Transaction: Freehold sale of a new commercial building (less than 3 years from completion); Liability: Standard-rated; Notes: Compulsory; the option to tax isn't needed.

cards.front: TOGC of let property where seller opted: what must the buyer do and by when?
cards.back: Opt to tax and notify HMRC by time of supply; tell seller option won't be disapplied
cards.evidence: - has opted to tax the property and notified HMRC no later than the time of supply (normally completion, or an earlier deposit paid to the seller as agent), and

cards.front: VAT: which form lets a TOGC buyer take over the seller's VAT number?
cards.back: Form VAT68
cards.evidence: - The buyer may take over the seller's VAT number (form VAT68), but then it also takes on the seller's VAT liabilities and history.

cards.front: VAT margin scheme: how is VAT calculated on a margin?
cards.back: 1/6 of the margin (selling price less purchase price)
cards.evidence: VAT is 1/6 of the margin, because the margin is treated as VAT-inclusive.

cards.front: Global accounting: maximum purchase price per item?
cards.back: £500 or less per item
cards.evidence: Each item must have a purchase price of £500 or less.

cards.front: Global accounting: what happens if purchases exceed sales in a period?
cards.back: Negative margin carried forward to next period, not repaid
cards.evidence: If purchases exceed sales in a period, the negative margin is carried forward to the next period. It isn't repaid.

cards.front: Margin scheme: what happens if VAT is shown separately on the sales invoice?
cards.back: VAT is due on the full selling price
cards.evidence: If a dealer shows VAT separately on a margin scheme sale (often because a trade customer asks for a "VAT invoice"), the dealer must account for VAT on the full selling price.

cards.front: Margin scheme part-exchange: what is the purchase price of the car taken in?
cards.back: The part-exchange allowance actually given
cards.evidence: On a part-exchange, the purchase price of the car taken in is the part-exchange allowance actually given, and the selling price of the car sold is the full price before deducting that allowance.

cards.front: VAT: input tax on buying a car with private availability?
cards.back: Blocked in full (unless used exclusively for business)
cards.evidence: Cost: Buying the vehicle; Car available for private use: Input tax blocked in full; Van or other commercial vehicle: Recoverable (adjust if there's significant private use).

cards.front: VAT: leasing a car available for private use - input tax blocked?
cards.back: 50% of the VAT on the rental
cards.evidence: Cost: Leasing or hiring; Car available for private use: 50% of the VAT on the rental is blocked; Van or other commercial vehicle: Recoverable.

cards.front: VAT: how is a car sold treated if input tax was blocked on purchase?
cards.back: Exempt: no VAT charged, no VAT invoice
cards.evidence: If input tax was blocked when the car was bought, the sale is exempt: no VAT is charged and no VAT invoice is issued (Notice 700/64 section 7).

cards.front: VAT fuel scale charge: what fraction of the charge is the VAT due?
cards.back: 1/6 of the charge (box 1; net charge in box 6)
cards.evidence: 3. The VAT due is 1/6 of the charge. It goes in box 1, and the charge net of VAT goes in box 6.

cards.front: VAT fuel scale charge: how to choose the CO₂ band?
cards.back: Round the V5C CO₂ figure down to the nearest multiple of 5
cards.evidence: 1. Take the car's CO₂ figure from the V5C and round down to the nearest multiple of 5.

cards.front: VAT fuel scale charge: bands if no CO₂ figure, by engine size?
cards.evidence: If a car has no CO₂ figure, use the band for its engine size: up to 1,400cc is band 140, over 1,400cc up to 2,000cc is band 175, and over 2,000cc is band 225 or more.

cards.front: VAT fuel scale charge 2026/27: quarterly charge for 140 g/km band?
cards.evidence: CO₂ band (g/km): 140; Quarterly charge: £294; VAT due (quarter): £49.00; Annual charge: £1,182; VAT due (year): £197.00.

cards.front: VAT: input tax formula on employee mileage allowance?
cards.back: Business miles × advisory fuel rate × 1/6
cards.evidence: Input tax = business miles × advisory fuel rate × 1/6

cards.front: VAT standard method: how is the residual recovery percentage rounded?
cards.back: Up to the next whole number
cards.evidence: Round the percentage up to the next whole number.

cards.front: VAT partial exemption: when is the recovery % rounded to 2 decimal places?
cards.back: Residual input tax averaging more than £400,000 a month
cards.evidence: If residual input tax averages more than £400,000 a month, round to 2 decimal places instead (Notice 706 section 4.7).

cards.front: CGS: threshold and adjustment period for land and buildings acquired on/after 29 July 2026?
cards.back: £600,000 or more; 10 intervals
cards.evidence: | Land, buildings and civil engineering works (acquired, built, refurbished, fitted out, altered or extended on or after 29 July 2026) | £600,000 or more | 10 intervals |

cards.front: CGS: threshold for land and buildings acquired before 29 July 2026?
cards.back: £250,000 or more; 10 intervals
cards.evidence: | The same items acquired or constructed before 29 July 2026 | £250,000 or more (existing items stay in the scheme until their period ends) | 10 intervals |

cards.front: CGS: threshold and adjustment period for aircraft, ships, boats and vessels?
cards.back: £50,000 or more; 5 intervals
cards.evidence: | Aircraft, ships, boats and other vessels | £50,000 or more | 5 intervals |

cards.front: CGS: where is the annual adjustment entered on the VAT return?
cards.back: Box 4, on the return for the second VAT period after the end of the interval
cards.evidence: Enter it in box 4 on the return for the second VAT period after the end of the interval.

cards.front: VAT: default liability of a supply unless a relief applies?
cards.back: Standard-rated at 20%
cards.evidence: The starting point is simple: every supply of goods or services is standard-rated at 20% unless the law specifically gives it another treatment.

cards.front: VAT: which Act schedules cover reduced, zero and exempt supplies?
cards.back: Sch 7A reduced (5%); Sch 8 zero; Sch 9 exemption
cards.evidence:
- Schedule 7A: reduced rate (5%).
- Schedule 8: zero rate (0%).
- Schedule 9: exemption.

cards.front: VAT: how is an exempt supply treated on the return versus outside the scope?
cards.back: Exempt counts in box 6 and can restrict input tax; outside the scope is left off the return
cards.evidence: Exempt supplies count in box 6 of the VAT return and can restrict input tax recovery under partial exemption. Outside the scope items (wages, dividends, donations) are left out of the return altogether.

cards.front: VAT: fraction of a price that is VAT if a zero-rated supply was actually standard-rated?
cards.back: 1/6 of the price charged
cards.evidence: Liability errors are expensive: if a supply you treated as zero-rated is actually standard-rated, the VAT comes out of the price already charged (1/6 of it).

cards.front: VAT: liability of a new dwelling build versus repairs to an existing home?
cards.back: New dwelling: zero; repairs to existing home: standard
cards.evidence: | Building a new dwelling (labour and materials by the builder) | Zero |

cards.front: VAT: liability of converting a non-residential building into homes?
cards.back: Reduced rate 5%
cards.evidence: | Converting a non-residential building (an office, a barn) into homes | Reduced 5% |

cards.front: VAT: liability of a cold sandwich eaten in the café?
cards.back: Standard-rated (catering)
cards.evidence: | | Anything eaten on the premises (catering), including a cold sandwich eaten in the café |

cards.front: VAT: compulsory registration threshold?
cards.back: £90,000 of taxable turnover
cards.evidence: Registration threshold: £90,000 of taxable turnover.

cards.front: VAT: deregistration threshold?
cards.back: £88,000 of taxable turnover
cards.evidence: Deregistration threshold: £88,000 of taxable turnover.

cards.front: VAT historic test: deadline to tell HMRC and effective registration date?
cards.back: Tell within 30 days of month end; registered from first day of second month after
cards.evidence: Test: Historic (backward look); When it's triggered: At the end of any month, taxable turnover for the previous 12 months is more than £90,000; Tell HMRC by: 30 days after the end of that month; Registered from: The first day of the second month after the month the threshold was exceeded.

cards.front: VAT future test: trigger for compulsory registration?
cards.back: Reasonable grounds to expect turnover over £90,000 in next 30 days alone
cards.evidence: Test: Future (forward look); When it's triggered: At any time, there are reasonable grounds to expect taxable turnover in the next 30 days alone to exceed £90,000; Tell HMRC by: The end of that 30-day period; Registered from: The start of the 30-day period (the date the business realised).

cards.front: VAT: late registration, how is VAT treated if it can't be collected from customers?
cards.back: Treated as included in the price: price × 1/6 at standard rate
cards.evidence: If it can't go back to customers to collect the VAT, the VAT is treated as included in the price it charged (so it's the price × 1/6 at standard rate).

cards.front: VAT deregistration: de minimis for output tax on stock and assets held?
cards.back: No charge if VAT due is £1,000 or less
cards.evidence: It must account for output tax on their current value on the final return, unless the VAT due would be £1,000 or less.

cards.front: VAT: time limit to notify HMRC of compulsory deregistration?
cards.back: Within 30 days
cards.evidence: | Compulsory | The business stops making taxable supplies (it ceases trading, is sold, or becomes wholly exempt), or the legal entity changes (sole trader incorporates). Tell HMRC within 30 days. |

cards.front: VAT: 14-day rule for tax points?
cards.back: Invoice within 14 days after basic tax point makes the invoice date the tax point
cards.evidence: If a VAT invoice is issued within 14 days after the basic tax point (and step 2 hasn't applied), the invoice date becomes the tax point.

cards.front: VAT: time limit to issue a VAT invoice to a VAT-registered customer?
cards.back: Within 30 days of the tax point
cards.evidence: A VAT-registered business must issue a VAT invoice within 30 days of the tax point for standard or reduced-rated supplies to another VAT-registered business.

cards.front: VAT: when can a simplified invoice be used?
cards.back: Retail supplies of £250 or less including VAT
cards.evidence: Type: Simplified invoice; When allowed: Retail supplies of £250 or less including VAT; What's different: No customer details; can show the VAT-inclusive total and the rate instead of the VAT amount.

cards.front: VAT: tax point for continuous supplies of services?
cards.back: Earlier of each payment received or VAT invoice issued
cards.evidence: there's no basic tax point. The tax point is the earlier of each payment received or VAT invoice issued.

cards.front: VAT: does a pro forma invoice create a tax point?
cards.back: No; tax point is the payment date
cards.evidence: It doesn't create a tax point and the customer can't reclaim VAT on it. When payment arrives, the tax point is the payment date and a proper VAT invoice should follow.

cards.front: VAT: how to correct an error on an issued invoice?
cards.back: Issue a credit note and a new invoice
cards.evidence: Errors on invoices: don't just alter or delete an issued invoice. Issue a credit note and a new invoice so there's an audit trail.

cards.front: VAT return: normal filing and payment deadline?
cards.back: 1 calendar month and 7 days after the end of the VAT period
cards.evidence: Filing and payment: 1 calendar month and 7 days after the end of the VAT period.

cards.front: VAT Direct Debit: when does HMRC collect?
cards.back: 3 working days after the extended deadline
cards.evidence: Direct Debit: HMRC collects 3 working days after the extended deadline, so the client needs the Direct Debit set up in time.

cards.front: VAT Annual Accounting Scheme: return deadline?
cards.back: 2 months after the year end
cards.evidence: Annual Accounting Scheme: 2 months after the year end.

cards.front: VAT: annual liability triggering monthly payments on account?
cards.back: More than £2.3 million
cards.evidence: Payments on account: businesses with an annual VAT liability of more than £2.3 million make monthly payments on account.

cards.front: VAT return Box 1: private use or gifts threshold?
cards.back: Gifts over £50
cards.evidence: Box: 1; What goes in it: VAT due on sales and other outputs; Watch out for: Also includes reverse-charge output VAT, postponed import VAT, fuel scale charges, and VAT on private use or gifts over £50. Credit notes issued reduce it.

cards.front: VAT review: quarter-on-quarter swing worth investigating?
cards.back: Swings over about 20%
cards.evidence: Compare with the last four quarters: sales, purchases and net VAT. Investigate swings over about 20%.
